title: Care, Human Enfeeblement, and the Existential Implications of AGI
summary: Stuart Russell has named "human enfeeblement" as a long-term societal risk of advanced AI. This paper gives a new interpretation of the enfeeblement danger by interpreting it in light of recent work by Brian Christian, Alison Gopnik, and David Spivak on care and caregiving, and connecting it with the ontological design tradition of Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores. The enfeeblement that threatens is not merely a matter of cognitive off-loading and loss of knowledge, but a form of disengagement with the world which I explain in terms of an erosion of our capacities to care. This paper articulates a conception of care as a constellation of cultivable skills that involve us in the world and with each other, while making life worth living. Designing AI to support our capacities to care addresses the worry recently raised by Demis Hassabis and others regarding the questions of "meaning and purpose" that are looming in a post-AGI world.

title: EasyFoam: Skill-Oriented OpenFOAM Agents with Evidence-Driven Evolution
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of automating end-to-end OpenFOAM workflows for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, current progress is bottlenecked by two critical limitations. First, existing evaluations are dominated by tutorial-level cases and execution-oriented metrics, masking a substantial executability--acceptability gap: successfully executed simulations often fail to satisfy prescribed numerical or quantity-of-interest (QoI) criteria. Second, domain expertise in existing systems is tightly coupled with bespoke agent architectures, limiting its reuse and continual refinement across agent implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce ExtFoamBench, a challenging benchmark for OpenFOAM agents that spans five axes of workflow variation, and separately assesses execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction. Complementing this, we propose EasyFoam, an agent framework that decouples CFD expertise into modular, externalized skills driven by a dual-loop mechanism. An execution loop constructs workflows from explicit task requirements and uses structured simulation evidence to diagnose failures and guide targeted repairs. Meanwhile, an evolution loop distills task experience into reusable skill updates selected through paired evaluation. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, establishing this work as a starting point for future research toward self-improving CFD agents.

title: Enhancing Resolution and Reliability with Attention Mechanisms in Nuclear Accident Surrogate Modeling
summary: Severe accident (SA) analysis of nuclear power plants relies on system codes such as MAAP, whose computational cost limits large-scale applications including dynamic probabilistic safety assessment and reinforcement learning. This study proposes the Accident Binary-Continuous Transformer (ABC-Transformer), a decoder-only surrogate combining causal self-attention with temporal attention pooling. It jointly embeds continuous thermal-hydraulic variables with binary safety-system and severe accident management guideline (SAMG) states, enabling 5-minute-resolution forecasting over 72-hour transients. Trained on 11,000 MAAP simulations of a total loss of component cooling water scenario for the OPR1000, it achieved lower one-step teacher-forcing error than CNN and recurrent baselines at fine resolutions. Autoregressive reliability was characterized as a full per-scenario distribution over 1100 held-out scenarios. For scheduled-sampling (SS) training, the median $R^2$ is $0.947 \pm 0.006$ and $3.8 \pm 1.0$% of scenarios fail ($R^2<0$; mean $\pm$ SD over four training seeds), while errors accumulate with rollout length. A Mahalanobis self-distance computed from each surrogate rollout, before comparison with the MAAP reference, ranks these failures (ROC-AUC 0.895, reference seed). A threshold at the 40th percentile of calibration scores accepts $36.8 \pm 0.5$% of 550 evaluation scenarios, with no accepted rollout below $R^2 = 0$ for any seed, and routes the rest to MAAP.

title: Learning Nonlinear Transient Dynamics in Fluid Flow Networks with the Neural Basis Method
summary: Fluid flow networks, from pipeline infrastructure to biological vasculature, are governed by nonlinear edgewise hyperbolic laws coupled through continuity and conservation at junctions. Many-query tasks require rapid evaluation across unseen parametric settings, but conventional methods re-solve the system for each query at prohibitive cost. Existing physics-informed neural approaches impose the governing equations through penalty losses over generic neural approximators; these losses act only as optimization surrogates, with no guarantee that their reduction reduces solution error, and the resulting optimization is prone to ill-conditioning, particularly for hyperbolic systems. Building on the "representation-then-projection" principle of the neural basis method, we introduce a new approach for modeling fluid flow networks. Fixed neural bases define the representation space on each edge, while projection of the discretized equations determines the expansion coefficients, embedding edgewise laws into a conservative formulation. Edge subdomains are coupled through non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns, directly in this reduced space, the parametric map to the expansion coefficients. On looped and branching network topologies, we reproduce references with relative $L^2$ errors below 0.02%, whereas the physics-informed neural network baseline fails. Across unseen boundary conditions in both interpolation and extrapolation, we maintain mean pressure errors below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the physics-informed DeepONet baseline reaches 8-18% pressure errors and 85-95% flux errors. These results highlight the framework's potential for real-time monitoring, design exploration, and uncertainty quantification of fluid flow networks.

title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
comments: 54 pages, 3 figures. Code and models: https://github.com/GerhardTrippen/Zugwise
summary: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent expert transcription move for move on 34 of 45 games, and adjudication against the sheets found errors in both records, on different plies. We do not establish that either workflow is faster or more accurate. The system runs entirely in the browser and is free, private, and offline-capable; alongside it we offer a three-way adjudication protocol for a domain where no single record is ground truth.
comment: 54 pages, 3 figures. Code and models: https://github.com/GerhardTrippen/Zugwise

title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs
summary: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.

title: SideTaskBench: Measuring Unauthorized Side-Task Delivery in Coding Agents
summary:
Can a coding agent fix a user's repository while also completing and delivering work the user never requested? In this paper, we introduce SideTaskBench to measure this failure where third-party technical references induce agents to produce independent side-task artifacts during an authorized repair. Repair success alone misses this behavior. Our key measurement contribution is to pair each repair with a self-contained side task and verify side tasks' delivery success rate along with the repair success rate. The benchmark contains 25 Python repairs and 190 side-task units. Its four-level similarity index defines 300 executable repair--side-task pairs.
  The experiments show roughly 40% valid delivery under wrapped requests for two models, alongside repair success close to their clean baselines. The completed v10 similarity run uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash on all 300 pairs, with eight repetitions per pair (2,400 runs). Conditional delivery ranges from 20.48% for L0 unrelated tasks to 57.44% for L3 mechanism-overlapping tasks, while the L1-L0 difference is 5.37 percentage points and remains sensitive to task composition. The central insight is that technical relevance may blur the authorization boundary for an agent, such that an agent can solve the requested problem and still deliver unauthorized work. SideTaskBench emphasizes this potential weakness of existing agents and provides a testbed for defenses that preserve repair capability while preventing unauthorized delivery. The code is available at: https://github.com/xywen97/SideTaskBench.

title: Probe Before You Preach: Conformal Ambiguity Sets and Neuro-Symbolic Counterfactual Probing for Diagnosing Algebraic Misconceptions in Middle School Mathematics
comments: 19 pages, 1 figure. Theoretical framework, method, and public-graph audit; withdrawn hardcoded offline/classroom outcome tables omitted; classroom study proposed for future validation
summary: Distinct mathematical misconception rules can produce the same incorrect answer, making diagnosis from a single response ambiguous. We formalize this algebraic collision and derive a conditional Bayes error bound; internally generated reasoning does not add student-specific information beyond its inputs under an explicit conditional-independence assumption. We propose Mondrian Adaptive Conformal Misconception Sets (MACMS) and Symbolic-Verified Counterfactual Micro-Probing (Sym-EIG). MACMS has curriculum-group marginal coverage under exchangeability, not a per-student correctness guarantee. Sym-EIG searches for probes whose outputs separate modeled candidate rules; identification additionally depends on the candidate set and response model. An audit of a local public Eedi graph finds 2,118 of 2,258 linked constructs associated with at least two misconception IDs; construct-level associations alone do not establish same-answer collisions. Other project performance tables require recomputation because their script assigns numerical results directly. No diagnostic performance or classroom learning benefit is claimed here. A classroom study is proposed for future validation.
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure. Theoretical framework, method, and public-graph audit; withdrawn hardcoded offline/classroom outcome tables omitted; classroom study proposed for future validation

title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
comments: Main text: 44 pages, 13 figures, 7 tables. Supplementary Information: 19 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary:
A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average.
  Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.
comment: Main text: 44 pages, 13 figures, 7 tables. Supplementary Information: 19 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables

title: A Neural Physics Solver for Richards Equation
summary: A new approach to discretise and solve Richards equation based on the finite element method (FEM) is presented. The novelty of the approach, called the Neural Physics method, is that it expresses the discretisation as a convolution neural network (CNN) whose weights are predetermined by the integrals of the basis functions in the FEM. The Neural Physics method is physically consistent as it represents a discretisation of the governing equation and can run on CPUs, GPUs and the latest AI accelerators, resulting in an increase in computational speed. The Neural Physics method is demonstrated for two different discretisations of Richards equation, including a multigrid method that is realised through a U-Net architecture. The accuracy and speed of these methods is tested on a problem with a known analytical solution and compared to a standard FEM, and shows that the Neural Physics method is almost an order of magnitude faster than a comparable FEM. Finally, the Neural Physics method is applied to a real-world test case with integrated experimental data and simulates the infiltration of water through a rain garden. This new approach therefore provides a route to efficiently and accurately solve Richards equation for a wide array of hydrological applications.

title: The Market Is the Reward: Design Markets, Not Just Traders for Human-AI Collective Intelligence
summary: Learning agents are becoming market participants, yet machine learning still treats the market as a fixed environment, although its payoff rule is the reward agents learn from. This position paper argues that financial AI should build HyperMarkets for human-AI collective intelligence, and not only the agents that trade in them: markets whose liquidity provision, information production, outcome determination, and trading rule are performed or adapted by learning agents and designed jointly toward explicit market-level objectives. In a pre-registered simulation with Claude agents trading for principals, joint design raises a market-level objective by 79% over separately tuned functions, through a trading rule that helps only when slow traders are present, and how evidence is paid for decides whether a stronger agent earns more for its principal. We state when fixed rules or non-market aggregation should be preferred and what findings would refute the case.

title: MechFoundry: An agentic loop that poses and performs engineering analyses and optimization of real-world objects
summary: AI agents can automate software engineering because a compiler or a test suite checks that the code does what the user or the agent intended. In engineering analysis, however, the steps that precede the computation have few easily verifiable checks: modeling a design or an object, deciding how it is used, where supports and loads are applied, and what material each part is made of. A human expert therefore makes these decisions, carries out the steps, and judges the result, one object at a time. We present MechFoundry, an agentic loop coupled with bespoke software that automates structural analyses of real-world objects without a human in the loop. From an object's lexical description, it generates a shape, poses a loading case relevant to how the object is used, assigns a material to each part, solves the nonlinear structural response, and improves the design against the loads it carries. A differentiable GPU solver built on an adaptive octree that need not conform to the surface enables the transition from shape generation to simulation and optimization. Across 50 everyday and engineering objects, the agent posed and solved a loading case in 6.5 minutes and for US$1.3 per object on average. Without a test suite to check against, we had language-model reviewers grade each session, as a first indication of where the agent's engineering judgment holds and where it fails.

title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
comments: 48 pages, 1 figure (3 panels). Exact-arithmetic certificate data and verification code included as ancillary files
summary: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.
comment: 48 pages, 1 figure (3 panels). Exact-arithmetic certificate data and verification code included as ancillary files

title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
comments: 45 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material (37 pages, 4 figures) appended
summary: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.
comment: 45 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material (37 pages, 4 figures) appended

title: Designing Collaborative Virtual Environments for Software Engineering Education
comments: Submitted to Computers and Education: X Reality
summary: Collaborative virtual environments offer opportunities to make software models available for shared inspection, but educational design and usability need to be examined separately from claims of learning effectiveness. This article presents MetaSEE, an approach connecting requirements guidance, a Web XR feature model, a reusable UML component, and a browser-based multiuser platform. We synthesize documented formative evaluations of the framework (16 participations), feature model (15), UML component (9), and platform (14). These counts represent evaluation participations; the same 12 developers took part in the first two evaluations. The principal platform study involved six teachers working individually and eight students working in four pairs through desktop or notebook computers, keyboard, and mouse. The documentary synthesis traces educational intentions to implemented features and reported difficulties. Participants identified potential value in shared modeling and simulation, alongside navigation, interaction, visualization, and distraction concerns. A numerical audit reconstructs a student System Usability Scale mean of 67.50 from published item frequencies, conflicting with the reported 79.38; an incomplete teacher item distribution prevents recovery of that group's overall mean. The contribution is a traceable account of educational design and formative limitations, with practical implications for onboarding, model readability, collaboration, and evaluation reporting. The evidence supports bounded feasibility and perceived usefulness, without establishing learning gains, sustained engagement, or adoption.
comment: Submitted to Computers and Education: X Reality

title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
comments: 38 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23683806. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1) is included as an ancillary file
summary:
Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are.
  We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness.
  The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.
comment: 38 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23683806. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1) is included as an ancillary file

title: CAFIN: CUDA-accelerated Adaptive Fisher Information Matrix Network Optimization via GPU-Native Kernel Fusion
summary: Second-order optimizers improve deep neural network training using curvature information, but their practical efficiency is limited by GPU execution overhead. AdaFisher reduces Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) approximation costs through diagonal Kronecker structures and exponential moving averages, yet its PyTorch implementation requires sequential CUDA kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. We introduce CAFIN, a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that improves AdaFisher execution efficiency without changing its optimization formulation. The proposed approach progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, exponential moving average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels. Shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations further reduce memory traffic and intermediate allocations. Experiments using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop GPUs demonstrate up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1-26.9% lower optimizer-step latency. The implementation also eliminates approximately 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per optimizer step. Numerical validation confirms consistency within the predefined FP32 tolerance, while convergence accuracy remains comparable across evaluated datasets and random seeds. These findings demonstrate that CUDA kernel fusion can substantially accelerate second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's underlying mathematical formulation and learning behavior.

title: An Asynchronous Federated Learning Platform for Lung Adenocarcinoma Grading via Foundation Models and Structural Pruning
summary: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.

title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer
summary: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.

title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
comments: neurips 2026, 10 pages, position paper on adversarial risk, certified robustness
summary: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.
comment: neurips 2026, 10 pages, position paper on adversarial risk, certified robustness

title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs
summary: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. For DQN on three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 (DoorKey), 0.10 to 0.80 (KeyCorridor) and 0 to 0.50 (ObstructedMaze); plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. For SAC on continuous PointMaze, graph-derived direction labels raise final success from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. Distilling the graph policy into a fresh Q-model gives a DoorKey 6x6 controller that reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN. Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.

title: VASTRA: Efficient Agentic Top-K Interactive Video Analysis
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable natural language video retrieval, bypassing traditional hand-engineered pipelines. Integrating agentic reasoning frameworks (e.g., ReAct) further advances this paradigm by allowing models to dynamically inspect video content rather than relying on a single visual pass. Applying this pattern naively to video retrieval inherits problems that video systems cannot afford: results vary from run to run under identical conditions, and cost and latency scale with every reasoning step the agent takes rather than with the work the query actually requires. We present VASTRA, an agentic video retrieval system whose execution is dictated by query complexity rather than an open-ended reasoning loop: cheap, reliably answerable queries are ranked directly from pre-ingested summaries, while harder queries trigger targeted verification only where relevance is genuinely uncertain. This keeps control flow external to the model rather than latent in a growing chain of thought, establishing deterministic control flow by construction and end-to-end rank reproducibility under greedy serving. Across 40 benchmark queries, VASTRA exposes explicit presets: VASTRA-Fast runs 12.2x faster (4.2 s vs. 51.2 s) and 10.4x cheaper ($0.0044 vs. $0.0458) than best performing ReAct agent at a 5.0-point mAP reduction, while VASTRA-Max matches peak ReAct agent accuracy (0.653 vs. 0.649 mAP) at comparable latency, trading higher spend ($0.1022 vs. $0.0458) for zero run-to-run variance.

title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation
summary: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks expressed as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. To build the solutions and trajectories, our agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization with reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively, while increasing the fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager at every level. Further training experiments show that supervision from the curated trajectories substantially outperforms direct responses and promotes sustained testing and revision. These results demonstrate that KernelMosaic enables a general-purpose model to achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation.

title: Discovering the Relation Between Architectural Models and Reference Architectures
comments: Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027). 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. \c{opyright} 2027 IEEE
summary: Assessing whether concrete software architectures are consistent with their reference architecture (RA) is essential to ensure that architectural decisions scale coherently across projects, preserving the quality attributes the RA was designed to guarantee. In the absence of dedicated techniques, mapping the components of an architectural model onto a predefined RA can be addressed only with general-purpose model-comparison algorithms. Our experiments show that these algorithms are inaccurate when applied to RAs. To address this gap, we propose Reference Architecture Mapping Discovery (RAMD), an LLM-based workflow that combines model analysis with structured prompting, and refines results through an iterative RA compliance-checking mechanism. We evaluate RAMD on 64 open-source architectural models spanning three RAs from the IoT, self-driving, and smart parking domains. With domain knowledge and GPT-4o, RAMD reaches 85.8% mapping accuracy and outperforms the strongest baseline by 44.6 percentage points, while ensuring structural consistency with the RA.
comment: Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027). 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. \c{opyright} 2027 IEEE

title: FreeDeshadow: Shadow Removal for User-Specified Objects With Multimodal Prompts
summary: Existing shadow removal methods either perform global shadow removal or rely on precise shadow masks to guide restoration. Such paradigms limit their ability to selectively remove the shadow cast by a user-specified object in practical applications. To this end, we introduce an object-aware controllable shadow removal task, which allows users to specify a target object through a simple prompt and removes only its cast shadow while preserving other content. However, object-shadow asymmetry makes it challenging to establish accurate correspondence between the specified object and its spatially separated cast shadow and to confine restoration to the target shadow region. To address these challenges, we propose FreeDeshadow, a unified controllable shadow removal framework that supports both visual and textual prompts. It consists of an object-aware generator and a shadow-aware local refiner. The former interprets the user prompt and produces a high-quality shadow-free proposal, while the latter establishes the correspondence between the object and its cast shadow and constrains the generated changes to the target shadow region. To support training and evaluation, we further construct PCSRD+, a large-scale dataset containing 154,571 quadruples at 1024$\times$1024 resolution and covering six types of user prompts. The visual prompts include a dot, a line, and an object mask, while the textual prompts describe the target object using attributes, spatial relations, or states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FreeDeshadow accurately removes the shadow of the target object under both visual and textual prompts while effectively preserving non-target regions. It also outperforms existing methods in shadow removal performance and controllability. Project Page: https://wzlwlm13.github.io/FreeDeshadow

title: Evaluating AI Musical Creativity: Towards a Quantitative Multi-Dimensional Framework Based on Value, Novelty, and Surprise
summary: Despite the increasing sophistication of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), research on the evaluation of AI-generated musical creativity remains limited. To address this gap, this paper proposes a quantitative framework for the formalization and evaluation of AI musical creativity. Building on Margaret Boden's theory, which conceptualizes creativity in terms of value, novelty, and surprise, the framework adapts and operationalizes these three dimensions for the musical domain. On the hypothesis that certain aspects of musical creativity can be assessed with a degree of objectivity, a domain-specific set of quantitative metrics for evaluating the creativity of AI-generated music is introduced. Rather than reducing musical creativity to a single unifying measure, this article proposes an ensemble of complementary metrics that capture its different dimensions, recognizing the complexity of musical artifacts and the difficulty of defining meaningful multi-objective compositional criteria. The framework has two implications. First, it gives researchers and developers a principled methodology and quantitative tools for empirically evaluating creative outputs, enabling more informed model development and reducing unnecessary computational costs. Second, it lays the groundwork for future generative models to optimize directly for creativity by adopting these metrics as learning objectives.

title: Evaluating the Performance of LLMs in Drafting NIH Data Management Plans
summary: Sharing research data is essential to promote transparency, enable reproducibility, and fuel scientific discoveries. To ensure consistent sharing, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and other funding agencies require applicants to submit data management plans (DMPs) with their proposals. They aim to encourage researchers to consider their data management and sharing strategies early on. However, researchers often face challenges when developing DMPs due to a lack of knowledge about data-sharing practices. Here, we evaluated the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in drafting DMPs compliant with the 2023 NIH guidelines. The goal was to investigate whether LLM-supported DMP creation could reduce the burden on researchers and librarians. We compared Llama and GPT performance against NIH-provided DMP samples. We also asked domain experts to evaluate LLM-generated DMPs. Overall, we found that LLMs can accelerate the creation of initial drafts but still require expert review before submission to ensure clarity and completeness. Moreover, open-source LLMs may not be as ready off-the-shelf as commercial ones for drafting funder-compliant DMPs.

title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions
summary: We study the multiple-choice secretary problem, in which candidates arrive in uniformly random order and the goal is to select at most $k$ candidates to maximize their total value. We consider a setting where predictions of individual candidate values are available before any candidate arrives. Fujii and Yoshida's Learned Kleinberg algorithm achieves competitive loss $O(\min\{\log k/\sqrt{k},\eps\})$, where $k$ is the selection capacity and $\eps$ is the maximum multiplicative prediction error. We remove the logarithmic factor through a sharper analysis of the same switching algorithm with a retuned threshold. The resulting competitive ratio is at least $\max\{0,1-\min\{32/\sqrt{k},4\eps\}\}$. In particular, exact predictions ($\eps=0$) achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
comments: 23 pages, 6 figures; code and data in ancillary files
summary: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures; code and data in ancillary files

title: Thompson Sampling using Prior-fitted Diffusion Transformers
summary: Thompson sampling is natural randomized strategy for optimizing unknown functions in a black-box manner. In continuous global optimization, Thompson sampling has largely been restricted to Gaussian process priors, as these are essentially the only class for which computing the posterior distribution has been tractable in practice. In this work, we introduce \emph{prior-fitted diffusion transformers}, which are diffusion models that perform Thompson sampling in-context at inference time, after being pre-trained using the prior-fitted network paradigm. To apply these models, we develop a set of practical non-Gaussian priors for general black-box functions---including those that have characteristics that cannot be achieved under Gaussianity, such as priors over unimodal functions. We also quantify the tradeoff between model size and the number of pre-training iterations, and show that these models follow scaling laws akin to those observed in transformers defined over other modalities. Across a set of global optimization benchmarks, we show that prior-fitted diffusion transformers with non-Gaussian priors can achieve improved performance compared to traditional pipelines built on Gaussian processes.

title: Closing the Loop: Co-Evolving EM for Irregular Time Series Generation in Lifted Representations
comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026; The first two authors contributed equally and are co-leading authors
summary: Regular time-series generation from irregular time series is typically reduced to one-shot imputation: complete each partial sequence once, freeze the completions, and train a generator on the resulting surrogate dataset. We show that this open-loop strategy is structurally flawed. Point imputers collapse ambiguous missing regions to conditional averages, while stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves; the binding constraint is therefore iteration, not imputer design. We introduce a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework that closes the imputer-generator loop. Each E-step samples missing values from the posterior of the current generator, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions, preserving unconditional generator training. Since our diffusion prior operates in a lifted 2D representation while observations live in time-series space, we further introduce Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR), which enforces operator-consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency during the E-step. Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score, 15% in predictive score, 73% in Context-FID, and 71% in feature-correlation error. Ablations show that our approach reduces average discriminative score by 73% over single-step baselines, closing most of the remaining gap to the clean-data oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/azencot-group/PSLR.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026; The first two authors contributed equally and are co-leading authors

title: Abstention Is Not Threshold Compliance: Stated Scoring Rules in Open Language Models
summary: Kalai et al. propose stating the scoring rule in the prompt with an explicit threshold t, so that a model should answer only when its probability of being correct exceeds t. We probe each requirement of compliance on shared items, in 12 checkpoints from three post-training stages of four fully open 3-8B recipes, with exploratory models up to 32B. At t = 0.75, a line limiting the reply to an answer or "I abstain" (the abstention format) raised the mean abstention rate from 20% to 91%. Yet within this format, raising t from 0.5 to 0.9 changed it by only -0.8 percentage points. Without the line, the higher threshold even lowered abstention, and up to 40% of a checkpoint's items received decisions that no compliant policy with threshold-independent beliefs could make. Given the probability that their answer was correct, the checkpoints barely responded to the threshold in a forced-choice probe. Comparisons with self-assessment signals such as P(True) depended on the grader and on answer drift between prompts. An external threshold on recalibrated P(True) made coverage non-increasing in t by construction. Calibrated on the evaluation distribution (post hoc), it beat the abstention format at t = 0.5; calibrated on TriviaQA and applied to PopQA, however, it fell below that format at 0.75. On OLMo 3 7B, decisions trained on threshold-conditioned targets did not follow unseen thresholds consistently. A post-hoc variant trained at four thresholds answered less as t rose but still failed a pre-specified test, mainly on agreement with its training rule. A high abstention rate is not evidence of compliance: evaluations using stated scoring rules should report how often models abstain, whether decisions respond to the stated threshold, and which items they answer.

title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.

title: Galop: Billion-Scale Genetic Programming on a Single GPU
summary: Genetic programming (GP) evolves populations of heterogeneous programs, whereas GPUs achieve their highest throughput when groups of threads execute the same instructions. To better align GP evaluation with GPU execution, we present Galop, a hybrid CPU-GPU linear GP system that assigns one individual to each CUDA warp, a group of 32 threads that execute the same instructions across different fitness cases. We compare Galop against EvoGP, a recent high-performance GPU-based tree GP system, on data-rich symbolic regression across two unique GPUs, varying population size and fitness-case count. Galop completes evolutionary runs faster than EvoGP in 27 of the 28 main comparisons, with speedups of up to 13.6 times. Solution quality comparisons favour EvoGP overall, although Galop remains competitive on several problems. Galop also completes a full generation with 2.15 billion individuals on a single H100 GPU, approximately 4.0 times the largest population achieved by any other tested GP system. All five runs at this population complete 100 generations, with a median wall-clock time of 2.23 hours. These results make it practical to study GP populations in the billions on a single GPU. Galop's source code, experimental data, and reproducibility scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/xavierhillroy/Galop.

title: Learning of LPV Models With Linear Fractional Representations: Initialization, Optimization, and Conditioning
comments: Preprint submitted to the IFAC Journal of Systems and Control
summary: Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) models with Linear Fractional Representation (LFR) can describe a wide class of nonlinear systems with a control-friendly structure. However, identifying these models together with their scheduling map from input-output data requires solving a non-convex optimization problem that is highly sensitive to initialization. Consequently, existing methods often rely on many random initializations. Instead, our work proposes an initialization strategy based on the Best Linear Approximator (BLA). Furthermore, motivated by an analysis of the impact of rational-dependency LPV-LFR models on the conditioning of the non-convex cost, two multiple shooting methods that improve the conditioning, unconstrained multiple shooting (UMS) and encoder-based multiple shooting (EBMS), are compared. The initialization and multiple shooting methods are evaluated on a nonlinear mass-spring-damper example, showing that BLA initialization consistently yields accurate results, whereas random initialization has a large spread. The results also show that both UMS and EBMS reduce the spread for randomly initialized models. UMS is simple to tune and well suited to few sub-records, whereas EBMS can exploit many short sub-records to further improve conditioning, at the cost of training an encoder and tuning additional hyperparameters.
comment: Preprint submitted to the IFAC Journal of Systems and Control

title: Where Should the Code Go? Locating Foundation-Model Errors in Bitemporal Inventory Simulation
comments: 22 pages. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS). Code and data: https://github.com/durga-sandeep/where-should-the-code-go
summary: Operational reports carry two clocks: when an event happened and when its report arrived; later reports can revise earlier ones. A foundation-model component that maintains the state supported by the reports visible at a cutoff, then rolls a supplied scenario forward, can be helped by exact code before it, after it or inside the call, or asked to reason harder. We ask which remedy removes which error, for which models, on an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment: 36,672 independently rescored requests over twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models, with a forced-answer-call interface as a control and protocols frozen before the calls. Weak models fail in separable ways. Canonical input removes report-selection error, exact continuation removes rollout error, neither repairs the other, and which error dominates differs by model; strong models are at ceiling on raw reports. Asking for more reasoning is no substitute and can depend on the interface: under a forced answer call high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, which gain or hold under automatic choice; on its provider the forced call disables reasoning for DeepSeek V4 Flash; and at high effort gpt-oss exhausts its output budget. The contribution is a controlled component diagnostic, released with every request, and evidence that for some model and provider pairs the tool-calling interface confounds reasoning evaluation.
comment: 22 pages. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS). Code and data: https://github.com/durga-sandeep/where-should-the-code-go

title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
comments: 17 pages, accepted to NeurIPS 2026 LP4FM Workshop
summary: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Samāsa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($Δ=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). Severe per-verse failures (MQM$<80$) fall from $9.0\%$ to $7.6\%$, at roughly $9\times$ the per-verse inference cost of the baseline. Additionally, $J_{\text{route}}$ scores its own family's outputs $2$-$7$ MQM higher than $J_{\text{report}}$ on every one of the 12 conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. These are small gains on a metric saturating near 85-86.
comment: 17 pages, accepted to NeurIPS 2026 LP4FM Workshop

title: Fast Slice-Wise Deep Learning Motion Correction for Spinal Cord Functional MRI
summary: Respiratory and bulk motion displace the spinal cord between the volumes of a functional MRI time series. Current methods such as the Spinal Cord Toolbox (SCT) take several minutes per time series, and general-purpose brain tools register whole volumes, whereas the cord moves mainly slice by slice. We propose a lightweight convolutional neural network that regresses the in-plane translation aligning each axial slice to a reference. Two models, trained without motion labels, correct large and then residual motion. On a 3T (120 scans) and a 7T (59 scans) dataset, the proposed method improves on SCT on every metric (tSNR +10 to +25%, DVARS -20 to -38%), leaves almost no slice displaced by more than one voxel (<0.1%), performs on par with a slice-wise AFNI variant and better than slice-wise FSL FLIRT, and runs in about 10 s per scan, about 30 times faster than SCT. The code is available at https://github.com/ivadomed/moco-dl and the method is available in SCT v7.4.

title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
summary: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.

title: Terrain-Aware Thompson Sampling for Multi-Drone Search and Rescue
comments: Accepted to the 18th International Symposium on Distributed Autonomous Robotic Systems (DARS 2026)
summary: In this work, we propose a decentralized terrain-aware multi-drone Thompson Sampling algorithm tailored for search and rescue (SAR) applications. A probability distribution of locating a lost person is informed by terrain data, using established SAR models (displacement ring, elevation, watershed, dispersion angle, and track offset) derived from historical SAR case data on lost person behavior. Exploration is conducted by a team of drones using Thompson Sampling, where candidate actions are selected by drawing samples from this probability distribution, represented by a per-cell Gaussian posterior whose mean and variance are updated through Bayesian inference. This approach balances exploration of uncertain regions with exploitation of high-probability areas to locate a lost person. Observation uncertainty is incorporated through fractional forest coverage, which measures the percentage of an observation occluded by tree coverage and accounts for reduced detection performance in densely vegetated areas. Simulations using real SAR case data (YOSAR) evaluate the proposed method against a coverage planner and a probabilistic active search method in search regions of 1.5 and 3.8 square kilometers, with 5, 10, 15, and 20 agents flying at 50 km/hr. We demonstrate that our method achieves a success rate of approximately 87% within 60 to 247 seconds in the 1.5 square kilometer region, and success rates of approximately 75% to 91% within 161 to 466 seconds in the 3.8 square kilometer region, across different agent configurations.
comment: Accepted to the 18th International Symposium on Distributed Autonomous Robotic Systems (DARS 2026)

title: What Entropy-Based View Selection Cannot See: An Audit of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshops on VLM4RWD
summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshops on VLM4RWD

title: Risk-Aware Joint Inference and Resource Control for Physical AI in 6G Networks
comments: Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Wireless edge inference enables Physical-AI devices to execute edge-inferred actions using transmitted sensory inputs. Since the risk of incorrect actions vary across observations and tasks, the associated uplink transmission of sensory inputs requires different levels of wireless reliability. For instance, applying a fixed signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirement can overprovision low-risk tasks while underprovisioning high-risk ones. Therefore, we propose risk-aware control for edge inference (RACE), which maps predicted action-failure probability and task criticality to adaptive SINR targets and combines them with deadline-derived SINR requirements. A slow-timescale large language model (LLM) proposes task requirements for deterministic validation, while a fast hybrid actor selects inference configurations and transmit power levels, complemented by analytical receive beamforming and finite power restoration. Simulations show $11\%$ improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective over fixed-high-SINR control, with near-zero constraint outage.
comment: Submitted to IEEE for possible publication

title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations
summary: Tables are compositional, with content spread across a schema, cell values, rows, and columns. Large-scale operations such as retrieval, overlap estimation, deduplication, and data curation need these local signals composed into one reusable embedding vector per table. Table representation methods, however, are mostly evaluated through row-level prediction or supervised downstream tasks, which do not measure table-level embedding quality directly. We introduce a benchmark that evaluates table-level embeddings through four desiderata: consistency under partial views, discriminability across label granularities, robustness to benign perturbations, and efficiency. Across twelve methods on synthetic and real corpora, lightweight schema- and text-based fingerprints are among the strongest. The sharpest contrast comes from two tabular foundation models, TabPFN and ConTextTab: although both are strong row-level predictors, their states, composed by mean, max, or three further parameter-free pooling rules, trail the strongest fingerprints. We therefore ask whether the gap lies in the encoder or in the compositional rule. Keeping ConTextTab frozen, we learn only the compositional rule over its cell states, using support-conditioned distribution matching (SCDM), a self-supervised loss we propose that matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps within and across tables. Across all fifteen head configurations, the learned rule raises the Spearman correlation between embedding similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43-0.50 on synthetic data and improves triplet ranking, clustering, and retrieval, with smaller but systematic gains on real data. A downstream parent-table retrieval task confirms these findings. How local states are composed, and with what objective, substantially affects the quality of table-level embeddings.

title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
summary:
Incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. Standard IVC schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise.
  We construct IVC schemes for oracle-aided computations under the LWE assumption by first constructing SNARGs, and then extending them to IVC. We consider the following two settings, where below, k is the security parameter, n is the input length, and T, S, and Q are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds.
  1. Robust computations: For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an eps-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct privately verifiable SNARGs and IVC. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length poly(k ,S, log T,1/eps), and verification uses O(k/eps) oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVCs with public parameters of length o(n), and o(Q) verifier oracle queries.
  2. Signed oracles: For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVC without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length poly(k,S,log T). For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths poly(k,log T), we remove the dependence on S, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths poly(k,log T).
  All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness.

title: Probe What-If Worlds Before You Ship: Persona Simulation for Real-World Decision Making
summary: User research and system testing reveal whether products and services meet user needs, yet recruiting specialized participants, designing controlled what-if comparisons, and repeating studies as designs evolve often bottleneck design iteration and data-driven decision-making. We present a framework and execution infrastructure that translates real-world industry inquiries into controlled experiments with simulated users. Our methodology formally defines the target cohort, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics, while the pipeline supports large-scale concurrent runs over cohort-stimulus-environment combinations (survey, web, chatbot, and OS app), auditable trial-level logging, cohort-level outcome aggregation, and cross-cohort and cross-variant statistical reports. Across twelve industry partner cases spanning five domains, we show how constructing hard-to-reach or what-if persona cohorts supports exploratory studies and distills simulated responses into testable design hypotheses. Cross-model comparisons on selected cases largely preserve primary conclusions, whereas perturbing or ablating persona attributes alters service outcomes, effect sizes, and inter-group differences, indicating that grounding target cohorts in detailed personas materially shapes simulation results. Together, these studies show that persona-enabled agents can test specified cohorts at design speed, diagnose systems under test, and deliver directional evidence that focuses problem definition, steers design and strategic decisions, and guides further study.

title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
comments: 30 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables, The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/code-as-explanations.
comment: 30 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables, The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
summary:
Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone.
  This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection.
  We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features.
  The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

title: A Three-Stage Unsupervised Online Physics-Informed Neural Network for Microgrid Optimal Power Flow
summary: Optimal allocation of generators is a key challenge in power systems to achieve economical dispatch while satisfying operational constraints. Conventional optimization techniques can be computationally expensive, limiting their applicability in real-time environments, and neural networks often require offline retraining under new operating conditions. This paper proposes a three-stage unsupervised online physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for optimal power flow (OPF). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework satisfies load demand and system constraints while achieving a $43,665 lower operating cost than fmincon-based optimization under the same operating conditions. The training process analysis further demonstrate the framework's ability to adapt its parameters online to variations in load demand and renewable generation in real time.
