We conducted experiments with two agent harnesses and real runtime controls, including Microsoft's agent governance toolkit and agentgateway. guardscope is available at https://github.com/VulcanLab/guardscope.

title: DGPExplainer: Generating Prototype Sequence Explanations for Dynamic Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been successfully applied to learning from graph-structured data. However, applying them to dynamic graphs-where nodes and edges evolve over time-presents significant challenges, particularly regarding explainability. While explanation techniques for static GNNs are well established, they do not readily extend to dynamic GNNs (DGNNs) due to the added complexity introduced by temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal dependencies, especially when generating model-level explanations. To address this gap, we introduce DGPExplainer, a post-hoc, prototype-based explainer specifically designed for DGNN models that transforms their complex decision-making processes into human-understandable, analogical, case-based explanations. DGPExplainer first employs local explanation methods to identify important elements within temporal snapshots of dynamic graph sequences. It then decomposes the graph at each time step into distinct prototypes, thereby symbolizing the dynamic graph sequence. Finally, we design a sequence generation method that uses these symbolized sequences to learn and generate class-specific dynamic graph pattern sequences that serve as prototype explanations. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method effectively produces prototype-based explanations for DGNN models across multiple classes.

title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark
summary: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

title: MOON-RL: Multi-Objective Optimization via Objective Space Navigation with Reinforcement Learning
comments: 66 pages, including appendices. Code, data and supplementary video links are provided in the manuscript
summary: Many engineering design problems involve multiple conflicting objectives and strict feasibility constraints. They are typically solved with population-based optimizers that require many evaluations and offer limited online control over where the search is focused. We present MOON-RL, a reinforcement-learning-based optimization framework that formulates constrained multi-objective search as preference-directed navigation in the objective space. In MOON-RL, a lightweight PPO policy receives objective-space and constraint-related observations and acts as an instance-specific adaptive search process. It learns how to update the design so that the current solution advances along a user-specified trade-off direction, while a simple meta-algorithm periodically resets the policy, resamples starting designs from a continuously updated archive of non-dominated solutions, and adjusts step-size and penalty schedules. We evaluate MOON-RL on real-world actuator-design problems and additional convergence-hard constrained benchmarks, comparing against established evolutionary algorithms under matched evaluation budgets. In focused search scenarios, MOON-RL achieves competitive performance in the region of interest, and ablation studies show that both the RL-driven adaptive sampling process and the meta-algorithm contribute to this behaviour, suggesting that repurposing RL training as objective-space navigation is a viable building block for interactive, preference-guided design tools. Additional experiments show that the framework also accommodates adaptive non-RL samplers, while PPO remains a strong choice for fixed-target, preference-directed objective-space navigation.
comment: 66 pages, including appendices. Code, data and supplementary video links are provided in the manuscript

title: TQIR: Trellis Quantization with Integer Reconstruction for Bandwidth-Efficient Edge LLM Acceleration
comments: submitted to IEEE transactions on circuits and systems for AI
summary: Autoregressive large language model (LLM) inference is often limited by external-memory bandwidth, while existing ultra-low-bit trellis quantization reconstructs floating-point weights and leaves runtime Hadamard-transform and decoder costs unresolved. This paper presents TQIR, an algorithm--hardware co-design that decouples storage precision ($S$) from decoded-weight ($W$) and activation ($A$) compute precisions, enabling a better accuracy--hardware trade-off. TQIR performs trellis matching with floating-point candidates offline while constraining each candidate to an INT8 or INT4 codeword that can be reproduced exactly for integer GEMM at runtime. To reduce transform cost while preserving the integer weight path, TQIR relocates the reverse Hadamard transform to the activation side and employs an $H_{128}$ Subspace Hadamard Transform, together with a subspace-aligned $128\times2$ trellis tile that preserves the original 256-weight sequence length. The configurable decoder, synthesized in a TSMC 16-nm process, delivers 307.2~Gweights/s in 0.0509~mm$^2$ and achieves 13.93$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ the normalized decoder-area efficiency of Ecco and Codeword Decomposition, respectively. These results show that fixed-rate trellis compression can reduce weight traffic while sustaining an integer-GEMM datapath matched to the evaluated memory and PE rates.
comment: submitted to IEEE transactions on circuits and systems for AI

title: Winter wheat improves soil carbon sequestration with reduced gains in warmer climates
comments: 19 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Published in Environmental Research Letters. Georgios Giannarakis and Vasileios Sitokonstantinou contributed equally to this work
summary: Sustainable agricultural intensification requires a precise understanding of how land use decisions influence soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration under varying environmental conditions. We apply causal machine learning to evaluate the heterogeneous impact of winter wheat-based rotations on SOC at the field-level across Lithuania. Using a nationwide dataset collected over five years (2018-2022), including crop types, management practices, soil properties, and environmental conditions, we estimate how the effects of winter wheat-based rotation vary across space and climate. Our results indicate that winter wheat generally enhances SOC levels, but its effectiveness is modulated by climate. Cooler regions experience higher SOC gains, whereas warmer regions show diminished or even negative effects. Future climate projections suggest that the potential for winter wheat carbon sequestration may decline under high-emission scenarios. These findings highlight the importance of localized agricultural strategies that account for climate variability to maximize SOC sequestration and ensure long-term soil sustainability.
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Published in Environmental Research Letters. Georgios Giannarakis and Vasileios Sitokonstantinou contributed equally to this work

title: Schedule-Calibrated Commitment Order in Blockwise Masked Diffusion Language Models
comments: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Includes appendices and ancillary code for algebraic verification
summary: Sequential block schedules can make token commitment in masked diffusion language models appear strongly left-to-right even when within-block order is random or reversed. For equal contiguous blocks processed without interleaving in positional order, with untied irreversible commitments, we use a Spearman-rank identity to express global position-commitment correlation as a deterministic schedule reference plus a weighted mean within-block correlation. In a reported paired study of LLaDA-8B-Instruct on 500 math and code prompts with 256 generated positions and updates, increasing block size from 64 to 128 lowers mean global correlation from 0.9845 to 0.9149. Uniform-random within-block references are already 0.9375 and 0.7500. After calibration, mean within-block correlations are 0.751 and 0.660, so the larger raw residual at block size 128 does not indicate stronger local positional ordering. We give sharp bounds and derive calibrated intervals from reported summaries, while documenting the limitations of the aggregate-only empirical release. The analysis supports schedule-aware interpretation of commitment order; its empirical scope is one checkpoint and two schedules, without evaluation of output quality or inference speed.
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Includes appendices and ancillary code for algebraic verification

title: Sub-100KB On-Device CNN Training via Dynamic Sparse Updates and Hardware--Software Co-Design
summary: The increasing demand for real-time processing and personalized deep learning has made edge-device training essential but challenging due to high memory and computational costs. To address this, we propose a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) training accelerator with a dynamic sparse update mechanism that selectively updates important parameters using a random channel strategy, avoiding costly evaluations. Combined with activation pruning, our approach reduces activation storage to just 3.4\% of the original. Our hardware features a fused forward dataflow that concurrently processes group normalization and convolution, reducing training time by 45\% through computation reordering and efficient zero-skipping. Implemented in TSMC 28nm at FP8 precision, the design operates at 800 MHz, achieving 8 TOPS peak throughput, 31.13 TOPS/W energy efficiency, and 14.8 TOPS/mm$^2$ area efficiency, with power consumption ranging from 257 to 272 mW. The design enables on-device training within a sub-100KB on-chip SRAM budget (95KB in silicon).

title: Regret Bounds for Quantum Linear Bandits
summary: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $Ω(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $Ω(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.

title: Towards Robust Vision-Language Reasoning: A Multi-Stage Optimization Pipeline with Masked Diffusion Model
summary: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.

title: Unifying Heterogeneous Dissipativity for Distributed Power-System Stability Analysis
summary: Compositional dissipativity is attractive for large-scale interconnected systems, but its application to modern heterogeneous power systems is limited by conservative descriptions of nodal dissipativity and inefficient distributed implementation. This paper introduces a common first-order dynamic lifting of the physical voltage-current port, providing an enriched dissipativity representation that captures complementary frequency-dependent energy behavior while preserving network composability. The resulting representation accommodates heterogeneous power system buses within a unified dissipativity description and enables less conservative compositional stability analysis. A centralized stability-certification problem is then formulated and solved through a dual-guided column-generation scheme. Its matrix dual reveals the network-critical dissipation direction, which guides parallel local certificate generation toward the current system bottleneck. This leads to a distributed Network-Critical Margin Exchange (NCME) method with early stability certification. Case studies demonstrate substantially reduced conservatism of the dynamic-port formulation and improved computational and communication scalability of NCME for heterogeneous power systems.

title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification
summary: Liver disease remains a major global health concern, highlighting the need for reliable and accessible early detection methods. Although recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and quantum machine learning (QML) have introduced promising diagnostic tools, many approaches suffer from limited interpretability and inflated performance caused by data leakage or overly simplistic evaluation protocols. These constraints reduce their reliability in real-world clinical practice. This paper proposes KQML-Liver, a hybrid framework that integrates QML with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to enhance predictive performance and interpretability. The architecture combines parameterized quantum circuits for expressive feature representation with KAN-based functional mappings that capture nonlinear relationships in an interpretable manner. Evaluated on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) under a rigorous preprocessing protocol preventing data leakage, the proposed model achieves 82% classification accuracy and 100% recall, detecting all positive cases, outperforming existing baselines while providing improved transparency in clinical predictions. These results suggest that hybrid KAN-quantum architectures offer a promising direction for interpretable AI-assisted medical diagnosis.

title: Computational Raga Recognition: A Theory-Driven Approach
summary: Raga recognition in Hindustani classical music is difficult because a raga is not defined only by the notes used in it. Its identity also depends on the way notes are emphasized, the movement between notes and characteristic phrases. In this work, we develop a computational approach to analyse these characteristics directly from audio recordings. The method uses pitch extracted from recordings and represents it using a 44-position note framework based on the 22-shruti system. From this representation, Raga features based on the Indian classical musicology are extracted.Each feature is compared with a reference representation of the raga and the resulting scores are combined to obtain an overall similarity score. The method is first studied using Raga Yaman and is then tested on recordings of other ragas. The computational results are also compared with the theoretical description of Yaman to identify which raga characteristics are captured well and where the method has limitations.

title: Dual Representation Enhanced Diffusion Policy for Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
summary: The Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) is a fundamental and challenging optimization problem in smart manufacturing. Although recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches can learn effective scheduling policies through interaction with the environment, their performance often degrades as problem scale and processing-time uncertainty increase. In this paper, we propose DredRL, a dual representation enhanced diffusion-policy reinforcement learning scheduler. DredRL first constructs enhanced dual representations of operations and machines through self- and cross-attention mechanisms to capture both intra-entity and inter-entity dependencies. A diffusion model is further employed as the policy network, generating scheduling decisions through iterative denoising conditioned on the encoded state to enhance policy expressiveness and robustness. Extensive experiments on synthetic, public, large-scale, and stochastic FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that DredRL outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based schedulers across most configurations. Compared with SOTA learning-based methods, DredRL reduces makespan by up to 5.44% on synthetic instances. It also achieves the best learning-based performance on three of four public benchmarks and outperforms the stochasticity-aware algorithms on stochastic benchmarks. These results demonstrate that combining enhanced dual representations with diffusion-based policies provides an effective and robust approach for large scale scalable FJSP scheduling in complicated environment.

title: Protected Unbiased Sparsification: A Sharp Loewner Curve
comments: 44 pages, 11 figures. Code, protocols, and saved results are included as ancillary files
summary: Random sparsification replaces a probability vector by a random vector with few nonzero entries. We ask for unbiasedness, exact preservation of prescribed linear statistics, and a covariance guarantee for every downstream linear response. Let $p$ have $k$ positive coordinates, let $A$ specify the protected statistics, and let $d\le k-2$ be their effective rank. For every $d+1\le m\le k$, we construct an unbiased random probability vector $Q$ with at most $m$ nonzero coordinates, $AQ=Ap$ on every realization, and $\operatorname{Cov}(Q)\preceq h C_{p\mid A}$, where $h=(k-m)/((m-d)(k-d-1))$ and $C_{p\mid A}$ is the categorical covariance after optimal linear adjustment for the protected statistics. This coefficient is sharp uniformly over instances, even among biased estimators when error is measured by its second moment. A residual covariance bridge extends the concurrent unprotected curve to arbitrary pathwise linear protection. We also characterize instance-optimal constants for partitions with uniform weights within classes and derive bounds for peaked weights. For rational inputs, an exact Las Vegas sampler attains the curve within a factor $1+ε$ in expected polynomial time. A separate fast block-pivotal sampler preserves block masses and is no worse in covariance order than independent sampling within blocks. Experiments illustrate the theory on synthetic weights and language-model attention. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct decoding, the fast sampler preserves block masses, while comparisons with VarOpt remain statistically inconclusive and top-$m$ truncation scores highest on RULER.
comment: 44 pages, 11 figures. Code, protocols, and saved results are included as ancillary files

title: Higher order schemes for the numerical solution of integro-differential equation-based age-of-infection models with time-dependent contact rates
summary:
Age-of-infection models, formulated as integro-differential equations (IDEs), provide elegant mathematical descriptions for the spread of infectious diseases. In contrast to ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based models, IDE-based models can accommodate general distributions of transition times between disease stages. Yet, the accurate numerical assessment of the solution of IDE models remains challenging.
  Here, we extend a recently proposed fixed-point method based on Gregory quadrature. We generalize the formulation to time-dependent contact rates whose changes at discrete time points are represented by continuously differentiable sigmoidal interpolants, and suggest additional finite difference approximations to obtain higher-order schemes for susceptible, infected and recovered subpopulations. The resulting numerical schemes achieve convergence orders of two, three and four for all three subpopulations, enabling accurate and flexible simulations of IDE-based epidemic models with general sojourn time distributions and changing contact patterns.

title: Driving World Models Move the Camera, Not the Scene
summary: Plan-conditioned driving world models are used to compare candidate plans, so their forecast should change with the plan as the real scene would, yet widely used control metrics check only whether the camera follows the command. Recorded drives already contain real outcomes of plans that were never driven: retiming a log gives pose-matched images and LiDAR for other speeds, and a stereo rig records a laterally shifted view. Against these references, released world models move their camera but barely move the scene: their scene response, the share of the real change in distance that the forecast reproduces, reaches at most about a third of real video's, and the trajectory score cannot tell an executed speed command from an ignored one. Interventions inside the generator trace the failure to the plan's channel. The forecast geometry follows the context frames; once they carry the planned geometry, plan tokens add little. ReTime-Compose therefore delivers the plan as geometry, without training. It transports the frames of one logged-speed rollout to the planned cameras, and the frozen model completes only what no frame covers. Frozen generators then follow a 0.54 m lateral shift nearly as the real scene does on KITTI, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, and respond more than re-sampling to slow-down plans in three generators and to speed-up plans in two.

title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy
summary: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.

title: Probe-Based Routing for Join Optimizer Selection
summary: In optimizers that choose a join-order solver by a size rule, join ordering is an algorithm-selection problem, because dynamic programming (DP), genetic search (GEQO), and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) each win on different queries. PostgreSQL nevertheless chooses among them by relation count alone, although queries with the same relation count can favor different solvers. This paper introduces two landscape features that a probe computes from random join orders in microseconds per query. The tail spacing $α$ describes how the costs of the best sampled orders are spaced, and the crossover surprise $θ$ describes how far the cost of a crossover child deviates from the mean cost of its parents. The router clusters training queries by these features and the relation count, assigns a solver to every cluster that this solver wins in total end-to-end time by a margin, and leaves all other queries to PostgreSQL's default rule. On JOB and IMDb-CEB, the router lowers mean end-to-end time relative to the default rule, and on IMDb-CEB the probe features nearly double the gain obtained from the relation count alone, so they carry information about the queries that the relation count lacks.

title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting
summary: One way to study language-model introspection is to test whether models can identify where their activations have been perturbed. We train a simple linear classifier to identify the perturbed sentence from the model's activations, then compare its predictions with the model's own answers across pretraining and injection strengths. This tests whether the model is being asked to report information that is already easy to recover. If so, successful localization may be less demanding than it first appears and may not extend to the broader uses that motivate introspection research, such as faithfully explaining a model's reasoning or helping researchers assess the reliability of its answers. With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and probe readout at layer 24 in OLMo~3 32B, the supervised probe reaches 98.3\% accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens, while the model's zero-shot answer remains at chance (11.1\%). At the released base checkpoint, these accuracies reach 99.1\% and 89.6\%, respectively. Across 7B and 32B, location is already decodable in randomly initialized networks, showing that the architecture can support these traces without pretraining. In these experiments, location information lies close enough to the surface for a simple linear probe to recover it, so successful reporting need not imply broader access to the model's internal computation.

title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent
comments: 18 pages, 5 figures, 15 tables. Code, data, and run records: https://github.com/Brightendata/knowledge-in-the-harness
summary: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $τ^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 15 tables. Code, data, and run records: https://github.com/Brightendata/knowledge-in-the-harness

title: MoE Pretraining:Parallelism Layout Changes the Model, Not Quality
summary: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are trained across many machines, and the way the work is split, the parallelism layout, often changes between runs: a job resumes on a different GPU count, a cluster is resized, or an ablation runs on a new setup. In exact arithmetic the layout should not matter, but in real arithmetic it changes the order in which numbers are added, and some MoE rules such as load balancing and expert capacity are often computed per machine. We ask whether the layout changes the trained MoE model. We pretrain the same small MoE language models (25M to 117M parameters, 20M FineWeb-Edu tokens) with the same seed, data and hyperparameters under 9 data-parallel and expert-parallel layouts, in fp32 on CPUs and fp16 on a GPU, and compare each run with the effect of a new random seed. Across 80 runs we find: (1) The layout does not change model quality, but it does change the model: final predictions differ about 80% as much as with a new seed, and over 90% of routing decisions differ. Any layout, a one-bit change to one weight, or a different CPU thread count has the same effect. (2) The cause is the router: decisions that flip are almost exactly those where two experts were nearly tied (AUC 0.97 to 1.00 in the first 16 steps). (3) More, smaller experts create more near-ties (2.7% with 8 experts, 23% with 64) and less reproducible routing (68% vs. 100% of decisions differ), but outputs do not drift further. (4) A dense model of the same active size is far more stable (0.12x the seed level in fp32, 0.58x in fp16), while the MoE reaches about 0.8x at both precisions and twice as fast. (5) When pretraining resumes on a new layout, timing matters: switching at 84% of pretraining barely changes the final model, while switching at 10%, just after warm-up, changes it substantially. We release code, run logs and data.

title: Multicontinuum Poroelasticity Model. Analysis and Computation
summary: In this work, we develop and analyze a macroscopic multicontinuum model for Biot poroelasticity. The full macroscopic multicontinuum system is derived by projecting the microscopic weak formulation onto continuum-dependent Galerkin spaces enriched with first-order multiscale corrections. This construction retains generalized pressure storage and coupling terms, with effective coefficients inherited from the microscopic bilinear forms. Under suitable coefficient assumptions, we establish well-posedness and energy stability of the macroscopic multicontinuum model. A fully discrete scheme combining the Galerkin finite element method in space with the backward Euler method in time is then developed. Its well-posedness and stability are proved, and a priori error estimates are derived using appropriate projection operators and energy arguments. Finally, numerical experiments for periodic and non-periodic high-contrast media demonstrate the accuracy of the multicontinuum model with respect to the averaged fine-scale solution.

title: Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback
summary: Agent self-improvement requires feedback about task success, yet external feedback may be unavailable at test time. Agents must then infer success from observable evidence, and incomplete verification can misguide subsequent updates. We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), a method that co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses within a single task while keeping model weights fixed. The Evaluator actively inspects artifacts and environment state with tools; its findings ground an internal signal for output selection and guide updates to both execution and verification procedures. Proposed Evaluators undergo comparative review on common candidates, while Actor updates require support from their own fresh outputs. Across AutomationBench, $τ^3$ Banking, and selected GDPval tasks, VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods operating without external feedback, with gains of 3.3, 4.1, and 2.3 percentage points over the strongest baselines on the main backbone. Ablations support the contributions of active verification and Evaluator evolution, and selection from fixed candidate pools shows that improved verification can recover successful outputs without generating new ones.

title: DroneDiffusion: Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Path Planner for UAV Navigation
summary: We present DroneDiffusion, a perception-aware diffusion planner for local 3-D UAV trajectory generation that explicitly models and avoids failure zones caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces. A vision-language perceptual safety estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that highlights regions of degraded sensing. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is conditioned on this map together with the onboard RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity to generate egocentric 3-D trajectories. To enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time without retraining, we apply training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D Euclidean signed distance field. The model is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a real drone. Reliability conditioning raises the mean perceptual reliability along generated trajectories to 0.71, compared with 0.63 for a geometric baseline, while guidance halves the collision rate of the learned prior from 14.7% to 7.8%. Perceptual safety conditioning and geometric guidance are therefore complementary: treating sensor reliability as a first-class signal reduces incursions into unreliable regions while maintaining competitive navigation performance.

title: PCLSegNet: Anatomy-Aware Deep Learning Framework for MRI-based Pancreatic Cyst Segmentation and Size Assessment
summary: Early detection and follow-up of pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are crucial, as some of their subtypes, such as mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, carry a significant risk of malignant transformation. Although most AI studies investigating PCLs rely on computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior soft tissue contrast, making it highly suitable for PCLs assessment. In this work, we propose an anatomy-aware two-stage deep learning framework for automated PCLs segmentation on abdominal MRI scans. First, a publicly available pancreas segmentation model is used to localize the pancreas. Then, we introduce the anatomyaware PCLSegNet, which incorporates anatomical priors as guidance for pancreas and PCLs segmentation. To address the class imbalance problem, we develop a Class-Specific ErrorWeighted (CSEW) loss function. Postprocessing is applied through anatomical constraints.Our proposed method outperforms multi-organ segmentation models such as TotalSegmentator, achieving substantially higher Dice scores for pancreas segmentation. Moreover, it also achieves a superior normalized surface Dice (NSD) and recall for PCLs segmentationcompared to other state-of-the-art models like nnU-Net, while also notably reducing the false negative rate, facilitating the automatic early detection and the noninvasive imaging-based assessment of PCLs.

title: Autonomous Trail Racing with a Bicycle Robot
comments: 35 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables (incl. appendix with supplementary figures and tables). Submitted to The International Journal of Robotics Research. Project page: https://pages.rai-inst.com/autonomous-trail-racing/. Code: https://github.com/rai-opensource/sem_map
summary: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.
comment: 35 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables (incl. appendix with supplementary figures and tables). Submitted to The International Journal of Robotics Research. Project page: https://pages.rai-inst.com/autonomous-trail-racing/. Code: https://github.com/rai-opensource/sem_map

title: Priority-Based Network Access with Strict-Priority Scheduling in PLCA Multidrop Networks
comments: 16 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Shared-medium Ethernet is gaining renewed attention across industrial domains, driven by the adoption of 10BASE-T1S. In such multidrop networks, collision-free and deterministic medium access is achieved through Physical Layer Collision Avoidance (PLCA). However, PLCA follows a node-based cyclic access structure that does not account for traffic priority, leading to high access latency for time-sensitive traffic and limited scalability with increasing network size. Existing PLCA extensions improve latency for selected devices but remain restricted to node-based access and do not support network-wide traffic differentiation. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a priority-based network access and scheduling mechanism for multidrop networks. The proposed approach decouples medium access from node-based ordering and enables class-based prioritization, allowing high-priority traffic from any device to be transmitted ahead of lower-priority traffic. It further supports a configuration that emulates Strict Priority (SP) scheduling, providing low and bounded access latency for highest-priority traffic. Analytical bounds on the worst-case access latency are derived, validated, and shown to be tight. Performance evaluation demonstrates that the proposed mechanism reduces the maximum observed access latency for high-priority traffic by over 65% compared to PLCA, with latency increasing by less than 1% as the network grows from 8 to 40 devices.

title: A hybrid machine learning-analog framework for downscaling unprecedented climate extremes
summary: Extreme weather events are critical for climate impact assessments. While physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes, for example, through ensemble boosting, this approach is computationally demanding, often restricting output to coarse spatial resolutions. Probabilistic generative downscaling offers a solution by enabling efficient sampling from the entire climate distribution, including its extreme tails. Here, we first demonstrate that machine learning generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic. We then leverage an emulated machine learning dataset to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. Our hybrid framework effectively bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling, providing an efficient tool for extreme event downscaling and capturing multi-model uncertainty.

title: Track4D: Representing Dense 3D Tracking for Video Diffusion Models
summary: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d

title: FineSpeaker: Reliable Speaker Representation Learning at Fine Temporal Resolution
summary: Speaker representation learning is fundamental to speech processing tasks such as speaker verification and diarization. Although long-context speaker encoders can produce stable and discriminative embeddings, short-duration verification and diarization require finer-grained temporal representations. Short temporal contexts limit the available speaker evidence and make speaker identity difficult to disentangle from phonetic and acoustic variability. This creates a temporal resolution-representation reliability trade-off: speaker representations should maintain local within-speaker consistency, between-speaker discriminability and remain sensitive to speaker changes at fine temporal resolution. Accordingly, we propose a framework for reliable speaker representation learning at fine temporal resolution. FineSpeaker first constructs resolution-controllable frame-wise speaker representations through mean pooling over an adjustable n-frame window, enabling flexible control of representation granularity. It then introduces a speaker encoder with local temporal modeling that exploits short-range speaker context to improve the stability and discriminability of short-duration and frame-wise representations. Furthermore, we develop a generative disentanglement strategy for optimizing frame-level speaker representations, combining VAE-based probabilistic modeling with flow matching to characterize speaker-related variation and suppress non-speaker interference. Experiments demonstrate competitive full-utterance performance, improved fine-grained speaker verification on VoxCeleb and CN-Celeb, and strong zero-shot diarization results, highlighting the benefits of balancing temporal resolution and representation reliability.

title: Fundamental Limits of Data-Driven Predictive Control
summary: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) has attracted substantial interest, and many variants have been proposed; however, comparatively less is known about the statistical closed-loop performance of these methods and the fundamental limits they are subject to. In this contribution, we apply the statistical decision framework developed in our earlier work to study fundamental limits of DDPC. The performance of a data-driven controller is measured by its risk, the expected deterioration in control performance relative to an oracle model-based controller at a given system, and by its total risk that measures the overall performance across all systems of interest. Lower bounds on these risks are derived using the bias-variance decomposition and the Cramer-Rao inequality. In particular, a lower bound on the total risk is obtained by a calculus-of-variations method. This bound applies to any DDPC design, thereby quantifying unavoidable performance limitations and providing a benchmark for assessing existing DDPC methods. In an illustrative example, we compare the risks of certainty-equivalence model predictive control, subspace predictive control, and data-enabled predictive control with the derived lower bounds, providing a quantitative performance assessment of these methods and some guidance on tuning regularization parameters in DDPC.

title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
summary: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

title: APG-Planner: Learning Vision-Based High-Speed Trajectory Planning via Analytic Policy Gradient
summary: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.

title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
summary: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

title: Browser Immune System (BIS): Innate and Adaptive Threat Detection in the Browser with a Cybersecurity Transformer
summary: Security decisions about a web page are best made where the page is: in the browser, before anything leaves the machine. We present the Browser Immune System (BIS), a browser extension that screens navigation with a cybersecurity transformer running entirely on the user's GPU, and alias-web, the model that powers it: a 4B-parameter model that starts from the dual-regime cybersecurity transformer (CT0), extends its public release alias3-micro with a context-category sensor, and is quantised to 4 bits and compiled to a 2.44 GB graph for WebGPU. alias-web is the first in-browser realisation of that model's typed decision mode, System 1, with its official pieces: the marker-token mapping, the complete pointer head and the final normalisation that the exported graph omits. It answers a typed security question in about 150 ms on a laptop GPU, and the same weights generate explanations at 10.5 tokens/s on demand. BIS treats the model as an immune system: an innate response, one System 1 question per threat class, runs on every page; an adaptive response, System 2 text, explains a verdict only when the user asks. On BISBENCH-8, eight synthetic sites of which six execute real but harmless malicious behaviour and two are adversarial controls, BIS returns the expected page verdict on 7/8 sites with both controls green and a class-level micro-F1 of 0.71, scans a page in 0.9 to 6.4 s, and gives identical verdicts across samples and across Chrome and Firefox. Single-variable diagnostics trace both benchmark errors to what the model was shown and, with a first pass over eleven real public pages, show that two of the seven questions answer yes on ordinary scripts and login forms: specificity on the real web is the open problem. We report every error, the engineering obstacles between a research checkpoint and a working extension, and what the evidence does not yet support.

title: Beyond the Explicit: Benchmarking and Detecting Implicit Harm in Short Videos
summary: Short videos have become a dominant online medium, where harmful content is increasingly conveyed in implicit and fragmented forms. Prior work largely focuses on explicit categories, such as violence and hate speech, and often fails to detect videos that subtly promote misleading values through narrative context, emotional framing, or cross-modal cues, partly due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks for implicit harm. To bridge this gap, we construct DeepHarm-7K, a large-scale harmful short-video dataset comprising 7,110 samples annotated according to a fine-grained harmful-content taxonomy. The dataset systematically covers implicitly harmful videos across diverse real-world scenarios and is constructed through a rigorous multi-stage quality-control process. Building on this dataset, we propose DeepHarm-VL, a multimodal detection framework that integrates visual, audio, and cross-modal reasoning. The framework employs a two-round reasoning strategy to progressively identify surface-level evidence and infer latent harmful implications. Experimental results show consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods across multiple open-source video-language models, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both explicit and implicit harmful short videos.

title: Floating-point, exact and certified computation for control: paradigms, pitfalls, and how to combine them
summary: Many questions in linear systems theory have a discrete answer: is a polynomial Hurwitz, is a 2-D system structurally stable, is the peak gain finite, which solution of a Riccati equation is stabilizing? Algorithms implemented in floating point usually answer such questions, but often with a limited, or even no, guarantee on the result, which depends on a tolerance fixed a priori. Computer algebra and interval arithmetic provide other ways of computing, which give guarantees on the result, but usually at a higher cost. In this paper, we propose a short guide to these approaches: floating-point, exact, multiprecision and interval arithmetic, certified root isolation and certified Newton methods. Using small examples from control theory (each of them runs in a few seconds), we show what each approach guarantees and in which situations it fails, and how several approaches can be combined, for example by certifying a numerical solution, or by reducing a problem exactly before solving it with certified real solving. We then revisit the structural stability of 2-D systems (with and without parameters) and the computation of the $H_\infty$ norm, and we list the available implementations. The main examples are given as reproducible worksheets based on the PACE ecosystem.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
summary: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

title: Technical Debt Risks in AI-Assisted Software Development: Insights from Practitioners
summary: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.

title: Arbor: When Labels Are Not Coarsened at Random
summary: Merging datasets labelled at different levels of a taxonomy leaves some images with only a coarse label, and some classes with no fine-grained label at all. Standard training scores a coarse label by the total probability of the classes under it. Coarse labels name superclasses, and the standard objective is exact only when every class within a superclass is equally likely to receive a coarse label. We call a class novel if it is never labelled finely, and known otherwise. A novel class violates the assumption, and the classifier assigns its images to a known sibling. We propose Arbor, which models how labels become coarse. In each superclass with a novel class, Arbor adds a virtual novel class, and a logistic gate divides the superclass's probability between it and the known classes. The gate is trained with the likelihood of the observed labels under this model, the coarsening likelihood. We prove that at its population optimum the gate equals the Elkan-Noto correction of positive-unlabelled learning, and show that training the correction into the classifier improves on applying it after training. Across Cars, CUB and Aircraft with 90% coarse labels, Arbor correctly assigns 76-85% of novel-class images to their superclass, more than hierarchical classifiers, hierarchical novelty detection and the Elkan-Noto correction. Its top-1 accuracy over the leaf classes on known-class images is within 1.6 points of the best baseline, although its final predictions return the superclass more often. On the more challenging iNaturalist-2019 benchmark, Arbor improves novel-class accuracy from 46% (uniform target, the strongest baseline) to 68%.

title: Influence of Assortativity on the SICP Spreading Process in Hypergraphs
summary: Many real-world systems involve group interactions that cannot be captured by pairwise graphs. They can be better represented by hypergraphs where each hyperedge could connect an arbitrary number of nodes. The Susceptible-Infected Contact Process (SICP) has been proposed to model the spreading of information and epidemics on hypergraphs. However, how higher-order topological properties of a hypergraph influence the SICP spreading process remains understudied. In this paper, we examine the impact of hypergraph assortativity based on the Neighborhood Coefficient (NC)-the average size of hyperedges incident to a node-on the SICP spreading process. By introducing a low-complexity measure of hypergraph assortativity grounded in analysis of variance, we apply hyperdegree-preserving rewirings to real-world networks and synthetic hypergraph models to tune their assortativity. We find and explain why lower NC assortativity yields higher average epidemic prevalence and lower prevalence variance across different seed selections. This phenomenon is evident when hyperdegree-preserving rewirings are applied to real-world networks with heterogeneous topological structures, but it is largely absent when comparing synthetic random hypergraphs to their rewired counterparts.

title: AcrossPlace: Do Vision--Language Models Recognize Places Beyond Their Source Views? A Comprehensive Benchmark
summary: Language-guided place recognition requires recovering geographic identity across visual observations beyond the image from which a description originates. However, aggregate retrieval scores often entangle observation transfer, gallery competition, and linguistic evidence, obscuring the underlying recognition capability. We introduce AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark establishing a systematic evaluation standard for bidirectional language--vision place recognition. Built upon GSV-Cities, AcrossPlace comprises 56,726 places across 23 cities, 156,800 automatically generated, rule-filtered descriptions, and 113,404 target images. Each description retains its source-image provenance, while retrieval operates on disjoint target observations. Text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval share a unified place-identity relevance criterion supporting multiple valid matches. Two geographic protocols evaluate unseen places within represented cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1). Paired observation comparisons, gallery-controlled evaluations, fixed-query scaling, and blinded annotation auditing systematically characterize retrieval performance. Across three training seeds, place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 decreases from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0. For fixed P1 queries, expanding the gallery from 500 to 8,425 places reduces Recall@1 from 14.67% to 2.87%. A 240-description audit further reveals discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence. These findings establish AcrossPlace as a reproducible evaluation standard for assessing transferable place identity across visual observations and geographic environments.

title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models
summary:
Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models.
  MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience.
  On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost.
  Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.

title: IoTPwnBench: A Synthetic Benchmark for IoT Firmware Security Analysis
summary: Building and evaluating security tools for IoT firmware requires targets whose weaknesses are known in ad- vance and can be reproduced in a running device. Two problems remain: (1) firmware collected from real-world products provides realistic software, but hardware dependencies and undocumented defects make it difficult to establish what a security tool should be expected to find; and (2) existing benchmarks typically collect sets of vulnerable or misconfigured firmware images without providing purpose-built vulnerable services with explicit weaknesses that a security analysis tool can target. We present IoTPwnBench, a synthetic, modular benchmark that brings these requirements together. IoTPwnBench contains 716 vulnerable firmware images covering 86 weakness scenarios and 28 CWE classes across 11 device profiles, including industrial controllers, health monitors, and household devices. Each vulnerable image runs a plausible device application with simulated sensors and actuators that generate live readings over its native interfaces while exposing one target weakness mapped to a primary CWE. A documented exploitation payload and observable signal establish the expected behavior independently of the evaluated tool. Every vulnerable image is paired with a corrected twin that preserves the device and service while removing that weakness. Researchers can therefore compare the same target before and after correction to assess detection and false positives for the target weakness. The benchmark produces kernel and filesystem binaries for static inspection and dynamic testing under QEMU. Device profiles and weakness modules remain separate, allowing the same scenario to be reused across device contexts. Vulnerable targets were validated manually, and the open source build workflow regenerates the firmware bit-for-bit.

title: BiPOP: Partial-Order Planning for Long-Horizon Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
summary: Bimanual robotic manipulation is versatile, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills and a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. We propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end to end on the real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. Code: https://github.com/Kchu/BiPOP

title: Delaunay-Based Nearest Neighbor Search with Grid-Accelerated Queries and Parallel Construction
summary: Nearest-neighbor search is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, with applications in distance field computation, surface reconstruction, and point cloud registration. In many graphics applications, data points lie on a surface manifold embedded in 3D space, whereas queries are distributed throughout the surrounding volume, a setting in which spatial partitioning structures such as k-d trees and grids can become inefficient. Dynamic-programming-based nearest-neighbor search (DP-NNS) offers an alternative: it traverses a successor DAG that records the history of incremental Delaunay construction and often outperforms spatial partitioning structures. However, its sequential construction is slow, and naive parallelization degrades query performance, limiting its practical adoption. We accelerate both queries and construction in DP-NNS. For queries, we introduce a grid-based initialization strategy that precomputes valid starting points on the successor DAG, shortening search paths while preserving exactness and enabling a twofold speedup. For construction, we analyze how parallel insertion affects query cost and develop a parallel algorithm that preserves logarithmic expected query cost under stated geometric assumptions. Our parallel construction algorithm achieves a 10x speedup over the sequential baseline while maintaining nearly the same query cost. We further reorder query points to improve cache locality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms widely used libraries in nearest-neighbor query performance.

title: Surface evolution under conformal map and linearized energy-stable parametric finite element methods
summary: In this paper, we aim to develop a linearized, energy-stable, second-order-in-time parametric finite element method without Lagrange multipliers for surface evolution equations on surfaces with or without boundaries, including (volume-preserving) mean curvature flow and surface diffusion. We first reformulate the original equations into a new unified form in which the tangential motion is determined by requiring the flow map to be conformal. Based on this new formulation, we present a family of parametric finite element schemes that employ a linearized Euler or Crank-Nicolson discretization in time. We prove the existence and uniqueness of the resulting linear system, as well as the energy stability of the schemes. Our discrete methods can be applied to general surfaces although the second-order scheme may degenerate to first-order accuracy in certain cases. Numerical results verify the robustness of our method and demonstrate its ability to preserve mesh quality.

title: CaseScope: A Multi-Field Benchmark for Case-Level Pathology Diagnosis with Multimodal LLMs
summary: Pathologists rarely diagnose from a single image: they scan a section at low power for architecture, zoom into selected fields for cytology, and integrate the evidence across views and scales. Pathology benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, mostly ask about one image or require whole-slide pipelines, and the few that show several fields draw nested regions from cancer slides of one public cohort. We introduce CaseScope, a benchmark of diagnosis from several curated fields of one lesion: CaseScope-Teaching, 436 cases from a residency-training image library, reconstructed, de-identified, harmonised against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist wherever an automated pre-review raised a doubt, and CaseScope-Atlas, 800 cases from 88 published atlases (387 of them figure series of one disease), labelled from the captions by two LLMs that must agree. They cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems and pose 4,679 items in six tasks, from open-ended and ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation to the verification and location of morphological findings. Across twenty-eight open and four proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses are unstable -- the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of the teaching cases -- and wrong answers favour the classic look-alike; open models make little use of the additional fields on teaching cases, where the one-line specimen site matters more, although on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields count about as much as the site; and most open models verify findings barely above chance (median 62.0% vs. 50%, best 81.5%), gaining a median +3.4 points from images; proprietary models reach 83.2-93.2%. Rankings broadly replicate between the sources. The evaluation code is available at https://github.com/Wenchuan-Zhang/CaseScope.

title: Vision-Grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment for Scalable Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval
summary: Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval (TBPR) aims to retrieve individuals with texts in multiple languages. Despite its practical importance, it has been overlooked by existing research, which mainly focuses on English-only retrieval. The only prior attempt at multilingual TBPR suffers from (1) the absence of a large-scale, multilingual pretraining dataset and (2) a suboptimal model architecture for multilingual text encoding and cross-modal alignment, which employs a shared encoder that overlooks linguistic heterogeneity and relies on English as a pivot for cross-modal alignment, introducing English-centric bias. For this, we contribute MultiPedes, the first large-scale, pedestrian-centric multilingual pretraining dataset. It contains 10 million image-text pairs across four languages, constructed by a multilingual quality-aware data construction pipeline. We also propose ViSeLA (Vision-grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment), a novel framework featuring: (1) a semantic-aware multilingual learning module that extends the mixture-of-experts architecture by routing language-invariant semantics to specialized experts for improved multilingual feature learning; and (2) a vision-grounded cross-modal alignment module that employs a semantic probe to capture fine-grained semantics across modalities, enabling direct cross-modal alignment without relying on a pivot language. Extensive experiments on both multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/ViSeLA

title: TabOmics: A Small, Open Tabular Foundation Model for Wide Omics Data
summary: Omics studies often produce tables with thousands to tens of thousands of molecular features and few samples. Tabular foundation models use diverse strategies to predict labels for such tables, with some relying on in-context learning, while approaches to wide tables may involve subsampling, grouping, or compressing features. We present TabOmics, a small, open family of tabular foundation models with 7.3M parameters, pretrained exclusively on synthetic tables. TabOmics processes all features retained after preprocessing jointly and derives predictions, attention-derived feature-importance scores, and test sample embeddings from the same forward pass. On 46 classification tasks from three benchmarks of high-dimensional, low-sample-size tables, TabOmics v2.5 with eight ensemble members achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) among the evaluated models (0.943), outperforming TabPFN-3.5 with eight members on 32 tasks despite having about 30 times fewer parameters. With a single member, TabOmics v2.5 reaches a mean AUROC of 0.941, versus 0.942 for TabPFN-3.5 with eight members, with no significant paired difference under the reported task-level analysis. On synthetic tables, its feature-importance scores achieve feature recovery similar to that of TabPFN-Wide, and its predictions remain above chance at 30,000 features. On breast cancer tasks, the top ranked genes include PAM50 genes, which define the subtype labels, indicating concordance with the label definition rather than independent biological validation. The code, model weights, training recipes, and experimental artifacts are publicly available.

title: Numerical solution of the Cauchy problem for second-order evolutionary equations with damped sinusoidal memory
