Our community-based participatory study, conducted across the platform's Discover and Define phases, combines qualitative sessions with doulas and mothers to identify these breakdowns. We close with tensions this approach surfaces and open questions for the workshop about how these findings will inform future participatory AI infrastructure for doula care in rural and other under-resourced communities.
comment: Presented at the CSCW 2026 Workshop on Women's Health as Cooperative Work: Participatory AI Across Care, Community, and Policy (arXiv:2611.03776)

title: The Golden Ratio: EF1 and Ordinal-MMS for Additive Goods
summary: Every complete allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1) guarantees each of the $n$ agents her $1$-out-of-$(2n-1)$ maximin share. Can we construct allocations that satisfy EF1 together with stronger ordinal maximin share guarantees? For additive valuations, we prove that there always exists a complete allocation that is simultaneously EF1 and ($1$-out-of-$\lfloor\varphi n\rfloor$)-MMS, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ is the golden ratio. For bivalued valuations, where each agent may have her own two non-negative values for the goods, we obtain a complete allocation that is simultaneously envy-free up to any good (EFX) and ($1$-out-of-$\lceil(7n-1)/6\rceil$)-MMS.

title: Your Secrets Are Showing: Deep Image Hiding Models Are Surprisingly Easy to Attack
summary: In this work, we ask whether an attacker can go beyond detecting a hidden image and tell what it depicts, even without knowing which model hid it. We show that, for deep image hiding, this is surprisingly easy. To test this, we build an evaluation dataset of stego images generated by 11 hiding models. These models span two families (invertible neural networks and autoencoders), use different backbones (CNN, Transformer, and Mamba), and include both spatial- and frequency-domain hiding methods. We demonstrate that training HiNet [17] in the usual way yields a single decoder that can extract secret content from unseen models across these settings. Both humans and machines can recognize what it reveals. A frequency analysis shows that most models favor mid- and high-frequency embedding. Guided by this finding, we strengthen cross-model extraction by enhancing cover textures and suppressing secret textures during training. The attack extends to out-of-distribution secrets and to multi-image hiding. It even exposes private content hidden by AIRPNet [13], a recent image restoration method that uses steganography for privacy protection. What surprised us most is that decoders from every hiding model we test exhibit this ''universal'' extraction ability to varying degrees. Our code and datasets will be open-sourced.

title: AI4Plasma II: Geometry-Aware Surrogate Modeling for Variable Electrode Gap GEC Plasmas
summary:
Industrial plasma process development requires broad exploration of operating and geometric parameters. Geometric parameters, particularly electrode spacing, affect discharge structure and processing uniformity. Exploring these parameter spaces through repeated high-fidelity simulations can be computationally expensive. Surrogate models can offer rapid predictions, but geometric variation complicates their application because the computational domain and discretization may change across samples.
  In this work, six geometry-aware surrogate models based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates, and geometry-native discretizations are compared in terms of their data requirements for accurate predictions of full plasma fields and ion density profiles near the wafer. The simulation dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency, and electrode gap, with each reference case requiring an average simulation cost of 5.32 CPU h.
  To achieve a 2% mean error across the four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver require 100 training cases, compared with 250-1000 for the other models. Predicting ion density profiles near the wafer is more demanding and reveals larger differences among models, with prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO requiring the fewest training cases for the profile accuracy targets considered. To further reduce the data required for accurate predictions near the wafer, we introduce charge-separation weighting into the training loss, which reduces the prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO's minimum tested training requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases.
  These results support prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO as a practical starting point for the variable-gap problem studied here when a suitable geometry mapping is available, while Transolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy with sufficient training data.

title: Marginal-Preserving Coupled Diffusion Composition for Long-Horizon Planning
summary: Compositional diffusion planners extend short-horizon trajectory models to long-horizon goal-conditioned planning by generating and stitching multiple local trajectory chunks. However, in multimodal environments, local plausibility is not sufficient for global consistency: independently initialized chunks may denoise toward incompatible overlap modes, producing plans that are individually feasible but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies typically add search, guidance, pruning, or graph-based structure at inference time, increasing computational cost or relying on task-specific machinery. We instead investigate graph-structured dependence among chunk-wise initial diffusion noises as a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning. We propose \textbf{M}arginal-Preserving \textbf{C}oupled \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{C}omposition (MCDC), a training-free inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners. Instead of sampling chunk noises independently, MCDC constructs coupled Gaussian initializations whose per-chunk marginals remain exactly standard Gaussian, as required by the pretrained denoiser, while neighboring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. This preserves the standard-Gaussian initialization marginal of each chunk while biasing adjacent chunks toward compatible overlap-mode choices. We prove exact marginal preservation and show, under a simple multimodal overlap model, that positive coupling increases the probability of compatible mode selection. On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling while retaining nearly the same inference time, and achieves a favorable success--cost trade-off compared with search-based composition methods.

title: VWEN: A Curated Small Language Model for Vietnamese Paraphrasing
summary: We present VWEN, a 0.8B-parameter model for Vietnamese paraphrasing at a requested level of change and for five related tasks: generating several paraphrases, simplification, gist, register transfer and paraphrase judgement. VWEN is Qwen3.5-0.8B fine-tuned on about 7k samples chosen by a four-stage pipeline: rules and deduplication, a bidirectional entailment filter, a divergence score that assigns low and high paraphrase levels, and selection for coverage and instruction-following difficulty. We compare it with paraphrase-only recipes from the same pipeline and with training on the ViSP corpus under matched and larger step budgets. On high-divergence paraphrasing, VWEN reaches a success rate (requested level reached and meaning preserved) of 0.61 against 0.46 for the ViSP model at matched compute, a difference that holds on inputs resembling ViSP. Given four times more training examples, the ViSP model closes the gap on such inputs but not on questions, which ViSP lacks and which it often turns into statements. Across all comparisons the entailment filter is the most effective stage. Training on paraphrases alone erases abilities of the base model that the multi-task data preserves.

title: EMS-Nav: Embodied Multi-Scale Navigation
summary: Industrial inspection robots must reach work areas and specific equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.

title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
summary: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.

title: From Isolated Protocols to Integrated Pipelines: Benchmarking IoT Communication in the MASA Living Lab
comments: Accepted for publication at the IEEE 2027 Consumer Communications and Networking Conference; track T3: Testbeds, Experimentation and Datasets for Communications and Networking
summary: The performance of real-time IoT communication systems depends not only on individual transport protocols, serialization formats, and data-processing stages, but also on how these components interact within the complete communication pipeline. Selecting an appropriate communication stack is therefore application-dependent and requires considering processing capabilities, network characteristics, communication patterns, and reliability requirements. This paper provides an experimental, evidence-based analysis of these interactions through a controlled benchmark of integrated communication pipelines deployed in the MASA living lab. We jointly evaluate local processing overhead, end-to-end latency, jitter, throughput, and delivery reliability across different combinations of transport, messaging, serialization, and compression mechanisms. Results show that component-level processing costs do not directly predict end-to-end performance. In particular, differences of only tens of microseconds in serialization or compression costs can coexist with several-millisecond differences in end-to-end latency, while middleware buffering and transport behavior substantially affect timing performance. The results demonstrate that communication-stack components should be evaluated as integrated pipelines and under representative operating loads rather than ranked independently.
comment: Accepted for publication at the IEEE 2027 Consumer Communications and Networking Conference; track T3: Testbeds, Experimentation and Datasets for Communications and Networking

title: Bug Finding With Agentic Symbolic Execution
summary: Symbolic execution, in tools such as CrossHair for Python, is a powerful technique for finding bugs, but two barriers hinder its adoption: the human effort of annotating code with assertions, and the need to model the execution environment outside Python, such as an external database. To overcome both, we design an agentic harness that orchestrates the symbolic execution tool CrossHair together with an AI coding agent. Without human intervention, it instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs symbolic execution, and constructs a concrete test as evidence for each bug it reports. We evaluate our harness on 1,156,044 lines of Python code over 11 popular open-source Python web applications (Zulip, NetBox, Apache Superset, and others). With the synthesized environment, CrossHair executes 81% of the 5,406 contracted functions, against 4.5% without it. Our pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, each reproduced by a test against the unmodified application, 221 of them by CrossHair, and 312 of them are missed by a baseline in which the same LLM inspects the code. The two find different kinds of bugs: CrossHair's are mostly crashes on input-domain corner cases that validation admits, such as empty strings, missing fields and unusual characters, while inspection's are mostly bugs that produce wrong output. Our framework thus lets symbolic execution supplement inspection-based bug finding.

title: When Local Definitions Are Missing: Stable Errors in Language Models
summary: Contracts, technical manuals, and online communities often give familiar words special meanings and define them in one place. A language model that reads a passage without that definition may use the usual meaning and give an answer that sounds right but is wrong. We study this with multiple-choice questions whose correct answers depend on a local definition. The questions come from a synthetic vocabulary, commercial contracts, Reddit community glossaries, and the documentation of a decentralized exchange. We ask three language models each question with and without the definition. Without using the answer key, we then test whether their repeated answers and stated confidence reveal their own errors. Separately, we give a small open model the answer key and test whether it can predict which questions larger models get wrong. We report three findings. (1) Familiar words that a source redefines cause the most errors. Models often repeat the same wrong answer, and neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flag it. (2) The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions, but a definition drawn from the model's own prior knowledge does not. In real contracts, the source definition fixes only about half of the errors. (3) Given an answer key, a small model can rank questions by how likely larger models are to get them wrong. These results call for tests that check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.

title: Imputing Missing Near-Surface Air Temperature using Graph Attention Networks with Distance-Aware Edge Features
summary: We introduce a graph attention network for reconstructing near-surface air temperature fields from incomplete observations. The model represents each grid cell as a node connected to its $k$ nearest neighbors, with attention weights that depend on node features, distance, and land-ocean transitions. This graph representation avoids the polar distortions associated with treating the globe as a flat latitude-longitude image, as most deep learning reconstruction methods do. This is particularly relevant for historical temperature records, which extend back to the mid-nineteenth century but remain incomplete, with the largest gaps early in the record and at high latitudes. We train our model on CMIP6 CESM2 historical simulations masked with the time-varying HadCRUT5 observational coverage from 1850 to 2014. We then compare our approach with ordinary kriging, GraphEM, and the LaMa inpainting network on a held-out realization. The graph model achieves the lowest spatial RMSE (0.997 K), 10.1% lower than LaMa and approximately 31% lower than kriging and GraphEM. The largest gains occur in the Arctic and Antarctic, while LaMa remains slightly more accurate in the densely observed tropics. The graph model's error also falls faster as coverage increases, so its advantage over LaMa grows by more than a third from the 1850s to the 2000s. An ablation study shows that the model's skill comes mainly from the geometric graph construction rather than from auxiliary physical covariates.

title: MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

title: Cat Royale Comprehensive Dataset: A Dataset for Pose Detection, Segmentation, Animal Action Recognition and Scene Understanding
comments: 26 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Computer Vision. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19498943
summary: Animal focused computer vision datasets are of a growing interest in the fields of both Computer Vision and Animal behaviour. The ability to make sense of complex scenes via a variety of Computer Vision tasks has substantial implications for behavioural understanding and welfare. The perfection of these tasks will help lead to better health and emotional outcomes for wild and domestic animals. In this work we present the Cat Royale Comprehensive Dataset (CRCD), a large, comprehensive, multi-modal dataset for feline understanding, based on a huge database of over 500 hours of video captured during the Cat Royale artwork and research project. Our dataset contains annotations for a range of computer vision problems including 20,000 images with instance segmentation masks, 5000 images with multi-subject pose coordinates, over 800 video clips with action classes, and over 800 clips with detailed text description. This is the first such dataset to link this wide range of annotation types together for multi-modal use. We release this entire dataset, and our custom annotation tools will also be made available, in order to allow for ongoing expansion. We also provide a series of benchmarks for the tasks of Instance Segmentation, Pose detection, Temporal Action Localisation, and finally video-text retrieval. The totality of this multi-modal dataset is the data needed to solve both these individual computer vision tasks as well as enabling more complex multi-modal tasks making use of a combination of annotations.
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Computer Vision. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19498943

title: CoCode-World: Shared 3D Proxy Representation for Multi-Player World Models
summary: Multiplayer generative world models must produce observations that agree on shared entities despite different camera motions and occlusions. Explicit world representations provide spatial control, but precise modeling of individual game maps limits scene diversity, while shared geometry alone cannot ensure consistent appearance across views. We present CoCode-World, a shared 3D proxy framework that separates structural control from visual synthesis for two-player video generation. Programmable proxies specify scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references guide character and scene appearance. To coordinate visual details across players, we concatenate paired proxy videos, appearance references, and target views in a consistent spatial layout and generate both views jointly with a pretrained video model. This formulation uses the model's native attention for cross-view communication within a single generation branch, with LoRA adaptation learning proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations. We construct a two-player GTA~V dataset that pairs synchronized RGB observations with proxy videos derived from shared map geometry and game-engine state. Experiments demonstrate appearance transfer to characters and scene styles unseen during training, with improvements in video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline. Ablations further examine how proxy construction and cross-view communication affect generation. Project page: https://iapple233.github.io/CCW/.

title: Are Scaling Laws of Universal MLIPs Universal?
summary: Neural scaling laws enable the prediction of returns from larger training datasets, but machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) datasets are heterogeneous and expensive to generate, and equal numbers of structures need not contain equal amounts of useful information. We study data scaling under fixed model configurations for M3GNet, MACE, and PET trained on subsets of a combined MatPES-MP-ALOE training pool. Across training structure subsets from 10,000 to 640,000, together with the full 1.16-million-structure training set, we compare uniform random sampling, three chemistry- and structure-informed stratification policies, iterative DIRECT, and furthest-point sampling using embeddings from three pretrained MLIPs. Models are evaluated using cohesive-energy, force, stress, and aggregate losses on both a held-out test set from the parent distribution and the distribution shifted MP-r$^2$SCAN test set. We observe power-law scaling improvements with increasing data, but the fitted scaling exponent, apparent error floor, and relative sample efficiency depend on the model architecture, target quantity, data sampling policy, and test set distribution. Sampling-policy rankings can reverse across test distributions: chemical stratification can improve cross-dataset performance while degrading in-distribution performance, whereas the embedding-space diversity policies frequently under-perform random sampling. Relative loss is strongly associated with test-to-train chemical-space divergence. These results show that structure count is a necessary but insufficient scaling variable for MLIPs. For training MLIPs, the return on additional first-principles calculations depends not only on how many additional structures are included, but also on how their chemical and configurational content aligns with the model's intended use.

title: FADO: Learning Causal Explanations with Prior-Fitted Networks
summary: In regression and classification tasks with tabular datasets, most of the literature on explanation in ML (e.g. SHAP, permutation importance) has focused on predictive attribution: does feature $X_i$ help predict outcome $Y$? At its heart, predictive attribution captures correlation, not causation. We instead ask a causal question: would manipulating feature $X_i$ change outcome $Y$? We define a natural quantity to answer this question, the feature intervention effect: $Δ_i = E[Y\mid do(X_i=+1)]-E[Y\mid do(X_i=-1)]$. In general, estimating this quantity from observational data alone would entail strong causal assumptions. We propose FADO (Feature-wise Amortized Do-Operators), an amortized inference method using prior-fitted networks trained on synthetic tabular datasets generated by structural causal models. During training, the synthetic data-generating process is known, so we can compute ground-truth intervention effects $Δ_i$, and train a model to predict them at test time from a purely observational tabular dataset. As we demonstrate through extensive experiments, our new causal explainability method is easy to train and provides better explanations under a range of settings for which standard predictive attribution fails, including proxy variables, confounders, colliders, and placebos. We evaluate it on real, synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets, with and without hidden confounders, and compare it to existing predictive attribution methods and state-of-the-art causal inference methods.

title: GLCR: Global-Local Collaborative Routing for Multi-Task Electromagnetic Signal Processing
comments: 13 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Code available at https://github.com/Dawn-try/GLCR
summary: Deep neural networks for electromagnetic signal processing are typically developed as single-task experts with fixed inputs and objectives, limiting cross-task transferability. Electromagnetic foundation models offer broader task coverage but incur substantial pretraining and inference costs. To balance accuracy and efficiency, we adopt model routing to dynamically dispatch unknown signals to matched experts within a heterogeneous pool. We construct HeteroSignal-7, a multi-task routing benchmark with 140,000 samples from seven datasets covering six task types, paired with seven classification and waveform-recovery experts and a unified evaluation protocol. We then propose GLCR, a two-stage routing method combining global dispatch with local discrimination of similar tasks. First, a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) with an additive-margin head predicts one of seven routing classes. Second, a gradient-boosted-tree specialist uses four physical statistics to re-evaluate samples whose top two candidates match a confusion pair automatically identified from validation errors. The pipeline is trained across the full signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) range and requires neither SNR labels nor noise estimation at inference time. GLCR outperforms all 19 baselines, achieving 96.16% routing accuracy and a 76.30% system score, exceeding the respective second-best baselines by 1.16% and 1.14%. It achieves the lowest routing latency among the compared methods at 1.43 ms per sample and reduces expected overall system FLOPs by 5.9 times compared with executing all experts. This work provides a public evaluation platform and an efficient, reproducible baseline for heterogeneous expert routing in electromagnetic signal processing.
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Code available at https://github.com/Dawn-try/GLCR

title: Contrastive Bootstrap Representation Learning for Label-Efficient Agricultural Image Classification
summary: Expert annotation remains a major bottleneck in agricultural image classification, where collecting images is often easier than obtaining reliable labels from domain specialists. Self-supervised learning can reduce this dependence by pretraining transferable representations on unlabelled imagery. Contrastive and bootstrap methods provide two established but distinct training signals, motivating an empirical study of a formulation that applies both signals within one representation path under severe downstream label scarcity. We present Contrastive Bootstrap Representation Learning (CBRL), which jointly optimises SimCLR-style NT-Xent contrastive learning and bidirectional BYOL-style exponential-moving-average target prediction within a shared online projection space. Using a ViT-L/16 backbone and 10% of the downstream labels, we report single-seed point estimates on four primary agricultural test benchmarks plus an exploratory 33-image New Plant Diseases evaluation. CBRL records the highest macro-F1 point estimate on the four primary benchmarks. On DeepWeeds, its 79.77% test macro-F1 is 32.29 points above the random-initialisation, label-only baseline and 15.78 points above the next-highest comparison point estimate; on PlantVillage, its 98.14% macro-F1 is 10.43 and 0.43 points higher, respectively. On PlantDoc, however, all methods fail to reach practically useful performance. These results identify the evaluated joint formulation as a promising candidate for label-limited transfer, but they do not establish objective synergy, statistical superiority, or robustness across stochastic runs.

title: Learning-Based Interpolation of Detector Gaps in Photon-Counting X-ray Imaging
summary: Image detectors assembled from tiled modules have physical gaps in the field of view that must be filled before downstream processing such as phase retrieval or tomographic reconstruction. Unlike natural-image inpainting, detector-gap interpolation must leave all other pixels unmodified and preserve the intensity statistics of the filled region, since even a small shift in mean intensity can cause ring artifacts after reconstruction. We adapted two generative models, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) and a conditional Pix2Pix model, to this task. We implemented a masking strategy that restricts all changes to the gap pixels and loss terms that constrain the mean intensity and the intensity distribution of the filled region. Both models were trained on nanoCT projections with simulated gaps and compared with linear interpolation, Navier--Stokes inpainting, and the deep image-inpainting network MADF, quantitatively on simulated gaps and visually on real detector gaps. WGAN-GP and Pix2Pix achieved the best perceptual similarity (LPIPS) and histogram distance and, apart from linear interpolation, the shortest inference time. Pix2Pix required about five times fewer training GPU-hours than WGAN-GP. Ablation studies showed that masking the network output contributes by far the most to plausible inpainting results. Applied to sinograms, Pix2Pix produced the most natural gap filling but improved the reconstruction only slightly compared with linear interpolation. The source code and the weights of the final Pix2Pix model are available at https://github.com/J-3TO/detectorGapRemoval_Pix2Pix.

title: A Parallel Greedy Algorithm for Maximal b-Matching in Hypergraphs
comments: 19 pages. Accepted to the SIAM Conference on Applied and Computational Discrete Algorithms (ACDA 2027)
summary: We present \parallelBatchBMatch, a parallel batch-vote algorithm for maximal $b$-matching in hypergraphs. The algorithm is deterministic for a given ordering of edges and produces the same output as the sequential greedy algorithm, i.e., the lexicographically first maximal $b$-matching. Under a uniformly random priority order it performs $O(m')$ expected work in the binary fork--join model, where $m'$ is the number of pins, the total number of vertex--edge incidences. The algorithm performs at most $m$ rounds for every priority order, where $m$ is the number of edges. Every round of the algorithm has $O(\log^2 m')$ depth with high probability, and thus the total depth of the algorithm is $O(m \log^2 m')$ with high probability. We implement the parallel algorithm in CUDA and evaluate it on real-world hypergraphs with capacities $b \in \{1, 3, 5\}$. The parallel algorithm computes the same matchings as the greedy algorithms and for the case of $b = 5$ it is up to $19.07$ times faster than the existing state-of-the art greedy algorithm.
comment: 19 pages. Accepted to the SIAM Conference on Applied and Computational Discrete Algorithms (ACDA 2027)

title: WaveletLoRA: Frequency-Aware Content-Style Decomposition for Personalized Image Generation
summary: Content-style decomposition from a single image is a fundamental challenge in personalized image generation, aiming to separate subject identity from visual style for flexible recomposition. Existing approaches primarily operate in the spatial domain, without explicitly exploiting the distinct frequency characteristics naturally associated with content and style. In this paper, we propose WaveletLoRA, a novel frequency-aware framework for explicit content-style decomposition through wavelet-domain supervision. Specifically, we first apply a multi-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to decompose the reference image into low-frequency and high-frequency subbands. We then assign a dedicated LoRA branch to each subband, where the low-frequency branch models global appearance for style acquisition, while the high-frequency branches capture structural details for content preservation. To further improve disentanglement quality, we introduce a dense Mixture-of-Experts aggregation module together with a frequency-domain regularization objective, which reduces style leakage and enhance content fidelity. In addition, we establish WaveBench and develop a VLM-based evaluation protocol that explicitly measures both attribute similarity and attribute separation for disentanglement assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WaveletLoRA consistently outperforms existing methods and produces results that better align with human preference.

title: Data-Free Metrics Don't Work: The Missing Invariance Under Functionally Preserving Reparameterisations
comments: NeurIPS 2026 (Negative Results Track), 44 pages, 21 figures and 18 tables
summary: Data-free methods for analysing and understanding the layers of neural networks offer many metrics for quantifying notions of 'strong' versus 'weak' layers, with the promise of increased interpretability. In particular, random matrix theory (RMT) offers data-free metrics that claim predictive power over the quality of pre-trained models at a layerwise precision and the ability to identify model pathologies, indicating a unique relationship with generalisation. As a result, metrics from RMT are championed for pre-training optimisation strategies and post-training compression. We establish that RMT-based metrics are unrelated to performance or training by showing that functionally preserving reparametrisations of a pre-trained model can have arbitrary metrics. We show this across a range of architectures and scales. To create functionally preserving reparametrisations, we exploit the well-established phenomenon of criticality: some layers can be re-initialised or re-randomised without affecting the functional behaviour of the model -- they are called robust -- while others cannot -- they are called critical. Re-initialising or re-randomising robust layers provides functionally preserving reparametrisations for which RMT-based metrics are arbitrary. Moreover, we show that relationships between metrics offered by RMT are spuriously related to generalisation. We conclude by showing that if many pre-trained models have data-free metrics in a 'good' range, it is, in part, dependent on model initialisation. Project page available at: https://gmw99.github.io/data-free-metrics-dont-work
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Negative Results Track), 44 pages, 21 figures and 18 tables

title: Quota-Based Traffic Classification for Bounded Jitter in Multi-CQF under Redundancy Mechanisms
comments: 6 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: The demand for deterministic and reliable communication is rapidly increasing in industrial networks. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) addresses these requirements through deterministic scheduling and redundancy mechanisms such as Multiple Cyclic Queuing and Forwarding (Multi-CQF) and Frame Replication and Elimination for Reliability (FRER). Multi-CQF guarantees bounded end-to-end (E2E) latency and jitter, while FRER provides seamless fault tolerance through redundant forwarding. With static traffic classification, redundant paths with different hop counts can exhibit different E2E latency ranges. This can amplify jitter when a failure causes packets to be delivered over a longer redundant path. To address this, we propose a quota-based traffic classification mechanism that adapts class assignments hop-by-hop using a common E2E latency budget derived from the primary path, thereby mitigating jitter amplification. Simulation results show that the proposed mechanism reduces jitter amplification by up to 70% and latency degradation by up to 41% compared to static classification.
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

title: Decentralised model predictive control of recurrent neural network models
summary: This work proposes a decentralised nonlinear model predictive control algorithm for systems described by input-coupled recurrent neural network models. The proposed approach exploits closed-loop incremental input-to-state stability to design the local controllers and provide robustness to subsystem couplings. The resulting control scheme guarantees asymptotic convergence to a desired equilibrium while satisfying input and output constraints. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the proposed approach.

title: An Empirical Square-Root Law for the Degree Discrepancy of Binary m-Sequences
comments: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/fv2fm2z7rk-droid/An-Empirical-Square-Root-Law-for-the-Degree-Discrepancy-of-Binary-m-Sequences (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24139931)
summary: Let $k\ge 2$, $N=2^k$, $M=N-1$ and let $Δ(r)$ be the range, over all starting offsets, of the total-variation degree discrepancy of a length-$r$ window of a primitive binary linear feedback shift register (LFSR) of period $M$. Degree-discrepancy profiles for every $k\le 28$ support the scaling $\max_r Δ(r)=Θ(\sqrt{N})=Θ(2^{k/2})$. The tabulated peaks are maxima on a discrete grid, hence lower bounds on the exhaustive maximum. The normalized peaks $d_k=\max_{r\in R_k}Δ(r)/2^{k/2}$ oscillate between values near 1/2 and values that approach, but do not exceed, 1. The data suggest $\liminf d_k=1/2$ and $\limsup d_k\le 1$. We conjecture the same square-root law for the exhaustive maximum, with those normalized envelopes. A Brownian-bridge heuristic accounts for the square-root scale. The same profiles do not place the recorded maximizer at mid-path: after folding by the complement identity $Δ(M-r)=Δ(r)$, the median of $\min(ρ^*_k,1-ρ^*_k)$ is 0.35, and several $k$ (notably 16 and 28) peak on a short window. Mid-horizon $Δ$ remains a large fraction of the peak, so the square-root scale can still come from a Brownian-bridge envelope. The same range has two readings of the starting offset: a pairing fragment in serial-knockout scheduling, and a change to the plaintext on an LFSR orbit. The location of the maximizer is not part of the conjecture. Open questions that separate the conjecture from a theorem are listed.
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/fv2fm2z7rk-droid/An-Empirical-Square-Root-Law-for-the-Degree-Discrepancy-of-Binary-m-Sequences (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24139931)

title: Helping Hand: A Continuum Robotic Grasper for Traction in Single-Channel Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection
summary: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is a minimally invasive approach for removing large polyps from the colon and offers many benefits compared to other surgical approaches. However, ESD is technically very challenging to perform, leading to limited adoption by physicians. We propose the Helping Hand, a two-segment continuum robotic grasper that, together with an electrosurgical knife, enables tissue traction and cutting within a single 3.7 mm working channel. We achieve this functionality by creating a slot at the base of the Helping Hand that lets the electrosurgical knife extend out, enabling countertraction and cutting through one instrument lumen. We evaluate the Helping Hand's workspace and its ability to provide traction forces from different starting configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the full workflow by isolating and removing tissue in an ex vivo chicken thigh, illustrating the potential for the Helping Hand to help improve ESD procedures.

title: ChJGBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Legal Judgment Generation with Diagnostic Evaluation
comments: 25 pages, 3 figures. Published in EMNLP 2026 (main conference)
summary: With the rapid development of LLMs, increasing attention has been paid to whether they can reliably generate complete and legally valid judicial documents. This calls for a benchmark capable of evaluating whether models can accurately apply statutes and resolve outcome-critical issues, including claims, charges, penalties, and monetary obligations. However, existing benchmarks typically focus on isolated legal tasks or coarse-grained evaluation. We introduce ChJGBench, a benchmark for generating the reasoning and dispositive sections of Chinese judgments across civil, criminal, and administrative cases. Built from 3,462 real-world judgments, ChJGBench provides a case-type-aware diagnostic evaluation framework comprising 13 metric types and adopts a hybrid paradigm. Experiments reveal no uniform advantage for legal-domain models over general-purpose models, with model strengths varying across diagnostic dimensions. Performance is generally stronger on criminal cases, while civil and administrative cases continue to present substantial challenges.
comment: 25 pages, 3 figures. Published in EMNLP 2026 (main conference)

title: MemInStream: Memorizing or Merely Recognizing? Rethinking Streaming Video Memory Evaluation
summary: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.

title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions
comments: 15 pages; supplementary material (10 pages) is provided as an ancillary file
summary: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and draws the contour lines they imply. The contour map decomposes the evaluated region into peaks: in two dimensions a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, and in more dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates the peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. A memory of the explored peaks directs the search to new ones. The data-supported contours of each peak are extrapolated to zero size by an area law, exact for quadratic peaks and second-order accurate for smooth ones, that estimates a peak's location, height and shape before it is sampled. A contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) inserts contour steps with local search and peak memory into a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution or particle swarm optimization. A contour-assisted surrogate-assisted EA (CA-SAEA), for expensive problems, spends each evaluation on surrogate-screened offspring or on sampling around a peak, entered at the maximum of the interpolated surface. On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces the evaluations a plain GA needs by factors of 12 to 112; controls attribute its gain over classical memetic search to restarting local search on distinct peaks. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank, behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and the competition winner MVMO, although in 30 dimensions MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions and loses on 6; there the map beats sampling around the best point on 5 of 15 functions and loses on 3. Entering the peaks at their extrapolated locations brought no gain at these budgets, although, with enough samples, it improves the estimated heights on most two-dimensional functions.
comment: 15 pages; supplementary material (10 pages) is provided as an ancillary file

title: Differential Backpack Language Models: Sense Inhibition via Signed Contextualization Weights
summary: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

title: When Agents Need to Consolidate Memories: What RRR Consolidation Explains, and What It Does Not Explain, in Conversation ESAA
comments: 8 pages, 4 tables. Code, synthetic data and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/elzobrito/conversation-esaa-rrr-artifacts
summary: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
comment: 8 pages, 4 tables. Code, synthetic data and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/elzobrito/conversation-esaa-rrr-artifacts

title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
summary: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

title: Single-View RGB-D Force--Deformation Estimation for Robotic Manipulation of Elasto-Plastic Materials
summary: Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes. We investigate the force--deformation relationship using a standard robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates. A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume. Force--volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on 52 force--volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and $R^2=0.440$. A separate comparison shows lower error for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N. An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward. These results establish a practical measurement basis for deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates and single-view geometry.

title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
summary: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.

title: Taming Neural Fields with a Frequency-Lipschitz Curriculum for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
summary: Sparse-view computed tomography (SVCT) reduces radiation dose by acquiring fewer projection views, but the resulting under-determined inverse problem requires careful regularization to prevent reconstruction algorithms from fitting streak artifacts and hallucinated structures. Existing implicit neural representation (INR) methods rely on implicit spectral bias or iterative external denoising, yet they provide limited control over when high-frequency capacity is exposed during optimization. To address this limitation, we propose FLIC (Frequency-Lipschitz INR Curriculum), a capacity-controlled self-prior INR framework that makes the network's representational capacity explicit and schedulable. The core of our method is a joint frequency-Lipschitz curriculum that couples random Fourier feature encoding with spectrally normalized MLP decoding under non-uniform Lipschitz budgets, guiding reconstruction along a coarse-to-fine trajectory from stable global anatomy to fine details. The terminal capacity is automatically calibrated from FBP gradient statistics, enabling scan-adaptive regularization without per-scan manual tuning of the terminal Lipschitz budget. We further introduce a prior-guided adaptive ray sampling strategy that concentrates integration samples near high-gradient anatomical boundaries, improving forward-model fidelity. The entire framework operates in a single training stage without iterative denoising, enabling efficient per-image reconstruction. Extensive experiments on four public CT datasets under noise-free and low-dose settings show that our method achieves state-of-the-art unsupervised reconstruction quality with consistent performance across diverse anatomical structures.

title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. A condensed version was selected for an oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery
summary: Foundation models are increasingly used across the sciences, but whether their internal computations correspond to known scientific operations or proceed through different mechanisms remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for assessing reliability, identifying failure modes, and learning new science from the models. We present, to our knowledge, the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on its multimodal advantage in redshift prediction, where combining imaging with photometry outperforms photometry alone. We find that this advantage is largest for spatially extended and dust-attenuated galaxies, and that most of it is localized to the first of the encoder's twelve blocks. Within that block, how well a property is linearly decodable does not predict whether it can be localized. Spatial extent is causally used, and one attention head dominates linear probing for it, yet ablating that head has negligible effect on redshift prediction: the information is distributed across heads and is decodable again one layer after we erase it. Dust attenuation shows the opposite pattern: it is only weakly decodable anywhere in the encoder, yet a single head is necessary for most of the multimodal advantage, particularly for the most dust-attenuated galaxies, and keeping that head as the only active head in its block preserves nearly all of the advantage. None of the astrophysically motivated operations we tested explains what this head computes. Whether this reflects a limitation of current interpretability methods or a computation that does not correspond to any known astrophysical operation remains open, and resolving it is a prerequisite for using interpretability as a tool for scientific discovery.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. A condensed version was selected for an oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery

title: Can Agents Relive Past Experiences? Diagnosing Event-Affect Decoupling in Affective-Episodic Retrospection
summary: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/A412/.

title: Embedded Sim-to-Real Visual Servoing: Learned Reaching and Force-Guided Placement
summary: Embedded perception-to-control systems must combine visual targeting with reliable contact handling under tight computational constraints. We present a shared architecture on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin controlling a Franka Research 3 through Cartesian impedance control. RealSense D435i observations, YOLO11-seg segmentation, depth back-projection, and hand--eye calibration provide metric robot-frame targets. We compare two strategies: compact proximal policy optimization (PPO) policies transferred from simulation for object- and hole-region reaching, and force-guided Cartesian placement using approximately 2 N normal contact and spiral search. The PPO policies achieved 87.2% and 83.1% success over 1000 simulation episodes each. Across 50 real-robot trials per strategy, the learned hybrid and force-guided analytical pipelines achieved 70.0% and 74.0% completion, respectively. Mean perception latency with TensorRT was 34.55 ms. These results support an embedded architecture combining learned free-space reaching with explicit contact correction.

title: GraSLA: A Lightweight Spatial-Language-Action Model with Grasp Hypotheses as Geometric Priors
summary: This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning. Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity. For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments. This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors. In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction. On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.

title: ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard
summary:
Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked.
  We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.

title: Beyond Reweighting: Certified Improvements from New Transitions in Discrete MCMC
summary: Optimizing transition probabilities on a fixed grap may leave substantial limitations on the efficiency of reversible Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). We develop a framework for transition-support design that considers both allowed transitions and their stationary flows. For a fixed target distribution, observable, and node-flow budget, we derive a necessary and sufficient dual condition for support augmentation to strictly reduce the optimal value of the asymptotic variance, together with computable primal--dual certificates that establish improvements over every admissible original-support reweighting. We also construct a family in which adding a single edge reduces integrated autocorrelation time by an $Ω(n)$ factor relative to optimal original-support weighting, demonstrating that structural limitations can impose arbitrarily large relative losses in estimation efficiency. To realize these gains, we investigate energy-informed edge selection and constrained stationary-flow optimization. Experiments on molecular and Ising state graphs distinguish the potential value of new transitions from the performance of kernels constructed on them: on identical augmented Ising supports, full weight optimization certifies strict improvements in 24/24 conditions, whereas degree-based Metropolis--Hastings weighting certifies none. Our results provide a principled approach to characterizing, certifying, and exploiting transition-support improvements in explicitly represented finite state spaces.

title: Online Vertex Connectivity Augmentation
summary:
Network design problems form a classic subfield of online algorithms, but almost nothing is known about their more challenging vertex-connectivity variants. We initiate the study of online vertex-connectivity network design for arbitrary demand pairs by considering the fundamental problem of connectivity augmentation.
  In an instance of \emph{Online Vertex Connectivity Augmentation} (OVCA), we are given a $k$-vertex-connected graph $F$ and a set of additional purchasable edges (with costs). Demand pairs $(s_1,t_1),(s_2,t_2),\dots$ then arrive online. Upon each arrival, the algorithm must irrevocably purchase edges so that $s_i$ and $t_i$ become $(k{+}1)$-vertex-connected in the union of $F$ with all edges purchased so far.
  Our main contribution is an $O((k+\log n)\log n)$-competitive online algorithm for OVCA. We also give an offline $O(k+\log n)$-approximation algorithm. We obtain our algorithms via a structural dichotomy on the minimum vertex cuts of $F$.
  We note that some dependence on $k$ in the approximation ratio is necessary -- i.e., the problem is hard to approximate within any $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factor independent of $k$ -- which shows a separation from the edge-connectivity setting.
  Finally, specializing to $k=1$, our methods yield the first polylogarithmic-competitive online algorithm for a vertex-connectivity survivable network design problem, namely an $\widetilde O(\log^3 n)$-competitive algorithm for online $\{1,2\}$-VC-SNDP (i.e., an SNDP variant where each demand pair comes with a vertex-connectivity requirement of $1$ or $2$).

title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models
summary: A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different server instance, it may change how requests are batched, and on some stacks the library selects a different kernel depending only on which packages import. We measure each of these sources on the same 2,400 public decisions for two of Cloudflare's decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B), on an NVIDIA GB10, and state every quantization effect as the excess over them. Sources that are not quantization move between 0 and 0.92% of decisions. llama.cpp restarts are bit-identical on every record for both models. vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef; a third instance of Clef's quantized builds (exploratory) leaves FP8 at 0 and puts NVFP4 at 4 to 22, depending on which two instances are compared. An engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16, a batch-size change 8 to 15, and the Gated DeltaNet kernel transformers selects unasked 10 to 14. Quantization inside one engine moves more: for Clef-flash and Clef, 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4. On both models, every 4-bit interval excludes every non-quantization source. Two of our five pre-registered predictions failed, and the same two fail when the tests are rerun on the 27B: FP8 is not inside restart noise, and changing engine moves fewer decisions than 8-bit quantization does. Accuracy hides most of this. Over the full 31,275 public questions, Clef's Q4_K_M build moves accuracy by a net six questions (-0.02 points [-0.20, +0.16]) while 436 of its decisions get worse (exploratory), and NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 points and Clef 0.65. We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration.

title: Optimal-Time Independent Subset Sampling over Acyclic Joins
summary: Join results can greatly exceed their inputs even when applications need only a small random subset. We study sampling that includes each result independently with a prescribed probability given by the product of its input-tuple weights (PRODUCT). For fixed full acyclic joins with static weights, we achieve input-linear preprocessing and index space together with output-linear expected sampling work, eliminating logarithmic factors from previous bounds. A shared join-tree index supports weighted draws over the entire join and locates high-probability results. Direct Bernoulli trials handle high-probability results, allowing Poisson thinning to generate the remaining independent inclusion decisions with bounded overhead. Our exact sampler uses expected $O(N)$ preprocessing, $O(N)$ index space, and expected $O(1+mμ)$ time per call including output construction. Here $N$ is the input size, $m$ counts relation occurrences, and $μ$ is the expected sample size. The guarantees hold on a real random-access machine with unit-cost exact arithmetic and logarithms, continuous uniform randomness, and expected-time hashing. The time bounds are optimal, matching input reading and explicit output writing. Our floating-point prototype has lower sampling latency than the fastest applicable baseline in 17 of 18 PRODUCT settings on three queries over the STATS benchmark. Construction savings on large joins can offset indexed materialization's faster sampling over a limited number of calls. On a real-data path at $μ=100$, our sampler achieves a $20.5\times$ speedup over indexed materialization for construction plus 300 calls, measured after common data preparation and loading.

title: Newton's Method and Policy Iterations for Viscous Hamilton--Jacobi Equations
summary: We study Newton's method for the Cauchy problem for viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equations with Hamiltonians that need not be convex. Each Newton step solves a linear parabolic equation obtained by linearizing the equation at the current iterate. We prove that the iterates converge geometrically in \(L^\infty\) from any initial guess satisfying the initial condition, and quadratically in the parabolic Hölder space \(C^{2+α,1+α/2}\) from initial guesses close to the solution. When the Hamiltonian admits a control representation, the Newton iterates coincide with those of classical policy iteration, which therefore inherits both convergence rates. We extend the local quadratic convergence to uniformly parabolic fully nonlinear equations. For small viscosity, we introduce a Nash--Moser variant that smooths the iterate and the residual in space, and we give a convergence criterion with constants independent of the viscosity. Finally, we show how computable residuals certify the error of inexact Newton corrections computed with physics-informed neural networks.

title: SpaceMCP: Vision Language Model Spatial Reasoning via Model Context Protocol
comments: 13 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) at NeurIPS 2026

title: Energy Aware Optimization of Non-Deterministic Task-Based Intermittent Computing Nodes with Thimble
summary: Intermittent computing nodes run on harvested energy, which they store in capacitors and spend in short bursts of computation. Choosing those capacitors is a trade-off: large capacitors can power large tasks but leak more current, wasting harvested energy, while small capacitors leak less but cannot power large tasks. Recent work, LEACS, showed that selecting capacitors and mapping tasks to them at compile time improves inference throughput. However, LEACS optimizes the mapping for a predetermined workload, whereas sensor nodes often run data-dependent workloads in which the next task depends on the outcome of earlier ones. We present Thimble, an energy storage system that maps a node's tasks to capacitors at runtime. Thimble models the workload as a Markov chain over tasks and assigns each task to a capacitor by weighing capacitor leakage, the task's energy demand and, when it replans, the likelihood of each future task. We compare Thimble against a reimplementation of LEACS, which ranks every static plan by simulation. When the training trace resembles deployment, Thimble's single design-time solve comes within 0.3--4% of LEACS's throughput. When the deployment conditions drift from the characteristics of the training set, LEACS's throughput-focused static plans can fail sharply. On the lowest-power source we consider, LEACS's plan stalls on deployment traces that harvest less than its training trace, and on some never wakes; Thimble avoids this, with 22--29% higher throughput at the reference workload. A sensitivity sweep over 25 workload profiles on that source shows that Thimble with depth replanning leads LEACS by 22--42% throughout, and what run-time remapping adds: replanning at a fixed interval matches or improves on the static map at 21 of 25 points, by up to 7%.

title: Integrating Slides, Mathematics, and Simulation in One Page: GenAI-Assisted HTML Learning Objects for Engineering Courses
summary: Engineering courses spread their materials across slides (PPTX), typeset notes (LaTeX/PDF), and MATLAB, leaving students to connect them. We describe an instructor-in-the-loop workflow in which generative AI (GenAI) converts these assets into single-file HTML learning objects that combine presentation, mathematics, visualization, simulation, and assessment; a page is released only after its simulations pass numerical verification. Six open demonstrators implement 18 tasks from six engineering courses. In the eight tasks with quantitative cross-checks, every quantity met its tolerance at default settings (1\%, or 2\% for the finite-difference time-domain simulation) and agreed with a separate Python re-computation and a value-blinded MATLAB re-computation run by a colleague not involved in development; the checks also flagged under-resolved settings. In a perception survey, students (19 after post-hoc screening of 28 responses) reported that the pages linked equations with simulation, and 74\% preferred them to separate files, but usability was marginal (System Usability Scale 56.8). Twelve lecturers rated the approach as useful (item means 4.25--4.58) but were hesitant to adopt it; their median ratings on a 12-criterion capability rubric agreed moderately with the first author's ($κ_w=0.60$; individual median 0.31). The results show technical feasibility and preliminary positive perceptions; learning outcomes were not measured.

title: Algebraic coarsening of hierarchical splines with guaranteed error control
summary: We present a purely algebraic coarsening operator for hierarchical spline spaces, obtained by inverting locally the refinement matrix that relates the coarsened basis to the current one. Only the B-splines that interact with the coarsened region are involved, so that a coarsening step reduces to one small least-squares problem followed by explicit corrections of the surviving coefficients, without mass matrices or numerical quadrature. The operator is a left inverse of the refinement matrix, hence exact whenever the fine spline belongs to the coarse space, and leaves the spline unchanged away from the coarsened region. The residual of the least-squares problem bounds the $L^\infty$-error with no unknown constants and is available before the mesh is modified, which yields an adaptive multi-level algorithm that guarantees a prescribed tolerance. The construction carries over to truncated hierarchical B-splines, where the corrections disappear. In numerical experiments, the bound is sharp within an order of magnitude, the local transfer is nearly as accurate as a global $L^2$-projection, and much of the refinement left behind a moving front is removed without degrading the solution.

title: A posteriori space error estimates for the finite element approximation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations based on the variational multiscale framework
summary: This study introduces a novel a posteriori space error estimator derived within the variational multiscale (VMS) framework for the stationary incompressible Navier-Stokes equations.
