In this framework, the continuous problem is decomposed into coarse and fine scales. The fine scale, often referred to as the sub-grid scale (SGS), is modeled as proportional to the component of the residual orthogonal to the finite element (FE) space. This modeled SGS then serves as a reliable error estimator. Specifically, the approach employs a scaled norm of the SGSs as an a posteriori error estimate, evaluated within the stabilized norm associated with the problem. This methodology was previously applied to the stationary convection-diffusion-reaction equation (Codina et al., 2025) and is now extended to the stationary incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. The accuracy and robustness of the proposed space error estimator are assessed through a series of numerical experiments on both manufactured and benchmark incompressible flow problems. Additionally, its performance is compared in selected cases with the space error estimator proposed by Irisarri and Hauke (2021).

title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
comments: Accepted in CoRL 2026 Workshop on Do Robots Need World Models
summary: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.
comment: Accepted in CoRL 2026 Workshop on Do Robots Need World Models

title: Transversal Passivity and Equilibrium Forces in Formation Control
summary: We consider controller synthesis for distance-constrained formations, aiming to stabilize the target formation manifold while sustaining admissible equilibrium edge forces. Using the newly introduced notion of transversal passivity, we encode the target formation shape, the prescribed edge lengths, and a subspace of internally balanced edge forces as the port target manifolds of the agents and the edge controller. The synthesis task is thereby reformulated as the joint design of a transversally passive edge controller and its output-target subspace. We then propose a general constructive realization of output-strictly transversally passive systems and specialize it to derive a dynamic edge controller that sustains admissible equilibrium edge forces. Through a compatibility analysis across the interconnection, we establish a closed-loop dissipation margin in terms of the controller parameters and prove local convergence of all agent and controller ports to their target manifolds. Numerical simulations validate the results.

title: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
comments: Published at Interspeech 2026 (oral). 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Code: https://github.com/King-Rafat/Dynamic_Streaming_ASR
summary: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.

title: CGOcc: Learning Cross-Gaussian Dependencies for 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction
summary: In Gaussian-based semantic occupancy prediction, overlapping primitives can provide ambiguous class predictions, making their joint interpretation important for voxel classification. However, current methods using spatially weighted mixtures neglect explicit modeling of cross-primitive dependencies, limiting the readout's ability to utilize category-specific relational evidence. Hence, we introduce CGOcc, a supervised multi-camera framework that explicitly models Cross-Gaussian dependencies for 3D semantic Occupancy prediction. CGOcc integrates appearance and geometric observations to refine Gaussian states and encodes cross-Gaussian dependencies in a diagonal-plus-low-rank representation. To incorporate these dependencies into voxel classification, CGOcc uses a class-conditional projection to extract diagonal and signed cross-Gaussian statistics without constructing a dense dependency matrix. The readout then refines occupied-class probabilities using these statistics while preserving a learned reference's occupied mass and free probability. Extensive experiments on nuScenes demonstrate CGOcc achieves state-of-the-art performance, with larger gains at high Gaussian overlap and improved predictions near boundaries. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of covariance-aware prediction and support its synergy with geometric interaction.

title: Optimization of Finite Alphabet Message Passing Decoding on Fully Node-Parallel Architectures for 5G LDPC Codes
summary: In this paper, we propose a novel design method for the lookup tables (LUTs) of the minimum reconstruction, computation, and quantization (min-RCQ) LDPC code decoding algorithm. The proposed design method uses Bayesian optimization and samples from a subspace of the design space. The novel design method does not require knowledge about the channel or the modulation format and uses the frame error rate (FER) as loss function. The design method is applicable to irregular low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with puncturing and shortening. Furthermore, the design method creates a set of iteration-agnostic LUTs that can be used over all iterations, which makes this approach suitable for fully node-parallel decoder architectures. We show that our proposed approach achieves a 38.6 % better energy efficiency than a state-of-the-art normalized min-sum (NMS) decoder without loss in error correction performance.

title: A posteriori error estimates for the bulk--surface Cahn--Hilliard system with dynamic boundary conditions
summary: This paper develops reliable residual-based a posteriori error estimators for the full discretization of a bulk--surface Cahn--Hilliard system with a two-parameter family of dynamic boundary conditions on a curved domain. The main novelty are theoretically justified computable temporal, coarsening and geometric error estimators. The numerical method combines a linear bulk--surface finite element method in space and a linearly implicit backward Euler method in time. Based on the derived error indicators, a space--time adaptive algorithm is proposed and numerical experiments illustrate and complement the theoretical result.

title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
comments: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at HUST 2026 (13th International Workshop on HPC User Support Tools), co-located with SC26, Chicago, IL, USA, November 15, 2026. Camera-ready version
summary:
AI-based question-answering systems are increasingly used for user support, including at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities. However, existing systems lack a systematic, deployment-oriented approach for evaluating final-answer quality and attributing failures to specific components. They also remain largely static after deployment, apart from periodic knowledge-base updates.
  We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline for HPC user support. AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a fine-grained level, identifies whether failures arise from missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes each failure to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test that distinguishes information missing from the documentation corpus from information present but not retrieved. We further introduce a controlled harness-training process that uses expert references, null edits, and explicit ship, revert, or decline decisions to improve the diagnostic pipeline reliably.
  Across 2,174 support turns, AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, while harness training improved expert agreement from 108/150 to 123/150 turns. These results demonstrate a governed form of self-evolution in which production evidence drives targeted system improvements. By turning production interactions into fine-grained diagnoses and actionable repairs, AskALCF provides a systematic foundation for continuously improving deployed AI support systems beyond knowledge-base updates alone.

title: Assessing Data Center Hosting Capacity Considering Electromagnetic Transient Dynamics
summary: Hosting capacity is commonly assessed with steady-state optimization, which leaves the dynamic response of the data center and the grid at the resulting operating point untested. This paper assesses candidate data center capacities by coupling a unit commitment (UC) model with electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulation. During the capacity search, the UC model determines the economic dispatch for each tested data center capacity, and the resulting operating points are tested for settling with the generators committed online by the UC model and after a selected synchronous generator outage. Three nested capacities are obtained: the optimization-based steady-state capacity, the dynamic pre-outage capacity, and the post-outage dynamic capacity, each bounded by the previous one. On a test system with a detailed data center model, both dynamic capacities fall well below the optimization capacity, and the ranking of connection locations changes with the assessment stage and with the outage. In the most severe outage case at each candidate bus, the capacity is about 30% below the steady-state capacity. Thus, the dynamic response of the data center and the grid should be part of the hosting capacity assessment, and the comparison of connection locations should be made on the post-outage dynamic capacity.

title: Characterizing Predictive Multiplicity in Ranking and Its Fairness Implications
summary: Prediction problems often admit competing models that achieve comparable performance yet produce conflicting outputs, a phenomenon known as predictive multiplicity. While this challenge has been extensively studied in classification tasks, its implications remain largely unexplored in ranking frameworks, which are critical for high-stakes societal decisions such as the allocation of welfare resources and social assistance. This paper investigates the phenomenon of predictive multiplicity in score-based ranking problems. We introduce formal definitions to capture multiplicity in ranking settings, supported by foundational theoretical guarantees. Furthermore, we examine the dual relationship between predictive multiplicity and algorithmic fairness in ranking problems: we analyze how model multiplicity can act as a potential source of unfairness, while demonstrating how exploring this decision space provides a principled avenue for discovering less discriminatory rankings. Finally, we complement our theoretical contributions with insightful empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets, validating our analytical findings and illustrating their practical implications. Taken together, this work highlights the real-world relevance of predictive multiplicity in ranking and sheds light on the potential of leveraging this effect to achieve fairer outcomes.

title: Quantifying the Cost of Restoring AC Feasibility for Approximate Optimal Power Flow Solutions
comments: 5 pages, 4 figures, submitted to 2027 IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting
summary: Power system operations rely on approximate solutions of the AC optimal power flow problem, most notably the DC optimal power flow used in security-constrained unit commitment and economic dispatch, while convex relaxations, machine learning surrogates, and other approximations are studied extensively in the academic literature. Because these approximations neglect or relax parts of the AC power flow equations, their solutions must be adjusted before dispatch; for example, the DC optimal power flow, which neglects transmission losses, reactive power, and voltage magnitude variations, is known to produce solutions that are always infeasible. The cost of this adjustment is not adequately understood. This paper proposes a method that quantifies, for any approximate solution, the minimum cost of the adjustments that restore AC feasibility, which is a lower bound on the cost of the heuristic adjustments used in practice. We apply it to the DC optimal power flow, the second-order cone and quadratic convex relaxations, and the AC optimal power flow solved to a loose relative tolerance of $10^{-4}$ instead of $10^{-8}$. Relative to the AC optimal power flow solution obtained from a local nonlinear optimization solver, and even with the minimum adjustment, the DC optimal power flow requires adjusting, on average, generators that account for 15.6% of total generation capacity and incurs a 1.10% cost increase; the convex relaxations require more adjustment (17.2% and 16.9%) but smaller cost increases (0.68% and 0.78%); and the loose-tolerance AC optimal power flow requires 6.1% and incurs 0.42%. These results indicate significant value in operating markets directly on the AC optimal power flow, which avoids the distortion of the dispatch and prices caused by heuristic feasibility restoration.
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, submitted to 2027 IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting

title: Efficient Knowledge Transfer in Federated Bayesian Optimization through Neural Network Surrogates
summary: Federated Bayesian Optimization (FedBO) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing Bayesian Optimization (BO) in distributed, privacy-sensitive settings, enabling agents to accelerate the optimization of their local objectives by sharing knowledge about their similarities without exposing raw data. However, existing methods rely on restrictive assumptions, such as near-identical objective functions or shared Gaussian process hyperparameters that are often violated in heterogeneous real-world applications. We present GLOBAFED, a novel framework that enables efficient knowledge transfer across different but related objectives without compromising privacy. At its core is a probabilistic neural network surrogate with a shared feature-extracting backbone and agent-specific heads equipped with varia- tional Bayesian last layers to provide uncertainty estimates. During optimization, agents use federated learning on the shared backbone to collaboratively build a common latent feature representation, while agent-specific heads adapt to their individual objectives. Our empirical results demonstrate that GLOBAFED significantly accelerates convergence and reaches better final performance compared to state-of-the-art FedBO baselines, and enables agents to warm-start their optimization from previously learned global features.

title: Trust-region high-index saddle dynamics for ill-conditioned saddle-point computation
summary: We propose a trust-region high-index saddle dynamics (TRHiSD) framework for computing high-index saddle points in ill-conditioned problems. To address the deterioration of high-index saddle dynamics caused by inappropriate step sizes and search directions, we exploit its intrinsic local min--max structure and construct separate trust-region subproblems on the maximization and minimization subspaces to adapt the two trust-region radii to different local curvature scales. Under suitable assumptions and with exact spectral subspaces, we prove local linear convergence of the Cauchy-point variant and local quadratic convergence of the Newton-step variant. Numerical experiments on modified Rosenbrock functions are consistent with the predicted convergence rates. For the Landau--de Gennes model, a TRHiSD variant using a truncated conjugate-gradient step for the minimization subproblem substantially reduces the outer-iteration count and the wall-clock time in the tested cases.

title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
summary: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. Laboratory value prediction improved, with MAE 18--46% lower than that of Curiosity-0226-1B. We evaluated prediction of disease events across pediatric cohorts aged 2--17 years. AUROCs for new asthma diagnosis (0.742--0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829--0.852) were comparable to those in the adult reference cohort, while AUROCs for sickle cell crisis (0.820--0.847) were lower than in adults (0.915). Explicit representation of documented death enabled new mortality prediction tasks among adults across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory settings (AUROC 0.821--0.942). Scaling-law analysis guided compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension. The resulting Curiosity-0826-4B model has more parameters (4.3B versus 1B) and a longer context window (16K versus 8K). It processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training floating point operations (FLOPs) compared with its predecessor. By extending a common zero-shot prediction strategy to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, Curiosity-0826-4B broadens opportunities to develop clinical and operational applications without training separate task-specific models. Further validation should assess local calibration, performance across patient subgroups and event frequencies, timeline completion rates, and generalization to new settings, alongside prospective evaluation of clinical and operational utility.

title: Beyond Worst-Case Online Algorithms via Input Subsampling
summary:
We study whether classical competitive ratios survive input subsampling, when both the online algorithm and the offline optimum are evaluated on the same subsampled input. We consider the canonical problems of prophet inequalities and ski-rental. In these settings, for any single subsampling rate, the classical worst-case ratios remain unchanged. We ask a stronger question: can one adversarial input remain worst-case at two distinct rates $p>q$?
  For prophet inequalities, in the model where the policy knows the sampling rate and learns item survival online, every instance has competitive ratio strictly below $2$ at one of the two rates, and we determine the tight simultaneous guarantee. For ski rental, in the fluid model where sampling scales the horizon, the answer depends on $q/p$. Against adversarial distributions over horizons, one unrestricted randomized algorithm achieves a strict simultaneous improvement over $e/(e-1)$ for every distribution exactly when $q/p$ is below approximately $0.34$. Requiring the algorithm to buy by the breakeven time lowers this threshold to approximately $0.31$, showing that unlike classical ski-rental algorithms, buying later can provably help in this setting.
  Our results therefore reveal a new form of beyond-worst-case fragility under input subsampling: instances that are worst-case at one rate need not remain hard at two rates simultaneously.

title: Scalable Reference Electrical Architectures for Modern Data Centers
summary: The rapid growth of cloud computing, artificial intelligence (AI), and high-performance computing is driving the deployment of data centers with electrical demands ranging from tens of megawatts to multi-gigawatt campuses, creating significant challenges for utility interconnection and power system planning. This paper presents scalable, vendor-neutral reference electrical architectures for colocation, hyperscale, and AI data centers. The proposed framework integrates modular Power PODs, hierarchical HV/MV/LV distribution, standby generation, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), battery energy storage systems (BESS), and scalable utility interfaces into a unified planning methodology. Three representative Power POD configurations are developed to support systematic capacity expansion while maintaining consistent electrical topology and equipment sizing. The proposed architectures facilitate utility interconnection studies, equipment demand forecasting, transmission planning, and grid infrastructure assessment, providing an open and reproducible benchmark for evaluating the impacts of large-scale data center deployment on future power systems.

title: A Reliability Study of Explainable AI for Freight Mode Classification
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly used to support freight transportation decisions, but their predictions are rarely accompanied by evidence that the associated explanations can be trusted. In this study we investigate explainable machine learning for classifying shipments as Air/Air Charter or Truck/Ocean using the PEPFAR Supply Chain Management System Delivery History dataset, with 5,964 shipment records and 47 input features after cleaning, where freight cost and pack price are excluded as near-proxies of the transportation mode. We compare three Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architectures, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and gradient boosting with imbalance-aware metrics and paired significance tests across one hundred random replications. We then evaluate the explanations themselves, namely the stability of SHAP feature rankings across retraining and across models, the faithfulness of SHAP and LIME attributions under a feature-deletion test, and the geographic structure of the destination effects, which we map for all 38 destination countries. The results suggest that the tree ensembles significantly outperform the neural and linear models (86.8% against 83.3-85.0% mean testing accuracy) while their leading features remain the most stable across retraining. Removing the five features ranked most important by SHAP or LIME changes the predicted probabilities roughly four times as much as removing randomly chosen features. The destination effects form a coherent geographic pattern that simple port access does not explain. However, models with similar accuracy disagree substantially on which features matter most, and thus explanation stability and faithfulness should be assessed before such explanations are used to support freight transport decisions.

title: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training
comments: Accepted at the Foundations of LLM Post-Training in Changing Environments, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.
comment: Accepted at the Foundations of LLM Post-Training in Changing Environments, NeurIPS 2026

title: Orbit: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on IT Operations Reasoning
summary: LLMs now support IT operations (ITOps), but benchmarks rarely show why a model fails. We present ORBIT, a benchmark of ITOps questions in three formats, namely multiple-choice, open-ended, and troubleshooting, with each question accompanied by a reference answer and a recorded source. An audit found template defects in about a tenth of the generated items, so we drop them and rebuild the troubleshooting format from real practitioner threads with accepted answers. Under one independent judge, five LLMs answer most multiple-choice items correctly, between a third and just over half of the open-ended items, and a minority of the troubleshooting items, even under a more lenient root-cause rubric. When models judged their own answers, they accepted many answers to defective items, so we use one independent judge for every model. Word overlap with the question finds the correct option for more than half of the multiple-choice items. ORBIT is a diagnostic aid for selecting and supervising assistants rather than a deployment test.

title: Terms of Care: Designing for Participation in Data Governance by Disability Communities
summary: Improving disability representation in AI-generated media requires community-specific datasets, yet openly sharing such data can expose communities to misuse, decontextualization, and exploitation. We examine how disability communities can participate in dataset governance through context-sensitive licensing. Working with three disability advocacy organizations, we conducted semi-structured interviews, an educational webinar and modular license activity to promote community participation in data stewardship. Our findings show that governance in these high-context communities relies on organizational memory (especially situated harms); both formal authority and informal relational practices; communication; and resulting trust. The modular license activity made organizational data choices more accessible and values-led, allowing communities to adapt Creative Commons clauses to express permitted uses, sector-specific restrictions, safeguarding requirements, and commitments to respectful representation. Yet, concerns remain about monitoring and enforcing appropriate data use. We contribute (1) an empirical account of governance tensions, (2) a practical modular approach, and (3) design implications for AI data platforms that support relational, context-sensitive governance beyond standardized, one-size-fits-all frameworks.

title: DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory
summary: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.

title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: How Decision and Reasoning Alignment Shape Reliance on AI Advisors
summary: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
summary: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

title: Beyond the Diff - VulSpot: A Vulnerability Dataset Where No Vulnerability Goes Unlocalized
summary: A vulnerability detector is only as trustworthy as the benchmark that scores it, and today's real-world datasets tend to flatter detectors. They are often built once and never refreshed, so they quickly miss new vulnerabilities, their labels are either noisy or heavily filtered, and their random splits let models train on near-copies of test code and on future vulnerabilities. Above all, when a fix only adds code, such as a missing NULL check, they do not point at where the vulnerability was, preventing detectors from learning to localize some of the most common C/C++ weaknesses. We present VulSpot, a living benchmark for detecting, classifying, and localizing vulnerabilities, with over 500k functions in 21 languages from 24k registered CVEs, including over 15k vulnerable C/C++ functions. By linking the code added by a patch to the existing statement it protects, VulSpot locates the vulnerability in 99.3\% of the functions that previous diff-based datasets used to leave without a location. Rather than discarding uncertain labels, it tells users how reliable each one is, and it comes with leak-free splits, complementary code context, and hierarchical CWE labels. An automated pipeline refreshes VulSpot every month, so that each release brings vulnerabilities no model has seen yet.

title: Adaptive Model Predictive Control for Damping IBR-Induced SSOs
summary: We propose an adaptive model predictive control (MPC) approach to damp sub-synchronous oscillations (SSOs) induced by grid-following (GFL) inverter-based resources (IBRs). Unlike traditional model predictive controller designed considering the nominal plant that may not perform well in other conditions, we use plants that alter with changing operating point. To capture the plant dynamics, we use recursive least squares (RLS) based system identification with variable forgetting factor. This approach allows us to discount past data and avoid bias caused by large transient outliers while performing system identification. We present a proof of the convergence of the model parameters in the presence of finite outliers. We propose to update the model inside the MPC optimization problem periodically after a predetermined time interval instead of each sampling instant since the operating point changes slowly in a practical power system. The MPC design allows us to directly impose constraints on control inputs so that the IBR current limits are respected. Our approach also addresses the issue of unavailability of IBR models. We show the accuracy of the system identification and the superior performance of the proposed controller on the modified IEEE $4$-machine system and the modified IEEE $68$-bus system as compared with the traditional MPC.

title: Robot-Induced Bias in Movement Smoothness Metrics for Rehabilitation: Quantification and Correction in Simulation
comments: 7 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Rehabilitation Robotics (ICORR)
summary: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Rehabilitation Robotics (ICORR)

title: Latent Imagination for Parameterized Action Spaces
summary: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions; model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act. We introduce HyLI (Hybrid Latent Imagination), a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass. To address learning problems that the PAMDP structure creates, HyLI adds counterfactual mode evaluation, which gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay, which keeps rare successes in training. On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the published score of the strongest model-free baseline in our comparison on all 7 tasks, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps than that baseline (5.0x when its reward-free pre-training is counted), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published planner settings. It is the only method in our comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.

title: Sensitivity-Aware Surrogate Modeling with Random Feature Expansions
summary: Random feature expansions (RFEs) provide a flexible approach to surrogate modeling, but their accuracy depends on the distribution used to sample features. We propose spike-and-slab random feature expansions (SAS-RFE) to learn the feature sampling distribution from sensitivity analysis. The method employs a spike-and-slab distribution that assigns probabilities to the inclusion of individual inputs in randomly sampled Fourier features. These inclusion probabilities are determined by estimates of total Sobol' sensitivity indices, rather than by explicitly selecting important inputs or interaction terms. An information theoretic criterion shows that the total Sobol' indices yield a distribution that approximates the input interaction structure of the model. An iterative algorithm updates the sampling probabilities using sensitivity estimates from successive RFE surrogates. Analytical formulas for the Sobol' indices of random Fourier feature expansions enable these updates without additional evaluations of the target function. Numerical experiments on six benchmark problems, with up to 100 input dimensions, demonstrate improvements in surrogate approximation and sensitivity estimation.

title: MULTILOOP: Evolving Multi-Agent Harnesses for Complex Information-Seeking Tasks
summary: The performance of LLM-based agents depends not only on the underlying model but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, and orchestration logic around it. Recent works automate harness optimization with coding agents that analyze execution traces, diagnose failures, and edit the harness code; however, those focused on single-agent systems. Multi-agent harnesses are harder to optimize as fixing them requires changing how agents interact in addition to how each behaves. We study whether automated harness optimization can diagnose and repair failures in multi-agent systems through a case study on complex information-seeking tasks from DeepSearchQA [Gupta et al., 2026]. We apply MULTILOOP, a simple optimization loop in which a coding agent iteratively analyzes, evaluates and edits the harness. With only 10 training samples, the evolved harness improves accuracy by 4.6% over the base harness and by 3.2% over the best single-agent system. However, a taxonomy of failure modes before and after optimization shows that the orchestration failures that characterize multi-agent systems largely persist. Our findings motivate harness optimization methods that encourage structural changes to how agents delegate tasks and share information.

title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench
comments: "Technical report, EBMV @ ECCV 2026 Challenge. 13 pages, 9 figures
summary: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.
comment: "Technical report, EBMV @ ECCV 2026 Challenge. 13 pages, 9 figures

title: Image Deblending with Diffusion Models
comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. 22 pages, 10 figures. Code: https://github.com/DanBotchan/image-deblending-diffusion
summary: Image deblending is the task of decomposing a composite image back into its source images, which is an ill-posed problem, as a single blended image can be decomposed into multiple plausible source layers. While diffusion models are often used to solve inverse problems, they typically address single-output reconstruction problems. In this work, we formulate deblending as a joint inverse problem, employing diffusion posterior sampling to simultaneously reconstruct two source images, demonstrating that a single diffusion prior is expressive enough to disentangle two full images at once rather than just one. Drawing inspiration from human perception, where semantic understanding helps disentangle visual inconsistencies, we propose a training-free framework that leverages text prompts to constrain this solution space. We address the blind deblending task through a two-stage architecture: text-guided latent diffusion performs semantic separation using prompts as high-level cues, followed by a pixel-space refinement to recover fine details. Stochastic sampling produces multiple plausible decompositions that can be ranked without ground truth. Extensive experiments show that our training-free method achieves state-of-the-art results on unseen domains and extends to spatially-varying alpha maps, while remaining competitive with supervised baselines on standard scalar blending benchmarks.
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 22 pages, 10 figures. Code: https://github.com/DanBotchan/image-deblending-diffusion

title: AIFR: Adaptive Identity Feature Recovery for Diffusion-Based Makeup and Anime Portraits
summary: Diffusion-based makeup and anime portraits are increasingly popular in online content creation (e.g., virtual makeup editing and anime avatar generation), but their altered appearances can hinder face recognition (FR) in identity-based content screening. Existing methods mainly adapt FR encoders or restore input images. The former require costly gallery re-encoding, while the latter may be incomplete or distort identity-related facial details. To address these limitations, we aim to correct identity features within a frozen FR model to recover its output embeddings in its original space. Appearance changes vary in strength and affect facial regions differently. To this end, we propose Adaptive Identity Feature Recovery (AIFR), a framework that inserts a lightweight recovery module at a single intermediate layer to predict sample-level correction strength and spatially adaptive residual updates. Module training uses fused identity targets to guide embedding recovery in the original FR space and an identity-shift score to regulate correction strength and limit unnecessary changes. At inference, AIFR processes a single portrait in one forward pass without reference images, producing recovered embeddings that can be directly matched with existing gallery templates without re-encoding. With only 1.22M trainable parameters, AIFR improves the average TAR at FAR=$10^{-4}$ from 66.1\% to 90.2\% over the original ArcFace, and further experiments show improvements across unseen makeup styles, stylization strengths, and generators. Beyond recognition, the recovered embeddings can directly condition a pretrained Arc2Face model to generate faces with improved identity preservation, showing compatibility with embedding-conditioned downstream generation.

title: Prior-as-Skill: Remember Outside and Read Inside with On-Policy Self-Distillation for Self-Evolving VLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.

title: Privacy-Preserving Spectrum Data Obfuscation in Next-Generation Spectrum Coexistence Systems
summary: In spectrum coexistence systems, the primary user (PU) activity must be partially disclosed for interference avoidance and coordination, while the exact spectrum occupancy information is often restricted due to security and regulatory constraints. To this end, subset-based disclosures can be employed in which the true frequency is included while ambiguity is introduced. This paper shows that naive randomized subset disclosures remain highly vulnerable to information leakage through inference, as temporal structure can be exploited to recover spectrum usage information. Under Markovian dynamics of the PU's spectrum usage, hidden Markov model (HMM) filtering with online learning is applied, while under periodic dynamics, period and phase estimations with phase-aligned statistics are used for inference. To address this vulnerability, structure-aware obfuscation strategies are introduced. For Markovian dynamics, history-based and belief-based schemes are designed to induce model mismatch and limit posterior concentration, while for periodic dynamics, cycle-dominance and decoy-based schemes are designed to manipulate phase-wise statistics and bias the inference process. These obfuscation schemes significantly hinder inference of spectrum information and offer principled disclosure solutions for spectrum coexistence systems.

title: SAME: Semantic Watermark Embedding for Open-Source Large Pretrained Models
summary: Open-source large pretrained models (LPMs) have become increasingly valuable assets for model development and downstream applications, but their accessibility also facilitates unauthorised copying and modification. To protect their intellectual property (IP), existing approaches typically embed tailored trigger-response patterns as watermarks for ownership verification. However, such trigger designs need to be tailored to task-specific data that constrain their transferability across downstream tasks, and are not durable under subsequent benign fine-tuning. To address these limitations, we propose SemAntic waterMark Embedding (SAME), which introduces a semantically meaningful private vocabulary that enables flexible composition of adaptive and persistent watermarks. Specifically, SAME introduces a fixed private vocabulary that assigns each native token a private embedding counterpart, while aligning the semantic expressiveness of the two vocabularies within the model's representation space. This alignment allows private tokens to be flexibly composed into semantic triggers that elicit meaningful responses, enabling adaptive watermarks beyond predefined trigger-response pairs. By grounding the private vocabulary in the model's native semantics, SAME couples the watermark with its evolving semantic capabilities, allowing this connection to be preserved throughout downstream fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAME provides reliable and robust watermarks across LPMs of varying scales and architectures, enabling effective ownership verification for IP protection.

title: Coverage-Aware Routing with Approximate Equilibrium Guarantees for Location-Diversity Vehicular Crowdsensing
summary: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed. Location-diversity incentives pay vehicles more to travel where few others go, but our earlier mechanism sets how far each vehicle deviates without optimizing collective coverage in route selection. We add this step in two stages. First, a non-cooperative game with diversity-weighted rewards yields each vehicle's equilibrium deviation. Second, the platform recommends to each vehicle a feasible route whose deviation is within a tolerance of this value, chosen to improve coverage. The coverage gain is monotone submodular, so a greedy router with local search attains at least half of the optimal gain over generated candidates. If every active vehicle has a candidate within a tolerance that is small relative to the aggregate deviation, the recommended routes form an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with $\varepsilon$ first order in the tolerance, or second order under a stronger condition. On London and Monaco road networks, the router achieves 99.4% and 98.9% of the optimal reduction in the coverage penalty on small instances and exceeds closest-length selection by up to 27.9 points. Under heterogeneous costs, uniform deviation needs compensation averaging 42% of the budget to give every vehicle nonnegative utility; the equilibrium targets need almost none. They also yield more coverage per unit of added travel in most settings and up to 22.6 more points at small budgets, an advantage that depends on placement and reverses at large budgets, where detour limits bind.

title: Robust Safe Control Under Uncertainty: Estimation, Contraction, and Regret Bounds
comments: 15 pages, temporary, (optional) simulation to be added
summary: Disturbance uncertainty requires safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs) to leave a robustness margin, which can alter the nominal control input and degrade closed-loop performance. This paper studies safety and the resulting performance loss for discrete-time nonlinear systems with additive disturbances and polytopic input constraints. We develop a causal disturbance observer and construct two robust barrier conditions. The first uses a time-dependent bound on the estimation error. The second uses a constant margin when the disturbance increments are uniformly bounded and moves the requirement on the initial error from the online filter to an explicit initialization condition. For affine barriers, both filters are quadratic programs. We bound their input deviations from an oracle filter with access to the current disturbance and derive sufficient conditions for uniform contraction of the oracle closed loop. The contraction analysis accounts for state-dependent actuation, unmatched disturbances, and active physical input limits. Combining the sensitivity and contraction estimates gives finite-time dynamic regret bounds that quantify the effects of observer convergence, disturbance variation, and robustness margins. With sublinear cumulative certified disturbance variation and observer innovation error, the bounds yield sublinear regret.
comment: 15 pages, temporary, (optional) simulation to be added

title: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models
comments: 32 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://lichenlillc.github.io/SO-Arena
summary: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

title: From Link Prediction to Linear Community Detection: A Finite-Sample Guarantee for Graph Pretraining
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 47 pages, 8 figures. Code: https://github.com/YChen1103/LP-to-Linear-Community-Detection
summary: Link prediction (LP) is a standard pretraining objective for graph neural networks (GNNs): hide edges, train an encoder-decoder to predict them, and reuse the node embeddings for downstream node tasks. Despite its empirical success, there is little quantitative theory explaining why an edge-level objective should produce embeddings that are linearly useful for node classification. We study this question in the finite-sample stochastic block model (SBM). For any bounded GNN encoder paired with a symmetric bilinear decoder, we prove a conditional reduction: small population held-out LP excess risk implies small community-classification error for a transductive linear classifier on the learned embeddings. The bound decomposes into an optimization residual, an architectural approximation residual, and explicit statistical terms of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d/n})$ in bounded dense regimes. We further give a constructive few-label classifier: nearest-centroid classification under the positive semidefinite quadratic form $G = W Z^\top Z W$, whose label error is coupled to LP quality. The framework is architecture-agnostic through the approximation residual, and we instantiate this residual as $O(\log n / n)$ for a graph isomorphism network (GIN) with spectral positional encoding and a bilinear decoder. Synthetic SBM experiments validate the theorem chain from LP risk to score error to classification error, and show when the worst-case constants become conservative.

title: Honesty Is a Race: Predicting When Verifiable-Reward RL Teaches a Model to Bluff
summary: Two rewards with the same expected payoff at the start of training can end a reinforcement-learning run in opposite places, with an honest model or one that bluffs. We study rewards that pay $b$ for a verdict that a checker cannot verify ("this program is correct") and $r$ for a certificate that it accepts (an input revealing a bug). To first order, a GRPO step makes the model more honest exactly when $\tilde{p}\,r/b>1+κ$. Here $\tilde{p}$ is the rate at which the checker accepts the model's certificates, weighted toward the items on which the model still gives both verdicts, and $κ$ is the pull of the items on which the unverifiable verdict is right. Both terms move during training. A checker raises $\tilde{p}$, so near the threshold honesty is a race, which a run just below the threshold can win and a run under a lottery (random pay with the same mean) cannot. The term $κ$ starts large and falls as the other items settle, so a run just above the threshold first dips toward bluffing, on code nearly to zero, before climbing back. Paying the honest verdict also pulls the other items toward it, which predicts a ceiling on the payoff ratio, above which the model gives the honest verdict where it is wrong. On propositional Datalog, two code models, and abstention on grade-school math, with $p$ the model's success rate before RL, no run above $pr/b=1$ ends collapsed, and runs under the checker can survive slightly below it. At $pr/b=3$, above the ceiling, both code models call about half of correct programs buggy. On depth-3 Datalog, training generously under the checker and then cutting the payoff keeps the model at least 67% honest in three seeds, at a ratio where the same model trained from the start falls to 4-15% and is at most 47% honest after 160 steps. On depth-2 Datalog, when honesty collapses, a linear probe fit before RL still reads the truth.

title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack with Small Items
summary: The Multiple-Choice Knapsack problem is a generalization of the Knapsack problem in which items are partitioned into disjoint classes and exactly one item must be selected from each class. Besides the standard dynamic program running in time $\mathcal{O}(nc)$, where $n$ is the total number of items and $c$ is the knapsack capacity, no other pseudopolynomial-time algorithm is currently known. We present an $\mathcal{O}(n+w_{\max}^4)$-time algorithm, where $w_{\max}=\max_i (w_{in_i}-w_{i1})$ is the maximum weight range within a class.

title: Prediction-Error-Tightened MPC for Socially Compliant Crowd Navigation
comments: 9 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the European Control Conference (ECC 2027)
summary: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.

title: A Linear-Time Construction on $\mathbb{S}^2$ Achieving a Sublinear Energy Gap on Smale's Seventh Problem
summary:
Smale's seventh problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm that places $N$ points on the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$ with logarithmic energy (the sum of $-\log$ of all pairwise distances) within $O(\log N)$ of the minimum. The minimal energy has an asymptotic expansion with explicit terms of order $N^2$ and $N\log N$ and a linear term whose constant is unknown. Brauchart, Hardin, and Saff conjectured this constant; the resulting expansion, $E_{BHS}(N)$, is known to be an upper bound on the minimum, up to $o(N)$. All previously analyzed constructions on $\mathbb{S}^2$ have energy exceeding $E_{BHS}(N)$ by an amount that grows at least linearly in $N$, i.e. $Ω(N)$, far from the $O(\log N)$ accuracy sought by Smale.
  We present TerracedZonal, a deterministic construction that generates $N$ points in $Θ(N)$ time and memory. Points are placed on latitude rings whose populations are held constant across bands ("terraces") chosen by a one-dimensional dynamic program, so that adjacent rings within each terrace lock into a staggered triangular lattice. Under a locality assumption, we prove that the energy exceeds $E_{BHS}(N)$ by only $Θ(N^{2/3})$, with an explicit constant; exact evaluation up to $N = 10^9$ confirms this rate. Under the same assumption, its distance from the true minimum is sublinear if the conjecture holds. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithmic construction with a sublinear excess over $E_{BHS}(N)$ of explicit order (proven under the locality assumption), a necessary step toward Smale's seventh problem. With one parameter changed, the same algorithm also gives an equal-weight integration rule on $\mathbb{S}^2$ that runs just as fast and whose error decays at an empirical rate of $N^{-4}$ on smooth functions, versus $N^{-3/2}$ for every previous fast construction we tested.

title: Small Maximum Likelihood on Fixed Cavender-Farris-Neyman Trees: An Approximation Scheme and Limits to Fully Polynomial Approximation
summary: Small Maximum Likelihood fits the edge substitution probabilities of a given phylogenetic tree to an observed alignment, summing over the unobserved ancestral states. For the binary Cavender--Farris--Neyman model, we assume a uniform root and an edge-specific substitution probability $p_e\in[0,\tfrac12]$ for each edge $e$, shared across all alignment sites. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme. The algorithm achieves a factor of $1+\varepsilon$ for both the negative log likelihood and the loss after subtracting the uniform-root contribution. Its main step fixes ancestral sequences at one periodically spaced class of depths while summing over all remaining ancestors. A posterior entropy bound controls the cost of this restriction, and dynamic programming optimizes the resulting components over a finite parameter grid. We also give a randomized reduction from Clique showing that an FPTAS returning feasible rational edge probabilities would imply $RP=NP$. These results separate fixed-accuracy approximation from fully polynomial approximation for the same fixed-tree model.

title: Quasi-Static Fault-Tolerant Feedback Control of a Quadrotor Carrying a Slung Payload under Rotor Failure
summary: This paper presents a nonlinear control law for a slung payload system (SPS) consisting of a quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) carrying a slung payload. We propose a fault-tolerant control (FTC) design for the case of a complete single-rotor failure, i.e., only three functioning propellers. The failure is not modeled as a disturbance to be handled by estimation. Rather, we model the faulty SPS in control-affine form and design a quasi-static feedback law directly for the faulty dynamics. The controller achieves local exponential convergence of the payload position to a geometric path in space, rather than tracking a timed reference trajectory. Moreover, the transverse dynamics are exponentially stable, and the path-following manifold is rendered controlled invariant by feedback. Controlled invariance allows motion along the path to be prescribed independently through a tangential command while the state stays on the path-following manifold. The UAV body angular velocity remains bounded under bounded applied torque despite the failure. To validate the control design, numerical simulations apply the controller derived from the faulty SPS model in coordinates to the coordinate-free SPS model. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/qs-sl/.

title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
summary: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

title: Bounded Knapsack in Truly Subquadratic Time
summary:
Bounded Knapsack asks how many copies of each item to take to maximize profit under a capacity constraint. Given $n$ records with binary-encoded multiplicities, we return optimal counts in randomized time with a fixed power saving in the maximum item weight $w_{\max}$ or maximum item profit $p_{\max}$.
  Fix $1<ρ<2$ and suppose integer $(\min,+)$-convolution on length-$m$ arrays can be computed with failure probability at most $η$ in $\widetilde O(m^ρ)$ time, up to polynomial factors in the entry bit length and $\log(1/η)$. Put $f(ρ)=4(3-ρ)/(8-3ρ).$ For any fixed $ε>0$, on inputs whose integers have magnitude polynomial in $n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})$, our algorithm runs in time $$\widetilde O\bigl(n\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{f(ρ)+ε}\bigr).$$ It returns optimal counts with high probability. If convolution saves $δ=2-ρ$ in its exponent, knapsack retains $δ/(1+3δ/2)$. With the integer convolution exponent $1.9601397040925$, a separate parameter choice gives $\widetilde O(n+\min(w_{\max},p_{\max})^{1.961})$, including for 0-1 Knapsack.
  We keep the copies compressed. Witnessed convolutions generate residual queries, and local linear programs filter them by cost. Resilient lattice cores allow recursive states to coalesce. Progression reserves support rounding, and a thin affordable fiber yields a lift that reduces the normalized column volume. This volume bounds the number of LP regions a grid lookup examines.

title: On Multi-Constrained Path Finding utilizing Grover Search and Decoded Quantum Interferometry
summary: Finding a path whose totals under several additive metrics all fall inside prescribed ranges is weakly NP-complete. We ask what two quantum algorithms can do for it, against strong classical baselines. For directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) we give a Grover search whose state preparation builds the uniform superposition over all source-to-destination paths with one qubit per arc and no ancilla. We prove it correct, give its exact gate count, and show that measured strings form an error- detecting code whose distance is a girth-like graph parameter. We complete the oracle and count its gates: one search on our largest instance, 136 arc qubits and 262,144 paths, needs about 4.4 x 10^5 Toffoli gates, while classical dynamic programming decides the same instance with 18,754 labels. Grover search needs O(sqrt(N/M)) oracle calls for M good paths among N . Classical meet-in-the-middle matches this exponent in the worst case, and known quantum algorithms with quantum memory beat it. For a staged fabric with node-independent linear weights, maximizing the number of satisfied metrics is max-LINSAT, and with power- of-index weights it is Optimal Polynomial Intersection, where no known polynomial-time classical algorithm matches decoded quantum interferometry (DQI). We verify this translation in simulation and run two small binary instances on IBM Heron processors, which keep 67 % and 15 % of the ideal gain over uniform sampling.

title: Early Reflections on How Large Language Models are Reshaping Software Engineering Research
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are radically reshaping software engineering (SE) research. Yet, their steep financial and computational costs raise questions about who participates in that change, and who does not. By analysing all 1,918 papers published in the ICSE 2019-2026 Research and SEIP tracks, we uncover a shifting and highly concentrated research landscape. China and the US dominate LLM-based SE research, appearing in 74% of LLM-based publications between 2023-2026, yet they diverge sharply in their use of commercial versus open-weight models. Beneath this national dominance lies extreme institutional concentration: just 5 institutions in China and 7 in the US appear in more than half of their respective nations' LLM-based output. In the US, only half of the unique institutions active in 2023-2026 participated in LLM-based research, whereas Singapore displays broader usage, with 11 of 15 active institutions participating in LLM-based work. Furthermore, across 2023-2026 Research-track papers, industry involvement is more prevalent in LLM-based work (23.4% vs 16.9%), and academia-only papers make up a smaller share (63.4% vs 70.9%). Crucially, we expose a gap in model usage across industry and academia. SEIP track papers lean strongly towards commercial LLMs, with 77.4% featuring them and 40.5% using them exclusively. In contrast, only 21.2% of Research-track work relies strictly on commercial models, making greater use of open-weight models that typically support more sustainable and reproducible experiments. However, this divide warrants reflection on the extent to which SE research aligns with industry practice.

title: Bag of concepts can enhance other text representations for medical systematic review screening
summary: The paper examines the choice of text representation for semi-automated systematic literature review (SLR) systems based on active learning. Motivated by the insufficient attention that the bag of concepts representation has received so far, the paper discusses the implementation and experimental evaluation of several variations thereof. The experimental study was performed on medical SLR case studies, with results reported for random forest classification, cluster initialization and uncertainty sampling. The utility of bag of concepts features obtained using different ontologies is evaluated by applying them within the active learning framework to sequentially create classification models based on training data iteratively expanded with expert annotations. Systematic experiments compare BoW, BoC, PubMedBERT, Jina, Gemma and Qwen3 representations, together with combinations of BoC and each of the other representations. The evaluation uses workload savings and performance profiles adapted from optimization benchmarking. The results suggest that concept-based features can provide complementary information, with the BoC-augmented representations achieving higher mean workload savings on the DERP cases than their corresponding base representations. The Qwen3+BoC representation gives the best average performance in this comparison. The effects of augmentation vary across case studies and base representations. The paper also concentrates on the impact of ontology choice on document classification outcomes. In particular, the paper compares the predictive value of bag of concepts representations based on chosen ontologies with that of representations obtained using MedCAT with a UMLS-based dictionary.

title: RUMI: A Robotiq-Matched Universal Manipulation Interface for Robot Learning with Augmented Reality and Haptic Feedback
summary: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.

title: Computational Explanations of Semantic Universals
comments: submitted to Cambridge Elements in Semantics
summary: Despite their differences, the languages of the world share many deep features when it comes to how they express meaning. These semantic universals are likely to reflect shared aspects of human cognitive, communicative, and social structure. Recent advances in cross-linguistic semantics and computational linguistics allow us to develop explanations of the sources of such properties. This Element presents a body of work doing just that: we explicate a framework for providing computational explanations of semantic universals and then describe several such explanations using principles of ease of learning and efficient communication. Empirical domains include quantifiers, color terms, modals, and indefinites. After providing these explanations, we provide a discussion of future directions for advancing the explanatory power of computational methods in semantic typology.
