However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.

title: SBA: A Practical Memory Performance Denial-of-Service Attack
comments: Accepted for publication at the 3rd Microarchitecture Security Conference (uASC 2027)
summary:
Modern cloud platforms use memory bandwidth regulation to isolate co-located workloads, implicitly assuming that high aggregate bandwidth consumption implies high interference. We show that this assumption is fundamentally flawed.
  We present the Single-Bank Attack (SBA), a practical memory denial-of-service attack that induces extreme cross-core slowdowns---over three orders of magnitude on memory-intensive victims (e.g., LLM decode)---while consuming less than 1 GB/s of memory bandwidth. SBA exploits the gap between peak and worst-case DRAM throughput by concentrating memory write operations on a single bank, forcing persistent row conflicts and frequent write draining, thereby collapsing the memory service rate. Across Intel and AMD systems, including DDR5- and HBM2E-based platforms, SBA consistently causes orders-of-magnitude slowdowns under realistic multi-tenant settings, revealing a fundamental limitation of bandwidth-centric memory isolation.
  We further show that this localized contention propagates system-wide: single-bank congestion saturates memory controller queues and induces back-pressure into shared cache and coherence structures, ultimately throttling memory request injection across cores. Consequently, severe interference can arise even at low aggregate bandwidth, evading existing bandwidth-based QoS mechanisms such as Intel RDT MBA.
  To address this limitation, we propose IQ-MemGuard, a lightweight, software-based memory bandwidth regulator that detects sustained contention using microarchitectural signals and selectively throttles pathological request injection. Our implementation on an Intel platform effectively mitigates SBA, whereas Intel's hardware QoS mechanism fails completely.
comment: Accepted for publication at the 3rd Microarchitecture Security Conference (uASC 2027)

title: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
comments: 70 pages. Also archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23842568. The AI use statement is in the paper
summary: Interpretability tools increasingly support safety claims, such as that a sparse dictionary has recovered most of a model's features. Such claims rest on measurements with arbitrary thresholds, and small changes to the model weights, a different training seed or a different threshold can reverse them. We study two widely used measurements in toy models and synthetic dictionaries with known ground truth: the feature dimensionality of Elhage et al. and the feature recovery rate (FRR) with a cosine threshold. We characterize exactly where feature dimensionality is discontinuous and replace it with a regularized (ridge) version with sharp stability bounds: the ridge leverage score changes by at most $3\sqrt{3}/(8\sqrtλ)$ times the operator-norm change of the weights, and this constant cannot be improved; for the regularized dimensionality the stability constant grows like $ρ/4$ in the scale $ρ=R/\sqrtλ$, with explicit upper and lower bounds. We also prove certificates stating when a claim "feature $i$ is recovered" must survive a given change of the dictionary. The certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but certify no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries; at the standard threshold, whether a feature counts as recovered changed with the training seed for 55 percent of features. Experiments use toy models only. The proofs, code and text were drafted by AI agents directed by the authors and checked by an independent blind AI reviewer and by numerical tests; the authors take full responsibility for the content.

title: Weak Composition Theorems for Randomized Communication
summary:
We present two results towards the randomized communication complexity of composed functions. Our contributions include:
  - \textbf{Lifting-by-Influence.} For any binary function $f$ and any outer gadget $g:\{0,1\}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we show that up to additive terms, computing $g \circ f^n$ information-theoretically requires solving at least $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ instances of $f$, where $\operatorname{Inf}(g)$ denotes the total influence of $g$. To our knowledge, this is the first composition lower bound for randomized communication that applies to \emph{every} choice of $f$ and $g$.
  - \textbf{Symmetric Composition.} When $g$ is a symmetric function with a value transition at Hamming weight $d$, we strengthen the number of required instances to $\min\{d,n+1-d\}$. As an implication, this recovers the previously known direct-sum theorem, XOR lemma, and majority lemma.
  Our proofs develop novel and distinctive usages of the classical \emph{input embedding} argument of Barak, Braverman, Chen, and Rao (SICOMP 2013). As an additional ingredient, we introduce a new public sampling framework that avoids auxiliary communication during the recovery phase of the protocol, ultimately reducing the extra cost from $O(n)$ bits of information to just $O(1)$.

title: GA-HEL: A Knowledge-Driven Expert System for Open-Set, Granularity-Aware Hierarchical Event Linking in Social Media
summary: Social-media event intelligence requires a system to determine whether a post belongs to a registered event space, identify the supported hierarchy path, and stop at the deepest level warranted by the evidence. We formulate this requirement as open-set hierarchical event linking over frozen Storyline--Episode--Atomic Event Cards. GA-HEL implements a three-stage, knowledge-driven expert-system funnel: open-set scope control limits candidate exposure before hierarchical reasoning, hierarchy-aware decoders select a supported path and depth, and deterministic legal-path validation checks each record before database-compatible use. A 200-post Pilot supports task and mechanism development, while a separately annotated 497-post Expansion set evaluates transfer across four held-out Storylines and a hard-negative pool. Method implementations, prompts, Event Cards, candidate order, and six systems' predictions were frozen before Expansion Gold annotation. The resulting evaluation combines end-to-end hierarchical matching, open-set rejection, structural validation, ablation, cross-Storyline analysis, and an independent expert reannotation of a fixed audited subset. GA-HEL remains competitive with strong global full-card reasoning while providing explicit scope control and hierarchy-valid structured records. Error analysis identifies unsupported descent from Episode-level evidence to Atomic Events as the dominant remaining challenge. The task definition, frozen resource, and auditable protocol provide a reproducible foundation for scope-aware event intelligence. Code, Event Cards, labels, frozen predictions, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/SHbiao/GAHEL_release.

title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
summary: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.

title: "We Are the Dirty Hands": Reimagining an Ambient Intelligence Care System with Professional Caregivers
summary: While ambient assisted living (AAL) sensing systems offer promise for aging in place, their impacts on professional caregivers are overlooked. We conducted two collective speculation workshops (N=24) with personal health aides (PHAs, n=18) and certified nursing assistants (CNAs, n=6) to examine the ethical implications and value tensions of a care system with ambient intelligence (CSAI), our conceptualization of an AAL. Participants anticipated different implications across care roles and settings. PHAs anticipated additional responsibilities from CSAI, including learning how it operates and supporting older adults in its use. CNAs, who had greater access to workplace resources and protections, similarly noted that CSAI could create additional work. Participants also identified tensions around visibility, as sensing could support caregivers by documenting difficult working conditions while simultaneously making their behavior more vulnerable to misinterpretation. Through their modifications and surfaced discussions, we propose design guidelines for AAL systems, such as integrating context-aware sensing.

title: An Extensive Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches for Sentiment Analysis: Insights from Amazon Customer Reviews
summary: The rapid growth of user-generated text on online platforms creates opportunities for understanding customer opinion and supporting data-driven decisions. This study compares five traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Bernoulli Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Classifier, and Multinomial Naive Bayes) and six deep learning architectures (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, RNN, Attention, and FastText) for three-class sentiment classification of 568,454 Amazon Fine Food Reviews. Machine learning models used Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF features limited to 5,000 terms; deep learning models used learned embeddings over a 20,000-word vocabulary. Models were evaluated on the original imbalanced data and on a random-oversampled balanced set of 1,070,469 reviews, using accuracy, macro and per-class precision, recall, and F1-score, and training time. On the balanced set, Random Forest with BoW achieved 99\% accuracy and the Attention model achieved 98.7\%. Linear SVC reached 89\% accuracy in 1 min 15 s, and Logistic Regression reached 90\% in 3 min 37 s. On the imbalanced set, the Attention model achieved 97.8\% accuracy, and FastText achieved 95.3\% in 3 min 26 s, while the RNN reached 91.9\% with a neutral-class F1-score of 0.08. Deep learning models were more stable across class distributions, whereas the best classical model depended on balancing. We also report a user-facing application that applies the trained Random Forest and Attention models to new review text. Because the labels are derived from star ratings, the results measure agreement with rating-derived sentiment classes rather than annotated sentiment; the dataset is a single source, and the findings should be read with that limitation in mind.

title: An Agentic Python Framework for LLM-Driven UVM Testbench Synthesis with Closed-Loop Compiler Feedback
comments: Accepted at IEEE ISVLSI 2026, Kolkata, India. Copyright 2026 IEEE
summary: Protocol bridge verification is a persistent bottleneck in SoC development: for every new bridge instance, engineers hand-craft a full UVM testbench from scratch, consuming 40--100 engineering hours of bring-up effort. We present an agentic Python framework that generates complete, protocol-aware UVM testbenches for arbitrary IP and subsystem configurations from a structured Verification Manifest---a JSON specification encoding interface topology, protocol semantics, and coverage intent. The framework employs a dual closed-loop architecture: an inner compiler feedback loop that injects categorised UVM diagnostics rather than raw tool output, and an outer coverage loop driven by intent-gap analysis against the Manifest. Validated on the AMBA AHB-to-APB bridge---a representative production protocol bridge with a 7-state control FSM, two-phase APB handshake, and non-trivial burst serialisation logic---the framework achieves 96.8% functional coverage, a $4.7\times$ bring-up speedup, and a Protocol Verification Completeness score of 0.87, with only 2.1% of the generated 4,623-line testbench requiring human correction. The generated scoreboard independently identified a critical RTL functional fault that the manual baseline missed entirely. Generalisation across four protocol families confirms that speedup increases with protocol complexity, ranging from $3.1\times$ (APB Subordinate) to $6.1\times$ (CHI Subordinate).

title: QVS-LIVO RiskMap: Health- and Information-Aware View Selection for Multi-Camera LIVO and Off-Road Risk Mapping
summary: Multi-camera observations in off-road environments vary significantly in reliability, posing challenges when complementing degraded geometric constraints. Motivated by this, we propose Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), which decouples visual processing for state estimation from that for semantic mapping. The front end evaluates camera observations through read-only pretracking on a shared lidar-inertial posterior, combining observation health with geometric complementarity. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis govern selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction fails acceptance. The mapping back end integrates semantic observations from all available views in a shared world grid. Vehicle-scale geometry constrains semantic risk corrections, while spatial and temporal evidence supports risk confirmation. The system also produces a local bird's-eye-view (BEV) risk map and a global 2.5D semantic-terrain risk map with obstacle instance voxels. On two field sequences, QVS-LIVO achieved horizontal root mean square errors of 0.910 m and 1.664 m. It reduced error by 43.3% relative to FAST-LIO2 on the degraded long-route sequence. Across 12 controlled camera-fault configurations involving dropout, black frames and 60 ms timestamp shifts, it maintained complete trajectories with errors of 1.54-2.23 m. When deployed onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the system generates local and global maps at 9.94 Hz and 2.00 Hz, respectively, with a median local mapping latency of 32.4 ms. These runtime results demonstrate the real-time feasibility of selective visual state updates alongside multi-view semantic mapping under challenging off-road conditions. The code and related resources are available at: https://github.com/zihanPan-HIT/QVS-LIVO.

title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at https://github.com/Camel-Prince/OPSD4MAS.

title: Core nonemptiness for $2/3$-convex games
summary: We study the core of $2/3$-convex games, a class of transferable-utility (TU) games that generalizes convex games, which requires at least two of any three distinct coalitions satisfy the supermodular inequality. We show that every $2/3$-convex game admits a marginal worth vector in the core, and hence has a nonempty core. Our proof is constructive and yields a linear-time algorithm for finding such a core allocation. We also show that $2/3$-convexity does not imply permutational convexity in general, while the implication holds under an additional superadditivity condition on pairs of singletons. As an application, we introduce a TU model motivated by the OSCE's consensus-minus-two procedure and show that the resulting game is $2/3$-convex but need not be convex.

title: One Fuzzer, Many Reasoners: Adaptive Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzing with Reliability-Calibrated and Context-Gated Guidance
summary: Neural-symbolic AI (NSAI) combines learned perception with programs, constraints, and compositional reasoning, but remains difficult to test because small semantics-preserving changes can alter grounded symbols and trigger discontinuous reasoning failures. Existing neural fuzzers mainly rely on neural coverage or representation-space feedback and do not provide a common testing interface for heterogeneous NSAI systems. We introduce NSAI-Fuzz, a unified semantics-aware fuzzing framework that separates task-specific valid mutation from architecture-neutral guided search and represents each candidate using five availability-aware, rank-normalized risk signals: boundary pressure, grounding uncertainty, representation drift, constraint violation, and archive novelty. We further propose Reliability-Calibrated Weighting (RCW), which learns dataset-model-level signal allocations from calibrated reliability, and Contextual Signal Gating (CSG), which adapts signal weights to the current candidate pool. We evaluate four NSAI systems across four reasoning tasks, nine compatible dataset-model cells, 20 policies, and 1,800 on-policy runs. Fixed five-signal guidance outperforms Random and Uniform in every cell, while RCW and CSG further improve over Fixed in all nine cells. Under matched mutation and query budgets, RCW and CSG achieve 16.17% and 16.06% aggregate failure discovery, compared with 6.06% for the strongest neural-fuzzing baseline. Wall-clock evaluation further shows that TensorFuzz requires 1.11x the runtime of RCW while achieving only 0.45x its failure throughput. These results show that effective and efficient fuzzing of heterogeneous NSAI systems benefits from a common neural-symbolic risk interface with adaptive signal allocation.

title: SPEM: Scan-Prior Entropy Modeling for LiDAR Point Cloud Compression
summary: LiDAR point clouds exhibit scan-induced spatial regularities that are informative for geometry compression. Existing scan-aware approaches often exploit these regularities by transforming coded geometry into spherical or beam-aligned coordinate systems. However, this couples acquisition priors with geometry representation, altering spatial partitioning and quantization, and potentially preventing exact recovery of the original Cartesian geometry. We argue that acquisition priors should guide probability modeling rather than dictate the coding representation. We propose SPEM, a Scan-Prior Entropy Modeling framework that exploits LiDAR scanning regularities within the entropy model without requiring coordinate transformation. We introduce a multi-frequency spherical rotary positional encoding that captures scan-aligned spatial relationships in both backbone self-attention and decoded-context retrieval. Building upon this encoding, we develop a decoded-memory autoregressive predictor that efficiently exploits previously decoded occupancy information through reusable key/value caches. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both lossy and lossless LiDAR geometry compression, highlighting the effectiveness of scan-prior modeling across different coordinate representations.

title: Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning with Task-Centric Perception
summary: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.

title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
comments: 7 pages, 6 tables, 1 figure. Code, data, prompts and model responses: https://github.com/MohannedAhmed67/kernel-sibling-migrations
summary: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.
comment: 7 pages, 6 tables, 1 figure. Code, data, prompts and model responses: https://github.com/MohannedAhmed67/kernel-sibling-migrations

title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
summary: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

title: A Coupled Control Barrier Function Approach to Deadlock-Free Multi-Robot Conflict Resolution
summary: Many robotic applications involve scenarios where multiple robots interact and the decisions of one robot influence the behavior of others. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based feedback controller for multi-robot conflict resolution with input constraints. Safety is enforced using coupled Control Barrier Function (CBF), while a yielding matrix encodes how robots influence each other. Unlike existing methods with fixed or hard priorities, the proposed framework enables yielding preferences while guaranteeing deadlock-free operation by design. Sufficient conditions are established for the controller to be locally Lipschitz. The optimal CBF sign- indefinite slack is shown to admit a finite uniform bound, which is compensated through an enlarged CBF safety margin to obtain a forward invariant set contained within the desired safe set. The analysis also identifies an irreducible slack component due to finite maximum deceleration that cannot be eliminated by increasing the slack penalty. Finally, sufficient conditions on the yielding matrix and nominal controller are derived to exclude deadlock states. Simulations demonstrate adaptive coordination across yielding preferences and robustness to robot failures.

title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
summary: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
summary: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

title: GridForge: A Tractable Network-Flow Method for Constructing Open, Continental-Scale Synthetic Power Grids
comments: 30 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables; supplementary material as an ancillary file. Submitted to the International Journal of Electrical Power & Energy Systems. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24096575; code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23826484
summary: The goal of this paper is to construct open, continental-scale synthetic transmission grids with an optimization method that stays tractable. Security restrictions keep models of the real grid out of open research and machine-learning datasets, and optimization-based construction is hard at scale: the number of candidate lines grows combinatorially, so electrically faithful methods prune the candidates in advance. This paper presents GridForge, which keeps every bus pair within physical length limits as a candidate, selects lines with Garver's length-weighted network-flow linear program instead of binary decisions, and resizes them with a sequential direct-current (DC) power flow. Two stages of 13 regional networks are evaluated. Their node-degree distributions are nearly as strongly log-linear as those of the real Eastern and Western Interconnections ($R^2$ of 0.92 to 0.98 against 0.971 and 0.981), although the areas under the fitted lines differ from the real ones by 39.9% on average. On the upper Midwest and Tennessee Valley footprints, resizing lowers the DC power-flow loss from 5.89% to 4.14% and from 14.55% to 7.05%, and the DC optimal power-flow loss from 4.03% to 2.02% and from 5.54% to 2.47%. Without relaxing any line limit, the DC optimal power flow is feasible in 78.81% and 0.82% of the scenarios. Most lines are built at 69 kV. The models span 250 to 78,484 buses, were built on single machines, and are freely redistributable.

title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
comments: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, and Zhuoshi Tong contributed equally to this work
summary: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
comment: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, and Zhuoshi Tong contributed equally to this work

title: Disentangled Embedding Optimization for Diffusion-Based Dataset Distillation
comments: 10 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: Dataset distillation aims to compress large-scale datasets into compact synthetic subsets that enable efficient model training with comparable performance to the original data. Recent advances show that diffusion models are highly effective for this task due to their strong generative capability. Existing diffusion-based approaches typically perform class-wise clustering and use the obtained cluster prototypes as diffusion inputs to generate distilled samples. However, the uniformly distributed original samples in a category inevitably lead to entanglement near cluster boundaries, pulling the cluster prototypes closer and reducing the inter-cluster separation. Consequently, the diffusion model receives overly similar latent inputs, resulting in synthetic data with limited diversity. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled Embedding Optimization (DEO), a simple yet effective framework that replaces static clustering with trainable embeddings. These embeddings are optimized to match the Gaussian statistics (i.e., mean and covariance) of the original data distribution, while a diversity regularizer is designed to encourage separation among these embeddings to improve the intra-class variability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DEO can generate more diversified and representative distilled data than existing cluster-based diffusion methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and superior generalization across multiple datasets.
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)

title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
comments: Accepted at the GlobalSouthAI Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.
comment: Accepted at the GlobalSouthAI Workshop, NeurIPS 2026

title: DER Aggregators in Wholesale Electricity Markets: A Hybrid Mean-Field Framework with Endogenous Price Feedback
summary: The rapid growth of distributed energy resources (DERs), including rooftop solar and energy storage, is transforming the grid edge, where customer-side assets increasingly interact with the broader power grid. DER aggregators, entities that coordinate the actions of many small-scale DERs, play a key role in this transformation. This paper presents a hybrid Mean-Field Control (MFC) and Mean-Field Game (MFG) framework for integrating DER aggregators into wholesale electricity markets. Unlike traditional approaches that treat market prices as exogenous, our model captures the feedback between aggregators' collective actions and electricity prices. The MFC component optimizes DER operations within each aggregator, while the MFG models strategic interactions among multiple aggregators. To account for various uncertainties, we incorporate reinforcement learning, which allows aggregators to learn optimal bidding strategies in dynamic market conditions. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a mean-field equilibrium and validate the framework through a case study of the Oahu Island power system. Results show that our approach reduces price volatility and improves market efficiency, offering a scalable and decentralized solution for DER integration in wholesale markets.

title: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching Through Image-Editor Controls
comments: 27 pages, 12 figures, 18 tables. Main paper 8 pages plus supplementary material
summary: Photo retouching models are trained on pairs of original and retouched photographs, usually edited by experts. Expert edits are costly, so the two main public sets, FiveK and PPR10K, hold only 16,161 originals. Good photographs on their own are far easier to find: commercial stock collections and free ones such as Pixabay and Unsplash hold millions. We learn retouching from them alone: we damage each photograph the way a camera or a careless edit would, which gives a worse and a better version of the same photograph. From these pairs, our model, ATune, learns how 13 measured attributes, such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, should change to raise a photograph's quality. The edit is declarative: ATune sets target values for the attributes, and a simple search adjusts the sliders of an out-of-the-box photo editor until the photograph reaches them. Every edit is a list of slider values a person can read and adjust. The same model can drive any editor that makes those changes; we test RawTherapee and darktable. We train on 10M photographs from a commercial stock collection and test on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ. Nine quality judges score every edit, and in a user study 157 human raters made 9,253 choices between our edit and another method's edit of the same photograph. When Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra edit the same photographs in the same editor, raters prefer our edits to GPT-6 Astra's (54.3%) and rate them even with Claude's (50.5%). We also compare with supervised retouchers on their home ground: NeurOP on FiveK and AdaInt on PPR10K, each trained on that set's own expert edits. Raters chose our edits in 46.3% of those comparisons. ATune, a 54M-parameter model trained without a single expert edit, now matches frontier models at setting an editor's sliders.
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures, 18 tables. Main paper 8 pages plus supplementary material

title: Fully Explicit Stabilized Runge--Kutta Methods for Allen--Cahn and Cahn--Hilliard Dynamics
summary: Stiff phase-field dynamics are typically solved by semi-implicit or fully implicit time discretizations, since the interfacial scales in the Allen--Cahn and Cahn--Hilliard equations impose severe step-size restrictions on standard explicit methods. In this paper, we investigate a different strategy based on stabilized Runge--Kutta solvers, in particular the Runge--Kutta--Legendre (RKL) and Runge--Kutta--Gegenbauer (RKG) families. These schemes possess enlarged stability regions and therefore provide a natural explicit framework for diffusion-dominated gradient flows without requiring implicit solves. For the Allen--Cahn equation, combined with Strang splitting, we establish a maximum principle in 1-dimensional case, and prove energy dissipation in all the dimensions. For the modified energy dissipation analysis, we further introduce two new first-order stabilized schemes of RKL and RKG type and derive a novel eigenvalue estimate for the second-order RKG method. We also conduct extensive numerical experiments with both constant and adaptive time stepping, on regular domains as well as on an L-shaped irregular domain. The numerical results show that stabilized explicit Runge--Kutta methods provide an effective and flexible approach for the numerical simulation of Allen--Cahn and Cahn--Hilliard dynamics while preserving key structural properties. The Python implementation is available at https://github.com/ZT220501/SRK-for-Gradient-Flows.

title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms
comments: 13 pages. Revised version of engrXiv preprint (doi:10.31224/osf.io/pm3hy) with a corrected, leakage-free evaluation protocol; original results retained for reference
summary: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli naïve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicated data (by 8--19 percentage points). For RF on the raw data and for Bernoulli NB, the differences (0.2--1.5 percentage points) may not hold for a different split. RF with 7 selected features reaches 99.90\% accuracy and 94.88\% Macro-F1 on the deduplicated data. On the same split, this exceeds our re-implementations of the deep neural network configurations of previous studies and the feature subset selected by particle swarm optimization in one of them, while the run time saved on this low-dimensional data set is small. These results suggest that the method can support automatic firewall log analysis, while evaluation over multiple splits remains future work.
comment: 13 pages. Revised version of engrXiv preprint (doi:10.31224/osf.io/pm3hy) with a corrected, leakage-free evaluation protocol; original results retained for reference

title: A Lower-envelope Eikonal Neural Operator
summary: We propose the Lower-envelope Eikonal Neural Operator (LENO), a physics-informed neural operator for eikonal equations with heterogeneous velocity fields and general source sets. LENO encodes the variational minimum principle of viscosity solutions by constructing source-wise candidate fields and taking their pointwise minimum. This lower-envelope structure enforces the source condition exactly and represents nonsmooth multi-source solutions without a soft boundary penalty. The model is trained without precomputed solution data, using a Godunov upwind residual as the sole training signal. Experiments on point sources and curve sources, sample-dependent piecewise velocity fields, and OpenFWI CurveVel-A and Style-A media show accurate agreement with references of Fast Marching Method (FMM). Additional validation shows that the Godunov residual outperforms conventional finite difference residuals on a high-resolution test, that velocity conditioning and the lower-envelope transform are essential in realistic heterogeneous media, and that the trained operator supports efficient batched evaluation and resolution transfer.

title: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders
comments: 84 pages, 3 figures. Also available as Cryptology ePrint Archive, Paper 2026/2841: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2841
summary: We introduce SEC, an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, particularly suitable for lattice-based distributed cryptography. It is everywhere-short: bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients, and the integer reconstruction vectors have bounded entries. Moreover, each participant receives exactly one share, regardless of the number of parties and the privacy and reconstruction thresholds. This improves on prior schemes with bounded share coefficients and bounded entries in the integer reconstruction vectors, in which the number of sub-shares or shares per participant grows either with the number of parties and the threshold or with the security parameter. The construction rests on a coding-theoretic observation: in the bi-adjacency matrix of a lossless bipartite expander, unique-neighbor peeling completes every sufficiently small set of columns to a square unimodular submatrix. We prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and give a publicly computable entrywise bound on the reconstruction vector our algorithm returns for each authorized set. For privacy, we introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, which strengthens the leakage-resilience notion of Nielsen and Simkin (EUROCRYPT 2020) to protect a hard-core function of the secret, and we prove that SEC satisfies it against correlated multi-query local leakage under the MatrixHint-MLWE problem, which admits a reduction from the standard MLWE problem. For $n=60$ participants and security parameter $κ=128$, SEC achieves privacy threshold 6 against $2^{64}$ leakage queries and empirical reconstruction threshold 46. The ideal entropy-coded secret and share sizes are about 3.5 KiB and 6.4 KiB, respectively.
comment: 84 pages, 3 figures. Also available as Cryptology ePrint Archive, Paper 2026/2841: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2841

title: Agentic Dashboards: A New Design Paradigm for Visual Analytics
summary: Visual analytics systems traditionally combine analytical methods and interactive visualizations into a fixed application specified at the design phase. Coding agents offer a flexible approach: experts could conduct analysis through natural-language instructions. We envision an agentic dashboard as a persistent visual analytics workspace where an agent makes decisions about analytical methods, views, and their coordination within a designer-defined decision space. This approach shifts part of the visualization designer's role from engineering a fixed interface to defining the decisions an agent may make at runtime. We illustrate how such a dashboard could operate with current capabilities and propose criteria for evaluating its behavior and potential failures. As analytical workflows become more fluid and agent-mediated, visualization can help experts maintain awareness, coordinate with agents, and exercise judgment.

title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
summary: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.

title: MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance
summary: Modern ML frameworks execute models using the kernel-per-operator paradigm, which runs each operator as a separate GPU kernel. This paradigm is modular, since developers can compose various kernel implementations and profile each kernel in isolation. However, this paradigm enforces dependencies at the granularity of entire kernels, which places a barrier between dependent kernels. These barriers cause streaming multiprocessors to idle, serialize computation and communication, and prevent a kernel from prefetching its weights while the preceding kernel runs. Megakernels remove kernel barriers by fusing the operators of an entire layer or model into a single kernel, but they give up the modularity of the kernel-per-operator paradigm. In this work, we ask whether a kernel-per-operator ML framework can perform on par with megakernels. Our key insight is that removing kernel barriers does not require fusing kernels. We develop MegaOps, a framework that launches dependent kernels on separate CUDA streams and enforces each dependency on individual tiles of the intermediate tensor that the producer kernel writes and the consumer kernel reads. Since kernels synchronize on data tiles instead of on each other's thread blocks, any two kernels that adopt the same data tiling can be composed without modifying either kernel. We evaluate MegaOps on dense Llama3 and Qwen3 models on single H100, A100, and L40 GPUs and on multi-GPU servers with 4$\times$A100 and 8$\times$H100. Our MegaOps framework matches the throughput of hand-tuned ThunderKittens megakernels, and achieves 1.09$\times$-1.10$\times$ the decode throughput and 0.98$\times$-1.10$\times$ the prefill throughput of the best-performing baseline, while reusing existing Triton, cuBLAS, and cuDNN kernels.

title: Direct-Ink-Writing of Soft Thin Film Force-Sensitive Resistors with Velostat and Printed-Carbon Sensing Elements
comments: 12 pages, 18 figures, to be published in: IEEE Sensors
summary: Flexible resistive force sensors are useful for wearable, rehabilitation, and human--machine interfaces, but their performance depends on sensing-material architecture and fabrication. This work presents a parameterized Voltera NOVA-based direct-ink-writing workflow using printed silver electrodes with multilayer Velostat sensing elements on PET and TPU substrates, together with an exploratory fully printed carbon architecture. Velostat sensors containing 1, 2, 4, and 6 sensing layers exhibited strongly nonlinear force--voltage responses, with the greatest sensitivity at low forces. Best-fit straight-line $R^2$ values ranged from 0.475 to 0.641, area-based hysteresis from 3.90\% to 7.47\%, and 5-min voltage drift from 1.9\% to 7.3\%, with no consistent monotonic relationship between layer count and these metrics. Selected PET6 and TPU6 devices showed less than 0.05~V change in peak output between the first and final 100 cycles of a 10,000-cycle test. Printed-carbon devices demonstrated the feasibility of a more fully printed architecture, but configurations with six or fewer layers saturated below approximately 0.5~N or were nonfunctional, while the eight-layer device responded primarily below approximately 2~N. These results establish the feasibility of the printed-electrode Velostat workflow while identifying printed sensing materials as a key area for further development.
comment: 12 pages, 18 figures, to be published in: IEEE Sensors

title: A Constructive Theory of Closed-Form Rate-Distortion Functions
summary: Rate-distortion functions are defined by a variational problem whose analytic solution depends on the source distribution and distortion measure. We develop a posterior-based construction framework using conditional entropy as a common distortion coordinate. Building on the rate-entropy formulation, we establish entropy-level attainability for discrete sources with finite entropy and absolutely continuous sources with integrable log densities. We give a constructive rate-entropy coding proof for finite-alphabet sources and such continuous sources, without a second-moment assumption. Marginal compatibility ensures that a candidate posterior and output distribution recover the source, while a Gibbs representation and a kernel mass bound certify attainment of maximum conditional entropy. The negative log posterior identifies candidate fixed distortions. Excess rate equals a conditional entropy gap and decomposes into budget slack and posterior mismatch. Convolution decompositions and conjugate posteriors provide two construction paths. They recover established results, including the Gamma-source rate-distortion function under Itakura-Saito distortion, and yield a closed-form parametric expression for zeta sources under divisibility-constrained logarithmic multiplicative distortion. Exact expressions are obtained on specified intervals for negative binomial sources under one-sided counting distortion and Gamma sources under one-sided mean error. A residual-count coordinate for Poisson entropy budgets and rate-entropy parametrizations of Gamma and Dirichlet counting channels connect model parameters to remaining uncertainty. The framework unifies distortion selection, compatible-channel construction, and optimality verification.

title: Few-Shot Cross-Subject Neural--Image Retrieval via Stimulus-Anchored Latent Bias Calibration
summary: In cross-subject neural--image retrieval, comparing the mean of a few stimulus-matched target observations with the global source mean conflates subject-specific representation shifts with stimulus-composition effects. To address this problem, we propose Stimulus-Anchored Latent Bias Calibration (SA-LBC), which estimates the first-order shift under fixed preprocessing and a frozen source-trained representation by averaging residuals between target responses and same-stimulus source-population anchors, then shrinks the correction using source-derived uncertainty. Under uniform sampling without replacement from a finite stimulus population, we derive exact finite-population MSE expressions for the unshrunk anchored and global-mean estimators, including residual--anchor cross-covariance, and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for anchoring to reduce MSE relative to global-mean estimation. In a 10-subject leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2, SA-LBC increases mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for the Attention--CLIP ViT-B/32 configuration from 0.1867 without calibration to 0.2013 and 0.2336 with M=2 and M=16 stimulus-level calibration samples, respectively. Across six neural--visual configurations and all calibration budgets, stimulus-matched anchors yield higher MRR than anchors with shuffled stimulus identities, but retrieval gains over no calibration remain representation-dependent. At (M=2), shrinkage improves MRR over the unshrunk anchored estimator in all six configurations, but its effects at larger budgets vary across representations; the relative ranking of translation and orientation corrections also depends on regularization strength. Thus, lower shift-estimation MSE does not guarantee higher retrieval performance. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Xizhang-Yao/SA-LBC.

title: Reconstruct What You Can: Distractor-free 4D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.

title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
summary: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.

title: Rectified Looped Transformer
summary: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.

title: Causals: An Open Knowledge Graph for Research on Causal Reasoning
summary: Applying causal knowledge to a new event requires connecting the event to relevant entities and the relationships through which its consequences may unfold. We present Causals, an open knowledge graph for research on this form of reasoning. Its initial release, constructed from news reports, contains 369,184 nodes and 1,272,418 edges linking reported events, organizations, commodities, financial instruments, and other entities. Structural relationships, observations, and attributed causal claims retain distinct semantics and links to source records. We describe the construction and representation of the resource and characterize its connectivity and multi-hop retrieval properties. Causals provides shared relational knowledge for studying how language models retrieve relevant context and apply mechanisms to particular events. The dataset is available under CC BY 4.0 at https://causals.org/, and we invite contributions to its ontology, records, and evidence.

title: FlowIR: Depth-driven Rectified Flow for Resolving Thermal Ambiguity in Infrared Super-Resolution
comments: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo (ICME 2026)
summary: Distinguishing different heat sources in low-resolution infrared (IR) images is inherently difficult, as multiple thermal emitters often collapse into ambiguous and overlapping responses. Existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structures from such ambiguous 2D evidence, leading to thermal drift, boundary merging, and unreliable restoration under infrared degradations. We propose FlowIR, a depth-driven rectified flow framework that resolves thermal ambiguity by injecting 3D geometric cues into the generation process. Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects, while cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss further enforces geometric alignment during refinement. Built upon a lightweight rectified flow backbone, FlowIR restores IR images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust, and geometrically faithful high-resolution results.
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo (ICME 2026)

title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference
summary: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.

title: A Binary Search Tree with the Unified Bound
summary: We give a deterministic online binary search tree (BST) that satisfies the unified bound of Iacono [SODA 2001], which subsumes the working-set and dynamic-finger bounds: it serves every sequence $X$ of $m$ searches on $n$ keys at total cost $O(m+\mathrm{UB}(X))$, and every single search at cost $O(\log n)$. Previously, no BST was known to satisfy the unified bound, even offline. As a consequence, the dynamic optimality conjecture implies Iacono's conjecture that splay trees satisfy the unified bound. We also show that the unified bound is $O((m+n)(1+\log c_σ))$ on every sequence of searches that avoids a fixed permutation $σ$, where $c_σ$ is the Füredi-Hajnal limit of $σ$. Hence every BST that satisfies the unified bound, including ours, serves such sequences at this cost. For permutations this bound is tight, and it improves the previous upper bound $O(nc_σ^2)$ on the optimal cost, due to Berendsohn, Kozma and Opler [STOC 2024]. Finally, we extend the tree to support insertions and deletions: a sequence $X$ of $m$ operations, starting from $n_0$ keys, costs $O(n_0+m+\mathrm{UB}(X))$ in total, where $\mathrm{UB}$ is now the extension of the unified bound to insertions and deletions by Bădoiu, Cole, Demaine and Iacono [TCS 2007]. Hence, if splay trees are dynamically optimal for searches, insertions and deletions, then they serve every such sequence at this total cost as well.

title: Strong error estimates for finite element approximations of the stochastic Burgers--Huxley equation with multiplicative noise
summary: This paper is concerned with strong error estimates for fully discrete finite element approximations of the stochastic Burgers--Huxley equation with multiplicative noise. We use the implicit Euler--Maruyama scheme for time discretization and continuous piecewise linear finite elements for spatial discretization. Moment bounds and exponential integrability estimates are established and used with the discrete stochastic Gronwall inequality to derive error estimates in full expectation. Sub-second-moment error estimates are first obtained in the discrete maximum-in-time $L^2$-norm and the discrete $L^2$-in-time $H^1$-norm. Second-moment error estimates in the discrete maximum-in-time $L^2$-norm are then established using a higher-moment argument. The convergence rates are of order $k^{1/2}$ in time and $h$ in space, with the spatial rate being optimal in the $H^1$-norm. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to examine the convergence rates and the influence of multiplicative noise on the solution.

title: Demo: Matter-Based IoMT Telemetry and Security Analysis
summary: Connected health devices increasingly support health monitoring outside clinical settings, making secure and accessible physiological data important for patients and caregivers. However, device-specific applications and interfaces complicate the integration of readings from different devices. The Matter standard provides standardized device commissioning and protected communication, but its cluster library does not represent the health attribute measurement. We present a preliminary demo study of a Matter-based IoMT testbed with a specific HealthVitals cluster. Implemented in the connectedhomeip SDK on a Raspberry~Pi~5, the cluster exposes simulated heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, and body temperature. We examine commissioning, attribute retrieval, communication under simulated packet loss, and operational traffic through a reference controller. The study demonstrates that this custom telemetry model can operate within the tested Matter configuration without modifying commissioning or secure-session mechanisms. The resulting testbed gives researchers and device developers a concrete platform for investigating health-oriented extensions. It also supports exploration of local telemetry integration that could help patients and caregivers access readings across connected devices.

title: Robot Navigation and Obstacle Avoidance from Randomly Positioned External Cameras
comments: 8 pages, 2 figures, accepted as a regular paper for the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration
summary: We study robot navigation in indoor environments from fixed exocentric cameras (infrastructure-mounted, external to the robot). We show that standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which succeeds with onboard cameras, fails to learn this navigation end-to-end in our setup. This failure results from the perspective mismatch between exocentric observations and egocentric action and goal formulations, which is too complex to resolve from the reward signal alone. To address this, we propose Viewpoint-Invariant Navigation from Exocentric Cameras (VINE). VINE uses an obstacle map estimation network, trained with supervised learning, that takes exocentric images, camera pose, robot pose, and room dimensions as input and produces a viewpoint-invariant obstacle map. This map can be used either by a PPO policy or by a planner such as A*. VINE's map estimation performs better than perspective mapping approaches, handles cameras placed across a wide range of positions and orientations without view-specific tuning, requires only approximate camera pose estimates (noise with a standard deviation of 30cm per axis in x, y, and z and about 20° of rotation error on average), is robust to intrinsic variation, and extends to two-camera setups with partial coverage. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera in simulated environments.
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, accepted as a regular paper for the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration

title: RiskLens: Human-Informed Incident Transfer for AI Risk Evaluation
summary: As AI capabilities advance, early-stage teams need better ways to judge whether historical incidents transfer to new products, demanding support beyond static risk checklists or one-off ideation tools. We present RiskLens, a human-AI workflow with an interactive system built around a live crawl, refreshable ranker, and extensible, human-informed schema. RiskLens analyzes 2,034 AI incidents and 10,443 AI products to rank transferable incidents using a feature schema spanning technical, operational, and user-facing attributes and supports an interface that presents ranked incident evidence, generated scenarios, risk metrics, and mitigation suggestions. In a study with 21 AI-familiar participants, users surfaced evaluation criteria that we added as 13 human-informed dimensions, including harm categories, failure mechanisms, and vulnerable groups. The feature-based model outperformed a generic baseline with an 86.2% win rate, and remained stable on a twenty-month future holdout; after human-informed schema expansion, the updated model outperformed the same baseline on 91.4% of pairs.

title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents often fail to meet all requirements in the task description. In some of these failures, the agent considers an implementation choice that meets a requirement, but later decides to commit to another one that does not meet the requirement for a reason it finds acceptable. We call this specification satisficing. It is challenging to identify and mitigate specification satisficing because the agent accepts such choices for its own reasons, and existing self-correction methods are biased toward them. We propose SatisFix, which guides a coding agent to report these choices and their reasons, and then check each choice against the task description. We evaluate SatisFix on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Pro with five LLMs as backbones and two different agent frameworks, and compare it with three self-correction methods. SatisFix improves the pass@1 of the base agent by an average of 5.09% on DeepSWE and 7.06% on the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro. On DeepSWE, it outperforms the best baseline by 3.98%. Our ablation study shows that both steps of SatisFix contribute to the improvement.

title: Parallel Computing Systems for the Optimal Selection of Process Equipment
comments: 99 pages, 29 figures, 9 tables, 18 listings. English translation, by the author, with minor corrections, of the monograph originally published in Russian (Tambov, 2026)
summary: This monograph addresses the optimal selection of equipment for chemical-engineering systems of multiproduct batch plants, a large-scale NP-hard discrete optimization problem in which, for each processing stage, a unit of standard size must be chosen so that the total capital cost of the equipment is minimized while the system remains operable and produces the required products within a given time horizon. We present the mathematical model of system operation and analyze its computational properties. We then develop a sequential branch-and-bound algorithm and its parallel versions for shared-memory systems (OpenMP), distributed-memory clusters (MPI, master-worker), and graphics processing units (CUDA), including recursive and iterative tree traversal, shared-memory optimization, and branch-divergence reduction. To overcome the exponential growth of the run time, we propose a hybrid metaheuristic in which Ant Colony Optimization finds a feasible initial solution and Simulated Annealing improves it, and we implement it on GPUs with thousands of independent threads. Finally, we propose random, constant, and multi-constant approaches to tuning the parameters of the ant colony algorithm based on statistical analysis of many parallel runs, and we study the program on GPUs of three generations and on nodes with several GPUs. Computational experiments on multi-core processors, clusters, and GPUs show that the parallel hybrid algorithm finds solutions within 0.01% of the branch-and-bound optimum in tens of seconds instead of tens of hours.
comment: 99 pages, 29 figures, 9 tables, 18 listings. English translation, by the author, with minor corrections, of the monograph originally published in Russian (Tambov, 2026)

title: Rasoi: Visual Diffs for Evaluating Structural Changes Made by Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents let developers modify software rapidly through natural language. However, as agents take on larger changes, developers can lose track of how the codebase is evolving. These edits may look correct on the surface while restructuring the system in unexpected ways: duplicating logic, changing modules outside the requested scope, removing functionality developers meant to keep, or introducing architectural drift. We investigate how visual diffs can help developers understand and evaluate the structural changes that coding agents make.
