title: Evaluating Video LLMs' Understanding of Corner Cases in Autonomous Driving
summary: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io

title: Class-Competence Aggregation: Output-Layer Routing for Federated Multiclass DDoS Detection under Class-Concentrated Non-IID Data
summary: Federated learning over distributed intrusion-detection sensors naturally produces \emph{class-concentrated} non-IID data, where an entire attack class is held by a single client and absent elsewhere. We show this collapses federated averaging in a specific, localized way: the output layer holds one decision boundary per class, and when a class's aggregation weight comes overwhelmingly from clients that have never seen it, its neuron receives an active anti-signal rather than mere dilution, collapsing to zero. On CIC-DDoS2019, standard FedAvg drives the concentrated LDAP class to $0.00 \pm 0.00\%$ F1 across every seed. We propose Class-Competence Aggregation (CCA), which aggregates the output layer per class using each client's own locally reported validation F1 as the weight, while hidden layers remain under standard size-weighted FedAvg. CCA requires no server-held auxiliary data and adds only one F1 scalar per class per round beyond the feature-scaling and class-count exchanges common to any federated pipeline. On our primary CNN-LSTM architecture, CCA alone raises LDAP F1 from $0\%$ to $84.83 \pm 1.65\%$, and the full method reaches $91.64 \pm 0.57\%$ macro F1, closing the federated-to-centralized gap from $-42.53$ to $-4.05$ points. Benchmarked against four other federated methods under identical partitions and seeds, CCA is the only one that recovers the concentrated class substantially and reliably; a $178\times$ smaller MLP shows the same qualitative recovery, though less completely, confirming the effect holds across architecture scale even as its magnitude varies. Results are validated across three seeds and replicated on a second dataset, CICIDS2017.

title: Key Relay and Secure Network Coding: One-Shot Equivalence and Separation on Undirected Networks
summary: Motivated by quantum key distribution networks, we compare key relay protocols with secure network coding on the same undirected graph. In this comparison, we fix the finite field, terminal set, and wiretap family. Each edge supplies one independent uniform symbol to its endpoints for key relay, or carries one symbol once for network coding. The network code may choose its source terminal, edge orientations, and causal transmission order before execution. In this setting, the standard one-time-pad simulation readily converts every secure network code to key relay. We investigate the reverse conversion to linear network coding. For two terminals and a one-symbol key, arbitrary key relay is equivalent to scalar linear acyclic network coding over the prescribed field. The proof uses connectivity and flow conservation, related to the binary $st$-flow protocol. However, this equivalence fails in general when several terminals seek one common key. A doubled triangle separates key relay from acyclic coding but admits causal coding on a cyclic orientation. On the four-terminal complete graph, a linear key relay protocol over the ternary field withstands the three perfect-matching wiretap sets, whereas no linear causal network code distributes a source symbol of the same size, even with private randomness at every vertex and its use in decoding. We also establish a linear key relay normal form that removes interaction and private randomness and bounds public communication. All results concern one-shot feasibility with exact agreement and perfect secrecy.

title: Computation with Backward Feedback: Power, Observation, and Cost
summary:
How much can a computation gain by passing information back to an earlier stage, and how soon can an observer obtain the answer? We study deterministic programs whose runs are accessed at randomly selected stages. A program keeps a register, a finite block of memory. A random clock selects the current stage; each tick takes a random step, with a law fixed independently of input, program and register. When the clock moves backward, the register contents at the stage it leaves start a new run, and the clock continues where it lands. Equilibrium readout requires a distribution of clock position and register that one tick leaves unchanged, and a correct final answer under every such distribution.
  For bounded steps in both directions with negative average, we obtain an exact classification at each polynomial scale s. If running time and register length are both O(s), feedback gives exactly nondeterministic space O(s); without transmission the class is deterministic time O(s), which is strictly smaller.
  An observer that starts at stage zero with an all-zero register, reads sequentially and never accepts a nonmember sees, with fewer ticks than any exponential, only languages fixed by a bounded input prefix. Exponentially many ticks reveal every linear-time language. For a clock moving one step up or down, we bound the wait for useful backward moves and the rate of random erasures a stored counter tolerates. The results separate the power of feedback at equilibrium, observation from a fixed start, and the cost of obtaining and keeping information.

title: ScrewSense: Mapping the Invisible - Anomaly Detection and Error Classification in Screwdriving Processes
comments: Accepted manuscript, 59th CIRP Conference on Manufacturing Systems (CMS 2026). 6 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables
summary: The growing volume of process data generated by screwdriving systems, combined with advancements in computing power, data storage, and algorithms, is facilitating the application of artificial intelligence in this field. Accurately detecting and classifying screwdriving errors is crucial for ensuring product quality, avoiding costly rework in manufacturing, and supporting sustainability by facilitating the maintenance, reuse, and recycling of screw-connected products. In this context, machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional monitoring techniques, such as window-based methods or envelope curves. This study examines the use of deep learning techniques for anomaly detection and error classification in screwdriving processes. The data corpus consists of multivariate time series capturing process parameters, such as torque and rotation angle. For anomaly detection, the embedding space of a vector quantized variational autoencoder was analyzed. In terms of error classification, four different model architectures were evaluated. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of anomaly detection and confirm that deep learning models can distinguish between multiple error categories beyond traditional binary classification. This extends the capabilities of conventional monitoring approaches, achieving accuracies of up to 100%. Additionally, real-world data material was examined in order to further demonstrate model robustness. Overall the results indicate strong generalization capability and highlight the practical potential of the developed models for use in industrial screwdriving processes, eliminating the need for expert knowledge in error identification and significantly reducing manual effort and analysis time.

title: EG360: Efficient and Generalizable $360^\circ$ Depth Estimation via Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation and Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion
summary: Generalized panorama depth estimation has witnessed great advances in recent years. These methods typically achieve robust zero-shot generalization performance using large pretrained models, but their high computational cost makes real-time inference on embedded platforms challenging. In contrast, previous lightweight panorama models have mostly been developed for single-domain evaluations and cannot generalize well due to domain shifts. To reduce the gap between these two types of models, we introduce EG360, an efficient and generalizable panorama depth estimation model. Specifically, building on a lightweight depth model, we design an Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation (APPD) strategy guided by scene geometry, along with a Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion (SCFF) module for global semantic perception. As a result, with only 6.593M parameters after reparameterization, EG360 achieves strong zero-shot performance on real-world benchmarks and runs at 35 FPS on a Jetson Orin NX 16GB in MAXN mode, whereas a previous ViT-small model runs at less than 2 FPS. Our code will also be made public for future research.

title: KuaiRecV2: Benchmarking Large-Scale Continual Learning for Diversified and Multi-task Recommendation
comments: This paper has been accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary:
Recommender systems, which retrieve items of interest to users based on their interaction histories, have recently witnessed several key technological advancements, benefiting from the semantic representation space and model-data scaling. Nevertheless, practitioners and researchers have frequently encountered critical inconsistencies between simple offline evaluations and complex online results, and this gap still exists in the era of large models. In this work, we address several key factors that contribute to this inconsistency: 1) the \textit{large-scale continual learning challenge} that assumes a practical demand to maintain long-term model effectiveness under dynamic item pools and distributional shifts; 2) the \textit{combinatorial diversity challenge} that requires the generation strategy to solve the accuracy-diversity trade-off in both the finer token level and the holistic item level; and 3) the \textit{multi-task reward balancing challenge}, which is particularly critical for modern generative models that can accurately model the sequence distribution but are less controllable for the multi-task demands.
  To address these challenges and further pave the way for the development of more realistic recommendation solutions, we introduce KuaiRecV2, a deliberately constructed benchmark with industrial-level datasets from Kuaishou. Specifically, we provide a large-scale interaction dataset with million-scale multi-modal item information and long-term interaction records across 30 days, with a dynamic video candidate pool. Additionally, we provide a rigorous benchmark that evaluates retrieval accuracy, diversity, and multi-task performance in one rubric system, where an effective advancement occurs if and only if the new method improves all metrics. The code is available at https://github.com/cxli2333/KuaiRecV2

title: Structure-Preserving Learning for Nonlinear Nonholonomic Dynamics
summary: Learning the dynamics of mechanical systems subject to nonlinear nonholonomic constraints is challenging, as data-driven models may violate the underlying physical constraints, leading to inconsistent predictions. To address this problem, we develop a constraint-preserving learning framework based on the Lagrange-d'Alembert-Chetaev equations and tangency to the constraint submanifold, which together define an affine space of admissible accelerations. Using the kinetic-energy metric and the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, we construct a metric projector and the corresponding Chetaev correction. Embedding this geometric structure directly into a Gaussian process prior ensures that both prior and posterior dynamics satisfy the acceleration constraints exactly. We characterize the resulting reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), derive an adapted-coordinate representation, and establish nonexpansiveness and consistency transfer. Numerical experiments on a three-dimensional directional flocking system with up to 50 agents demonstrate exact constraint preservation and robustness to constraint-incompatible observations.

title: Transverse impact of a Hertzian sphere with an infinite Rayleigh beam
summary: We study the impact of a Hertzian sphere on an infinite Rayleigh beam, which presents both interesting possibilities for numerical approximation as well as new insights in the multiple-contact-event regime. Here, Galerkin projection using an abstract continuous variable replaces the history-dependent convolution in the impact equations by a system of local-in-time ordinary differential equations. The corresponding approximate solutions are validated against direct numerical solution of the convolution-based formulation and show agreement. Unlike the corresponding Euler-Bernoulli beam impact problem, which is governed by a single nondimensional parameter, the Rayleigh beam impact dynamics is governed by two nondimensional parameters. A parametric study reveals three distinct impact regimes: one regime with a single contact followed by permanent separation, a second regime with a single contact that is sustained thereafter, and an intervening regime with initial separation followed by multiple contact events with diminishing amplitudes, leading eventually to sustained contact. Short- and long-time asymptotic analyses are used to characterize the boundaries between the permanent separation and the re-contact regimes in different parameter regimes. The three significant new aspects of this paper are the system itself (Rayleigh beam instead of Euler Bernoulli beam), the model order reduction achieved through Galerkin projection in an abstract domain, and the detailed parametric study leading to a simple qualitative picture of possible behaviours.

title: A Code-Level Audit of X
summary: The transparency regime of recommender systems on Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) is undergoing significant change under the EU Digital Services Act (DSA). The DSA requires platforms to disclose information about their recommendation pipelines and grants vetted researchers access to non-public data, which may extend to recommender code. However, it is not known to what extent such code releases enable substantive and meaningful third-party auditing of a production recommender system. We address this question by proposing a code-level audit methodology for recommender systems and applying it to the X platform, which has voluntarily open-sourced its recommender pipeline. Our methodology is a backwards-walk traversal of the repository, tracing each decision-relevant component from the user-facing timeline back to its upstream producers, checking that it is reachable from the served pipeline, and classifying each under a four-tier inspectability scheme. Applying this procedure, we identify 13 transparency dead-ends on the live serving path: models, services, label lists, and configuration values that the public code depends on but the release does not contain. We find that the components that decide which posts are filtered and how they are ranked fall into the two least inspectable tiers, a pattern that intensifies with the 2025 integration of the proprietary Grok language model into moderation, annotation, and ranking. We further show that the release keeps 2023 code that the 2025 pipeline no longer reaches, with 36 parameter references that would pass for dead-ends without a reachability check. Finally, we discuss which additional artifacts would be required for meaningful auditing.

title: Agentic Orchestration for SLA-Constrained Network Slicing in Programmable Mobile Data Planes
comments: Accepted author manuscript for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC 2027), Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, January 9-12, 2027
summary: The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Technical Specification 23.501 (Release 17) defines Maximum Bit Rate (MBR) enforcement at the User Plane Function (UPF) in fifth-generation (5G) networks. Supporting differentiated service-level agreements across the radio access and core networks requires the UPF to enforce MBR limits according to configured slice priorities. During overload, the challenge is to adapt these limits while preserving that differentiation and avoiding oscillations. Building on programmable enforcement and intelligent orchestration, we propose an agentic control loop combining UPF telemetry with locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM) selection from a finite set of admissible rate candidates. Deterministic logic validates each selection and derives Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) updates. The evaluated runs show no oscillations or fallbacks and unchanged highest-priority rate limits. These observations establish configuration preservation; delivered per-class QoS protection remains unmeasured.

title: Detection Is Not Early Warning: Evaluating Token-Level Alarms on Language Model Failures
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability as a Science. 30 pages (10 main text), 6 figures, 16 tables. Code: https://github.com/swiss-ai/degeneration-probe
summary: Many failures of language models begin at a specific token, the onset. A monitor that reads the model during generation can classify the finished response, detect the failure once it is under way, or warn before it begins, and only a warning leaves time to stop or steer the generation. Monitors are usually evaluated with response-level metrics such as AUROC, which ignore when the monitor fires. We introduce PREWARN, an evaluation protocol for any failure with an annotated onset. It calibrates each monitor's threshold on validation data to an error rate chosen for the application, runs the monitor, and scores its alarms relative to the onset on all three tasks. As a case study we apply it to repetitive degeneration in three open language models, with early warning as the main task, using linear probes on activations and six untrained baselines. Response-level metrics saturate on this failure, and a rule that reads only the response length scores almost perfectly, while probes that AUROC ranks as equal warn very differently under PREWARN. Probes warn before the onset on most degenerate responses of two of the three models, low-rank adapters below the probe more than double the share of tokens just before the onset that it flags, largely by flagging degenerate responses long before the onset, and no untrained baseline warns much more often than random alarms. We release the probes with calibrated thresholds at https://huggingface.co/collections/marcodene/prewarn-degeneration-probes

title: FlatSeek: LLM-Driven Symbolic Discovery of Flat Outputs via Backward Data Generation
summary: Differential flatness enables efficient planning and control, but discovering explicit flat outputs for general nonlinear systems remains difficult due to the lack of general methods and supervised data. We propose FlatSeek, a framework combining backward data generation with task-specific large language model (LLM) training. By reversing the defining reconstruction of flatness, we generate system-flat-output pairs with known certificates, then fine-tune an LLM to propose symbolic flat-output candidates for unseen dynamics. On literature and synthetic benchmarks, FlatSeek outperforms both the traditional symbolic methods and the untuned reference models in flat-output discovery success, and uncovers alternative symbolic flat outputs not reported in the literature.

title: Quantum Network Flows That Solve Linear Equations
summary: We develop a distributed quantum network flow for solving linear equations from locally stored row data. Local pumping enforces each node's equation constraint, while neighboring registers interact through swaps. The node marginals obey an exact, closed flow combining consensus with local constraint enforcement. For consistent equations, all node states converge exponentially to a common state supported on the solution space; a unique solution yields full-network convergence to the product solution state. For inconsistent equations of full column rank, scaled encoding and readout recover the least-squares solution through successive large-gain and small-scale limits. For consistent systems, the marginal convergence rate is nondecreasing and concave in the swap gain, approaching a graph-independent limit for fixed local dissipators. Its leading finite-gain correction couples graph topology and row placement through the Laplacian pseudoinverse, enabling semidefinite optimization of edge rates under a fixed total swap-rate budget. For invertible systems, a dissipative HHL-type construction using the same pumping law provides a comparison of solution-state encodings, decay rates, and row-update locality under squared-row-norm pumping. Numerical examples are provided to validate the presented results.

title: Improved Deterministic Algorithms for $k$-SAT: Generalization of Chains and Recurrence Proof
summary: We present a deterministic algorithm for 3-SAT running in $1.32736^n$ time. The algorithm is built on a branching-and-chain framework augmented with a polynomial-time expansion procedure that joins short chains through additional clauses to form bounded-size blocks, which impose stronger constraints on the assignment space. After branching, the algorithm chooses between derandomized local search guided by the block structure and enumeration of block assignments together with selected port variables, reducing the remaining formula to 2-SAT. A weighted analysis of branching, partial-assignment, and local-search costs, together with inductive bounds for chains and block interactions, establishes the running-time guarantee. The framework is self-contained and also offers guidance for practical SAT solver design by identifying useful clause-overlap structures and suggesting when to switch between local-search and reduction-based strategies.

title: Selective Chaining of Parameterised Boolean Equation Systems
summary: Parameterised Boolean Equations Systems (PBESs) are used to verify properties of formal industrial models. We introduce a technique called selective chaining to simplify these PBESs by unfolding specific predicate variable instances when the unfolding results in a PBES that is likely to be simpler. For determining the latter we propose a set of heuristics. We show the formal correctness of the chaining operator and provide theoretical upper bounds using relevancy graphs on the size of the verification problem after chaining. Lastly, we study the effectiveness of our heuristics, showing that selective chaining can reduce memory usage and yield significant speed-ups solving PBESs that encode model checking problems for complex industrial systems.

title: Outcome-Mass Alignment: Controlling Length-Dependent Trajectory Influence in Multi-Turn LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: To keep long interaction contexts tractable, stepwise group-relative training for multi-turn LLM agents materializes each source trajectory into multiple response rows and valid tokens. This expansion creates an outer-accounting problem distinct from within-trajectory credit assignment: row-based outcome statistics can count one episode outcome multiple times, while token-level reduction can assign unequal aggregate objective mass across trajectories. We term these effects outcome-statistics multiplicity and objective-mass imbalance. We introduce Outcome-Mass Alignment (OMA), a two-component method that makes both accounting choices explicit. Outcome Alignment computes outcome statistics over unique source trajectories, while Mass Alignment controls aggregate objective mass after within-trajectory aggregation of optimizer-native token objectives. Neither redesigns the base optimizer's credit assignment, importance ratios, or clipping. Across matched ALFWorld GRPO comparisons at two model scales, where failed trajectories typically expand much more than successful ones, OMA improves matched-horizon endpoint success by 7.0-9.4 percentage points. Ordinary WebShop exhibits weak or reversed expansion-outcome coupling and correspondingly mixed effects, whereas in a success-oriented WebShop setting, WebShop-SOL, OMA improves success nAUC from 0.399 to 0.511. Component ablations and GiGPO and GSPO comparisons further support component separability and cross-optimizer compatibility. These results show that trajectory expansion always defines an implicit weighting rule, but its practical effect depends on how expansion couples to outcomes and optimizer-native updates.

title: Signed Dyadic Path Encoding for Efficient Non-Interactive Private Decision Tree Evaluation over TFHE
comments: 17 pages (15 + 2 pages of supplementary material), 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computing
summary: Private decision-tree evaluation lets a server classify a client's encrypted query without learning the input. In the non-interactive, path-based setting over TFHE, the server returns a single encrypted prediction by aggregating per-path comparison outcomes, and the standard per-leaf formulation pays one programmable bootstrap (PBS) per leaf, which dominates the cost. We propose a signed dyadic path-sum encoding that nearly halves this cost: each internal node receives a signed dyadic label so that every root-to-leaf path accumulates a distinct integer sum, which lets the two children of a leaf-parent be packed into a single test polynomial and resolved by one PBS, reducing the PBS count from the number of leaves to the number of leaf-parents. We formalize the distinct-sum property and prove that the dyadic labeling is the range-minimal encoding satisfying it, and its half-symmetric signed form is magnitude-optimal, tightening the comparison-stage noise bound at fixed parameters. We derive the two conditions under which the encrypted evaluation returns the exact prediction and instantiate parameters with per-inference failure below $2^{-64}$ at 128-bit security. We show that the ring degree grows linearly with the consumed plaintext range, which confines the profitable regime to depths $\leq 4$, where our method stays faster even when each scheme runs at its own cost-optimal parameters. We further extend the encoding to gradient-boosted ensembles. On standard UCI benchmarks at depths 1-4, our method reduces single-tree latency by $1.51\times$-$1.92\times$ and ensemble latency by $2\times$, without accuracy loss, while preserving the compact, non-interactive response.
comment: 17 pages (15 + 2 pages of supplementary material), 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computing

title: Canonical Truncation for Mixed-Integer and Combinatorial n-Fold Optimization
summary:
We consider a special block-structured integer program with $n$ blocks. Every block has a prescribed number of vectors that need to be selected while minimizing the objective $c^{\intercal}x + g(Ax)$, where $c$ is a rational cost vector, $A$ is an integral matrix with $d$ rows, and $g \colon \mathbb{Z}^d \to \mathbb{Q}\cup \{+\infty\}$ is an arbitrary function. We access $g$ via an oracle that minimizes $c^{\intercal}x + g(Ax)$ when all but $O(d)$ variables are fixed. Our algorithm runs in time $(ndΔ)^{O(d)}(Q + \text{poly}(|I|))$ where $Δ$ is the largest absolute value of an entry in $A$, $Q$ is the necessary time to evaluate the oracle for $g$ and $|I|$ is the size of the input. This model is a variation of the model studied by Dadush et al.~[IPCO 23]. Their model has only a single block but individual upper and lower bounds on the variables instead of prescribed block sums. For their model they present an algorithm with running time $t^d(dΔ)^{O(d^2)}Q$ where $t$ is the number of variables.
  We use our algorithm to solve mixed-integer linear programs with no upper bounds on the variables, a linear objective, and arbitrarily many constraints involving only fractional variables in time $(mΔ)^{O(m)}\text{poly}(|I|)$, where $m$ is the number of constraints involving integral variables and $Δ$ is the largest absolute value of coefficients of integral variables. This improves the dependence on $m$ in the exponent to asymptotically match the dependency in the integer setting. Further, we use our algorithm to generalize the parameterized algorithm for scheduling on uniformly related machines by Rohwedder~[ICALP 25] to obtain an algorithm for multiple knapsack with running time $w_{\max}^{O(d)}\text{poly}(|I|)$ where $w_{\max}$ is the maximum weight of an item and $d$ the number of different weights.

title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly tested on medical exam questions, but accuracy alone does not show when an answer can be trusted. I study the calibration and uncertainty of two open-weight models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Jais-adapted-7B-chat (both run in 4-bit precision), on 2,816 English multiple-choice questions from MedMCQA and 4,927 Arabic multiple-choice questions from MedAraBench. Accuracy was 0.561 (English) and 0.430 (Arabic) for Qwen, and 0.369 and 0.308 for Jais. Raw option probabilities were overconfident in all four settings (expected calibration error 0.242 to 0.486), and a single temperature parameter removed 82% to 93% of that error. Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options. The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged. Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at https://github.com/Mariyaaleem/arabic-english-medqa-uncertainty.

title: A Modular Framework for ESG Prediction through Domain-Specific Language Modeling and Graph Learning
summary: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores are increasingly used to evaluate corporate sustainability, supporting investment decisions, ensuring regulatory compliance and assessing risk. However, current ESG evaluations largely rely on proprietary methodologies that often produce inconsistent ratings. This motivates the development of data-driven prediction frameworks. In this paper, we present ESGPred, a modular framework for predicting ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modeling with graph-based learning over a network that models the relationships among the companies being evaluated. In addition to presenting the rationale behind ESGPred and detailing its ESG score prediction process, we show that ESGPred can effectively predict both overall ESG ratings and their individual Environmental, Social, and Governance components. We evaluated ESGPred using a dataset of 5,266 sustainability reports published by 2,134 publicly listed companies between 2020 and 2023. In this evaluation, we used ESG ratings provided by LSEG Data & Analytics as ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrated that integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.

title: Earlier citation practices are linked to signs of artificial intelligence use in scientific writing
summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more common in scientific writing, some authors show fewer signs of AI assistance than expected across successive periods. We analysed OpenAlex publication histories for 71,133 authors with at least one eligible first-authored English-language publication each year from 2023 through September 2026. Using abstract-based writing scores, we defined resistance as the predicted minus observed share of abstracts classified as AI-assisted. Positive scores indicate fewer such abstracts than expected. Early resistance was positively associated with later resistance, although the share with positive scores fell. Environmental characteristics contributed more than individual characteristics to predicting later scores, although overall predictive power was low. Having a collaborator with a non-positive early score was associated with lower subsequent resistance. Authors with positive mean scores in both 2023-2024 and 2025-2026 cited older work, drew on fewer subfields and more often cited sources they had used before than authors with non-positive mean scores in both periods. These differences were evident before 2023. The adjusted gap in reference reuse rose from 3.24 percentage points before 2023 to 7.95 in 2025-2026. The findings link variation in signs of AI assistance to earlier differences in how scientists used prior work.

title: Explicit Edit Codes via Multicoloring
summary: For any fixed integers $q\ge2$ and $t\ge1$, we construct explicit $q$-ary codes of length $n$ that correct any combination of at most $t$ insertions, deletions, and substitutions, with redundancy at most $2t\log_q n+O_{q,t}(\log\log n)$ $q$-ary symbols. This matches the leading redundancy term of Levenshtein's classical existential bound. Building on the standard graph-coloring approach, we use a prime-based multicoloring of the edit-confusion graph to assign multiple colors to each $q$-ary word of length $m<n$. Appending a short, edit-protected representation of an assigned color to the length-$m$ word yields a length-$n$ codeword. The choice among the assigned colors carries additional message information, thereby reducing the redundancy. The construction admits deterministic encoding and decoding in $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{6t+2})$ and $\widetilde O_{q,t}(n^{7t+2})$ time, respectively.

title: Kosmo-GFM: A Production-Ready Geometry Foundation Model
summary: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
summary: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
summary: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $Δ_0$ suffice for a $15(Δ_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $Θ(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(Δ_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((Δ_0+1)(d+\log(k/η)))$ slots with failure probability at most $η$; for fixed $Δ_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/η))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

title: Constrained intersection representations and forbidden patterns
summary:
We study the interplay between two types of graph classes: the ones defined by intersections of geometric objects and the ones defined by the absence of a substructure. More precisely, we study intersection graphs that are grounded, that is, the objects lie above a horizontal line that they touch, and ordered graphs with forbidden patterns, that is, ordered graphs that avoid a set of ordered induced subgraphs. These two approaches are fundamentally different, but it is known that several interesting graph classes have both types of characterizations, and we aim to understand whether this is a general phenomenon. Our contributions are the following.
  First, we identify a family of patterns on four vertices and a natural hierarchy of intersection graphs of strings whose classes are nicely interleaved. This raises hopes to prove connections between the two perspectives.
  Second, we dampen these hopes by proving that a class of (ordered) intersection graphs that we study cannot be characterized by a finite set of forbidden patterns.
  Third, we show a dual impossibility result: there exists a pattern-defined class of our hierarchy that admits no intersection representation, if we require this representation to be closed under natural operations such as translation and scaling. However, it turns out that if we allow slightly more exotic intersection representations, then we can find one for this pattern-defined class.

title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors
summary: Numerical simulations of fracture propagation require accurate computation of stress intensity factors (SIFs) to determine whether a pre-existing fracture will propagate. Even though displacement solutions from well-established numerical methods generally converge with mesh refinement, the convergence behavior of SIF estimates remains less understood. In this work, we propose a scaling law to improve the performance of SIF extraction using two-point displacement correlation methods. This scaling law relates sampling distance from the fracture tip to mesh resolution. It is developed by balancing the asymptotic truncation error against the numerical discretization error. Three numerical discretization methods--standard quadratic finite elements, quadratic finite elements with quarter-point elements, and a multi-point stress approximation finite volume method--are employed to validate the proposed scaling law on fracture benchmark problems under pure-mode and mixed-mode loading. We find that the conventional nearest-tip sampling strategy fails to compute convergent SIF estimates. In contrast, the proposed scaling-based approach yields decreasing errors in the SIF estimates as the mesh is refined. Across all three discretization methods, the proposed scaling law captures the sampling locations required for convergent SIF extraction, suggesting a general numerical characteristic of near-tip SIF extraction.

title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
comments: Accepted author manuscript for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC 2027), Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, January 9-12, 2027
summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.
comment: Accepted author manuscript for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC 2027), Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, January 9-12, 2027

title: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning
summary: While language-model agents excel at long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, this success relies on two conditions: explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. However, neither condition holds in real-world problems where critical information exists only in images, leaving it unclear whether long-horizon capability transfers from text to visual reasoning. In such visual settings, because rules and clues resist text transcription and lack test-case feedback, agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations, and autonomously cross-check clues. Despite this challenge, existing evaluations fail to capture such capability: visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, whereas agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that permit trial-and-error. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual Cipher Bench, a collection of 40 original visual puzzles across four categories: spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding. Each puzzle provides only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, requiring agents to discover the underlying solving mechanism entirely from the images. Across 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieves only 26.7% accuracy, while five of the eight models score below 1%. Yet on a ten-task subset, providing a single non-spoiler mechanism hint boosts accuracy from 7.8% to 55.6%. This sharp contrast shows that the primary bottleneck of current agents lies not in executing multi-step plans, but in autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. Visual Cipher Bench thus provides a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents.

title: Adjacent Heat Transfer Effects Can Bias Savings Estimates When Controlling Only Part of a Multi-Zone Building
comments: 10 pages. Accepted at the 2027 ASHRAE Winter Conference
summary: Field demonstrations of advanced heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning control often operate a few thermal zones within a larger building and report savings for those zones alone. A recent theorem showed that this practice overestimates whole-building savings, because heat drawn from the neighboring zones is paid for by their equipment and is not counted. The error grows with the thermal conductance between the controlled and uncontrolled zones, with how much colder the controlled zones run over the test, and with the price of the heat their neighbors supply. For one controlled zone with one neighbor, a single thermal price, and slowly changing prices, the relative error reduces to the ratio of two conductances, a screening number that can be evaluated from the two conductances before a demonstration begins. This paper tests how far that reduction can be taken. A two-story house with one thermal zone per floor is simulated over a 90-day heating season in West Lafayette, Indiana, with receding-horizon model predictive control on the first floor and setpoint control on the second, under four combinations of electricity tariff (time-of-use or flat) and heating plant (heat pump or electric resistance). The exact correction from the theorem recovers the true savings in every case, and the full theorem, evaluated from the controlled zone's temperatures, the prices, and the building parameters, reproduces the measured relative error in every case. The conductance ratio bounds that error from above in all four cases, tightly under a flat tariff, within 3%, and loosely under a time-of-use tariff, where most of the controller's savings come from shifting load through the thermal mass rather than from lowering the temperature.
comment: 10 pages. Accepted at the 2027 ASHRAE Winter Conference

title: Raysemble: Metric 3D Bone Reconstruction from a Single X-ray
summary: Raysemble reconstructs eight lumbar and pelvic bones from a single X-ray by separating shape and placement. Each 3D query samples regional and global features at its image projection. A shared decoder predicts normalized bone shapes. Predicted depth and camera geometry determine 3D centers and scales for resampling these shapes onto a common grid in millimeters. Evaluation uses 23 held-out patients with 43 CT scans, each generating one simulated anteroposterior radiograph. Without rigid alignment to CT,Raysemble leads 15 evaluated methods, averaging 65.24% Dice, 9.09 mm HD95, and 3.32 mm ASSD over three random seeds. With identical inputs, it improves Dice over VolumeNeRF by 5.86 percentage points.

title: DPA: Decentralized Primal Averaging with Quasi-Global Momentum for Highly Heterogeneous Data
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 7 figures. Code available at https://github.com/Diyako754/DPA
summary: Decentralized training of deep learning models keeps training data local and supports on-device learning over networks. In realistic scenarios, heterogeneity across agents' local data poses an optimization challenge and can severely degrade test accuracy, especially on sparse communication graphs. Building on recent advances in centralized primal averaging, we propose Decentralized Primal Averaging (DPA), a decentralized learning algorithm that combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer. DPA maintains three coupled sequences for optimization, gradient evaluation, and output averaging, while using consecutive mixed iterates to construct a network-aware momentum direction without transmitting an auxiliary tracking variable. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a convergence bound for DPA and identify conditions for linear speedup in the number of agents for sufficiently many iterations. We also introduce DPA-1G, a variant that uses one communication round per iteration and matches the per-iteration communication cost of DSGD-style baselines. Experiments following the GUT decentralized image-classification benchmark show that DPA compares favorably with DSGD, gradient tracking, QG-DSGDm, momentum tracking, and QG-GUTm across datasets, architectures, topologies, and heterogeneity levels, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. At the same total communication cost, both DPA variants achieve higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20. Our code is publicly available.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 7 figures. Code available at https://github.com/Diyako754/DPA

title: ACE-CaP-0: Real-World Code-as-Policies in the Era of Experience
summary: Recent advances in frontier models have pushed the boundaries of agentic robot control, enabling agents to perform complex robotic tasks through reasoning and interaction. However, repeated calls to these models during execution can substantially increase task completion time. Code as Policies (CaP) offers a route for coding agents to acquire physical skills through experience and retain them in executable programs, allowing the reasoning invested in development to be reused across runs. Developing reliable code policies while limiting the cost of physical experimentation remains a central challenge. We investigate human guidance as a source of priors for feasible actions and simulation as an auxiliary environment for exploring and testing candidate policies. Our findings favor robot demonstrations available on request and simulation used selectively during real-world policy refinement. These findings inform ACE-CaP-0, an agentic recipe that couples policy revision with experience acquisition through Demonstrations on Request and Simulation on Demand. Across eight real-world manipulation tasks spanning alignment, multi-object handling, and bimanual coordination, the resulting frozen programs achieve 92.1\% success (221/240 trials). Mean execution times across tasks range from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. The programs execute with runtime perception and control, without a human or coding agent in the loop. These results highlight CaP's potential to turn experience into reliable, reusable physical skills.

title: Informative Path Planning with Gaussian Processes: Error Bounds, Algorithms, and Benchmarks
summary:
Accurate environmental monitoring relies on Informative Path Planning (IPP) to deploy autonomous systems that maximize information gain. While Gaussian Processes (GPs) provide a robust mathematical foundation for modeling the environment, contemporary IPP approaches remain hindered by heuristic operational constraints and the lack of simultaneous theoretical guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality. Rather than introducing yet another heuristic, this paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of existing error bounds and algorithms to further develop the mathematical foundation for IPP.
  By evaluating probabilistic and deterministic bounds on reconstruction error, we establish that predictive variance is the theoretically ideal optimization objective for GP-based IPP. Furthermore, we analyze GreedyCover, a recent approach for optimizing predictive variance, and demonstrate that its near-optimal approximation guarantee matches the fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit for the problem. Comprehensive benchmarking confirms that this approach delivers superior estimation accuracy and computational efficiency compared to prominent information-theoretic objectives and optimization methods used in IPP. Finally, this theoretical analysis establishes a rigorous, near-optimal foundation for discrete offline IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints, offering clear and principled guidance for future work in continuous-space and online formulations.

title: Topology-Aware Handover Management for Service Continuity in LEO Satellite Networks
summary: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites are expected to play a key role in sixth-generation (6G) non-terrestrial networks. The high mobility of LEO satellites necessitates frequent handovers (HOs), posing challenges to service continuity and availability for user equipment. Conventional methods based on handover margin (HOM) and time-to-trigger (TTT) have limited adaptability to time-varying channel conditions and do not explicitly account for the impact of feeder-link and ground station (GS) connectivity on HO interruption time. To address these limitations, this paper develops a topology-aware HO framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). The framework uses reference signal received power (RSRP), satellite--GS associations, remaining visibility time, and elevation angles to determine when to initiate an HO and which satellite to select. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed policy achieves a service availability of 99.32% at a minimum elevation angle of 40 degrees, exceeding that of optimized HOM--TTT (O-HT) and least-delay (LD) satellite selection by 1.67 and 1.41 percentage points, respectively. The policy maintains service availability above 97.52% as the minimum elevation angle increases to 55 degrees, demonstrating its ability to sustain high service availability under stricter elevation constraints.

title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
comments: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

title: Tight Bounds for Downward-Closed Prophet and Secretary Problems
summary: We study online selection problems subject to arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints, under different arrival orders, with different distributional assumptions. We establish the following bounds: (1) $Θ(\log^2 n / \log \log n)$ for the standard (adversarial-order) prophet problem, (2) $Ω(\log n)$ for the (Bayesian, random-order) prophet secretary problem, and by extension, for the standard (prior-free, random-order) secretary problem, and (3) $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ for the free-order prophet problem. Together with complementary bounds established in prior work, these results pin down the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for all these variants of prophet and secretary problems subject to downward-closed constraints. Our results refine and reinforce the big-decisions-first principle by Rubinstein and Singla [2026], establishing a superconstant separation between the random-order and free-order models.

title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
summary: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.

title: Collision-Resilient All-to-All Broadcast Scheduling in Underwater Acoustic Networks
summary: This paper studies all-to-all broadcast scheduling for underwater swarms with collision-resilient physical layers that can decode asynchronously overlapping packets. Propagation-aware collision-free schedulers coordinate packet arrivals but do not account for this reception capability. We first design a data-driven neural reception model that captures per-interferer power and timing effects. The model improves prediction accuracy over SINR baselines while admitting an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. The resulting neural-network-embedded MILP (NN-MILP) optimizes transmission times while explicitly encoding schedule-dependent overlaps and the predictor's inference, enabling globally optimal scheduling for small-scale instances. For larger networks, a two-stage ant colony optimization (ACO) heuristic combines low-cost transmission-order search with neural-aware timing refinement. Simulation results show that ACO shortens broadcast rounds compared with existing schedulers. It approaches the NN-MILP optimum on small-scale instances while supporting larger networks at substantially lower computational cost.

title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
comments: 16 pages (excluding references), 20 pages including references; 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to FSEN 2027
summary: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.
comment: 16 pages (excluding references), 20 pages including references; 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to FSEN 2027

title: A New Analytical Method and Interpretation of Loss-of-Load Counts
comments: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, submitted to IEEE PESGM
summary: This paper establishes the relationship between loss-of-load expectation (LOLE) and loss-of-load frequency (LOLF). We show why LOLE generally does not measure distinct-event frequency, mean event duration, or shortage magnitude. We identify conditions under which peak-based LOLE admits a frequency interpretation as the expected count of deficient daily peaks per horizon and distinguish this quantity from LOLF. We also derive an analytical formulation for frequency-and-duration indices that combines a convolution-derived generation probability-and-frequency model with chronological load changes. Under stationary generation, it uses the prescribed load profile directly, without constructing a separate load model or discretizing load magnitudes. Studies using generation and load data from the 24-bus IEEE RTS reveal different event frequencies and mean event durations at identical peak-based LOLE, motivating their separate assessment. Numerical comparisons demonstrate the accuracy advantage of the proposed analytical calculation over the conventional analytical implementations, quantifying the LOLF errors incurred by load discretization.
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, submitted to IEEE PESGM

title: Control-Flow Profiling for Workload Representativeness
summary:
Workload characterization in performance engineering often replaces expensive target executions with lower-cost proxies, including reduced datasets, miniapps, and training inputs. Such substitutions require empirical verification that the proxy faithfully exercises the target's dynamic execution behavior. This paper presents an address-keyed control-flow profiling methodology and tool suite designed to evaluate workload representativeness directly from compiled, unmodified binaries. We pair time-ordered basic-block vector (BBV) recurrence analysis with exp-branchprof, an experimental Valgrind tool that captures five orthogonal structural profile families spanning branch direction bias, four-bit global history contexts, dynamic indirect targets, function call transitions, and intraprocedural CFG edges.
  Our method compares weighted event distributions from two executions of the same binary. It reports support coverage, reference event-mass coverage, distribution distance, entropy-derived quantities, and phase structure, rather than claiming that a single similarity score certifies a proxy. We validate the tool with exact-oracle microbenchmarks across AArch64 and x86-64, covering conditional and inverted exits, calls, returns, direct and indirect jumps, and forked processes. We then apply the workflow to SPEC CPU2017 and CPU2026 train/reference pairs and seven refrate/refspeed pairs. The corpus contains both close matches and cases where a shorter execution reaches much of the same code but misses substantial target, callgraph, CFG, or BBV event mass. The accompanying artifact supports the same analysis for proprietary workload/proxy pairs without requiring raw PC-level profiles to leave the collection environment.

title: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search
comments: 16 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security. Code: https://github.com/jaroslawjanas/llmw-codebook
summary: Attributing short LLM-generated texts to a specific source remains challenging for existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding to recover payloads reliably. We propose a codebook-based watermarking scheme that maps an $n$-bit payload to a longer $u$-bit codeword and embeds it during generation through token-level logit biasing. During extraction, the received bit sequence is matched to the nearest codeword in a precomputed secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show that our method achieves near-perfect recovery for 16-24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. Results are weaker on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts, where low-entropy output distributions reduce embedding reliability. We also study a BCH-based variant that avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging. We analyze collision probability, codeword separation, extraction time, tokenization consistency, and text quality, highlighting both the practicality and limitations of codebook-based watermarking for short-form attribution.
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security. Code: https://github.com/jaroslawjanas/llmw-codebook

title: Mode-in-Variance Participation Factors under Stochastic Excitation
summary: This paper investigates how the dynamic modes of a power system contribute to the stationary variance of its variables under continuous stochastic excitation. Using a modal decomposition of the covariance matrix, the variance of each state or algebraic variable can be resolved into components associated with individual modal responses and their interactions. These components are shown to correspond to within-mode variance and cross-modal covariance, respectively, and the corresponding normalized contributions are termed mode-in-variance participation factors (PFs). The proposed PFs can be used to identify modes governing the variability of important system quantities such as frequency and voltage, quantify the effect of modal interactions, and reveal control dynamics that can be targeted to reduce their stochastic variability. These capabilities are demonstrated through case studies based on the Kundur two-area and IEEE 39-bus systems.

title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
summary: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

title: TokenStream: Multi-Subject Personalized Video Generation with Token-wise LoRA and Guided Attention
summary: We introduce TokenStream, an optimization-based framework that composes independently learned subject identities in text-to-video generation without a reference-video training dataset or joint optimization of each new subject combination. Learning from a single reference image makes subject appearance difficult to separate from static-image bias, while merging independently trained adapters can mix identities. Token-wise LoRA (ToRA) restricts low-rank updates to the cross-attention value projections of subject-associated text tokens, providing a separate adaptation path for each subject. A T2V-guided stream copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to reuse its layout and motion priors while retaining personalized values. We also introduce Multi-DB, a 30-subject, 122-prompt benchmark with appearance-free prompts and varied interactions. On Multi-DB at 1.3B, TokenStream improves identity preservation from 0.422 for DreamBooth to 0.467 and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688.

title: Edge-wise Graph Alignments
summary:
Pairwise graph ``alignments'', usually defined as maximum common subgraphs, have been considered in many application domains, including the comparison of molecular structures. Most commonly, the problem is formulated as maximum common induced subgraph (MCIS) or maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) problems. Sometimes these formulations are restricted to connected common subgraphs. Common subgraph problems readily generalize to more than two input graphs. However, this concept is fundamentally distinct from the notion of multiple sequence alignments. Abstractly, alignments are defined as super-structures from which the individual input objects are recovered via structure-preserving projections. While the mathematical construction readily applies to common induced subgraphs, it does not fully encompass the common edge subgraph problem, which is the variant more commonly employed in cheminformatics applications.
  In order to consistently define multiple edge-based alignments of graphs we represent a graph $G$ as E-graph $(E,\mathscr{V})$, where $E$ is the edge set of $G$ and $\mathscr{V}$ is the set of sets of incident edges. This representation implicitly encodes the vertices in terms of edge data. Alignments of E-graphs are themselves E-graphs that contain the input (E-)graphs as subgraphs. Maximum edge subgraphs correspond to maximum induced sub-E-graphs, and they can thus be computed using a slightly modified version of the VF2 algorithm without the need to switch from graphs to line graphs. Furthermore, multiple alignments of (E-)graphs yield a natural definition of a consensus graph that is ``on average'' present in the input without having to be a subgraph of every (and in fact of any) input graph.

title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
summary: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.

title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
comments: NeurIPS 2026. 17 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam
summary: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam
comment: NeurIPS 2026. 17 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

title: Automated PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Scoring with Uncertainty-Guided Triage in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
comments: 55 pages (29-page main text with 5 figures and 3 tables, followed by 26 pages of supplementary material)
summary: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor proportion score (TPS) informs immunotherapy selection in non-small cell lung cancer. Near the 1% and 50% cutoffs, the score should also indicate when closer review is warranted. We designed a three-stage framework to follow the sequence of TPS assessment. Stage 1 identifies tumor regions and excludes macrophage-rich patches. Stage 2, a dual-branch cell counting network (D2Count-Net), counts PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative tumor cells in these regions to calculate TPS. Stage 3, TPS-Guard, an uncertainty-guided triage mechanism, reports model uncertainty as the disagreement among independently trained models, refers the most uncertain slides, and flags scores near the 1% or 50% cutoff when model estimates disagree across that cutoff. Flags state the reason for referral or alert the pathologist to possible scoring errors on auto-reported slides. In a retrospective, single-center study, 154 whole-slide images were scored by three pathologists, and the model and each pathologist were compared in turn with the mean of the other two. On the 114 slides unseen in training, model mean absolute error (MAE) was 6.96 percentage points, within the range of the three pathologists (4.24 to 8.29), and model uncertainty correlated with absolute TPS error (Spearman rho = 0.77) and inter-pathologist disagreement (rho = 0.71). After referral of the 15% most uncertain slides, model and pathologist MAE both decreased. Applied without retraining to an external, publicly available dataset, TPS-Guard still directed review to higher-error cases, and referring more uncertain cases raised sensitivity at the 50% cutoff. TPS-Guard provides reasons for reviewing individual automated scores and identifies slides that also produce greater disagreement among pathologists. Prospective reader studies should assess TPS-Guard's effect on TPS reporting.
comment: 55 pages (29-page main text with 5 figures and 3 tables, followed by 26 pages of supplementary material)

title: CADET: Construction of PCB Routing Instances with Executable Demonstrations
comments: 28 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/LGAI-Research/CADET
summary: Printed circuit board (PCB) routing is the stage of physical layout that finds paths connecting the placed pads of each net. Public datasets in this domain are few, and most contain only the final states of routed boards, not demonstrations of the electronic design automation (EDA) engine actions that produce them. To close this gap, we propose CADET (Constructing executAble Demonstrations for Engine-grounded Training), which jointly generates synthetic boards and demonstrations built from EDA engine actions. The resulting RouteDemos provides 100,000 synthetic boards routed with zero design rule violations (DRVs), together with their demonstrations.
