title: Multiobjective optimization-based design and dispatch of islanded, hybrid microgrids for remote, off-grid communities in sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Sizing an islanded hybrid microgrid requires evaluating candidate designs through a year-long hourly simulation. The resulting objective is non-smooth, which limits gradient-based methods and requires approximation for mixed-integer linear programming. We size a solar photovoltaic (PV), wind, lithium-ion battery and diesel microgrid for an off-grid community in Timbila, Kenya, using five objectives: levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), emissions, unmet load, dumped energy and fossil share. We benchmark eight solvers, including particle swarm optimization (PSO), over 30 runs each with a budget of 2,000 evaluations. PSO, the PSO--pattern-search hybrid, pattern search and surrogate optimization finish within 0.5% of the exhaustively computed integer optimum in all 30 runs; PSO is fastest (expected running time 2.9~s), and gradient-based multistart methods perform worst. We then approximate the Pareto front, select designs with knee-point and compromise rules and the technique for order of preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS), trace a cost--reliability front over the generator rating, and re-rank candidates over 500 Monte Carlo resource and load scenarios. The equal-weight design, 73~kW of PV with a 239~kWh battery and no wind turbines, supplies 97% of energy from renewables at 0.184~USD/kWh, 63% below diesel-only supply. The selected design that serves all load uses a 12.2~kW generator, and accepting 1% unmet load lowers LCOE to 0.163~USD/kWh. Under uncertainty, a design with a 31% larger PV array lowers the 95% conditional value-at-risk of LCOE by 10% for a 2% higher expected cost. LCOE is most sensitive to the interest rate over the ranges tested.

title: The complexity of bisimilarity on pointmass processes
comments: 37 pages (29pp with biblio + 8pp appendices), 3 figures. v2: Adapted to journal page limits. Addressed referee's remarks
summary:
We assess the descriptive complexity of *bisimilarity* or "equality of behavior" on a family of Markov decision processes over uncountable standard Borel spaces, namely *nondeterministic labelled Markov processes* (NLMP).
  We show that bisimilarity is analytic for processes with a uniform assignment of finitely-supported measures to each state and label. More precisely, we obtain that bisimilarity on the space of countable Kripke frames (or labelled transition systems) is classifiable by countable structures.
  We show that bisimilarity of well-founded ("terminating") processes is Borel. We also provide a lower complexity bound by reducing the relation of eventual equality of binary sequences, $E_0$, to the former. As a consequence, there is no countable fragment of basic modal logic with denumerable conjunctions that characterizes bisimilarity for processes of small rank.
  We finally apply the previous Borel-definability to study the well-founded part of discrete uniform processes over continuous spaces.

title: Deterministic sketching for Krylov subspace methods
summary: Randomized sketching is currently introduced into every area of numerical linear algebra. In Krylov subspace methods, it allows runtime savings at the cost of small accuracy reductions. This work offers a different view on sketching in Krylov subspace methods by analyzing what subspace embeddings are obtained by arbitrary sketching matrices. The analysis gives rise to a deterministic sketching approach leveraging row subset selection techniques that yield subspace embeddings holding with probability 1. We propose deterministically sketched Krylov subspace methods for matrix functions, linear systems, and eigenvalue problems that show a similar performance to their randomly sketched counterparts.

title: Appear2Meaning: A Cross-Cultural Benchmark for Structured Cultural Metadata Inference from Images
summary: Museum records express how people understand heritage objects through cultural and historical relations. Recovering these human attributions from images is a technical challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce Appear2Meaning, a cross-cultural benchmark of 750 museum objects for image-only recovery of title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Its evaluation framework distinguishes field-level from complete-record compatibility and uses human validation for semantic judgement. Across nine VLMs, mean field accuracy is 36.16--49.82%; 7.20--17.02% of records have all four contextual fields compatible, and 2.13--7.87% have all five, including title. For the two tested models, image-only input yields 12.6--32.2 percentage points higher reference compatibility for culture, period, and origin than a museum-and-title-only control.

title: Stability Despite Misalignment: Model Predictive Game Controllers with Objective Misspecifications
summary: Predictive control requires the controller to possess an embedded prediction model. In multi-agent control, this prediction model must consider the behavior that emerges from other agents' strategic decisions. Game theory offers a natural model for the emergent collective behavior of self-interested agents. Model predictive games (MPGs) are a class of controllers in which an agent iteratively solves a finite-horizon game to predict the behavior of a multi-agent system and synthesize their own control action. When all agents use the same game model to select their control action, conditions have been found that guarantee the closed-loop stability of the multi-agent system. However, when multiple agents implement their own MPG controllers, their respective game models may be misspecified due to inaccurate estimates or conjectures about other agents' objectives. This paper analyzes the consequences of these prediction misalignments on the system's behavior. We show that existing stability conditions for homogeneous MPG controllers do not extend to the heterogeneous setting, even when they hold for each agent's individual game. We provide sufficient conditions for the stability of multi-agent dynamical systems with heterogeneous MPG controllers adopting linear-quadratic (LQ) games. We also show that misaligned game models can destabilize a system that reaches stability when all agents share the same game model, using a financial duopoly simulation.

title: BLaFA: Bridging Language to 3D Functional Affordances for Dexterous Robotic Grasping in Tool Use
comments: Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/PopeyePxx/BLaFA
summary: In industrial assembly, equipment maintenance, and everyday tool-use scenarios, robots need not only to grasp objects stably but also to establish task-appropriate contact configurations according to task intentions and tool functionality. However, existing methods lack explicit mappings from open-vocabulary instructions to 3D functional contact structures and dexterous grasp configurations, limiting robots' adaptability to diverse tools and functional tasks. To address this limitation, we propose BLaFA (Bridging Language to 3D Functional Affordances for Dexterous Robotic Grasping), a structured framework for language-driven functional dexterous grasping. First, a Knowledge-guided Language Parsing (KLP) module leverages structured knowledge to transform natural-language instructions into semantic sextuples of manipulation constraints. Second, a 3D Gaussian Splatting based hierarchical semantic representation and a Triangular Functional Point Localization (TriLocation) module are developed to localize 3D functional contact keypoints under task-tool topology constraints. Finally, a 3D Keypoint Grasp Matrix Transformation (KGT3D+) module maps the localized keypoints and semantic constraints to executable wrist poses and finger-level joint and force commands. Evaluations on 100 open-vocabulary language instructions, 14 task-tool combinations covering four functional intents, and real-world robotic experiments in representative scenes demonstrate that BLaFA can effectively translate natural-language instructions into task-aligned 3D functional contact structures and corresponding dexterous grasps, thereby enabling language-driven robotic tool use across diverse tasks. The source code will be made publicly available. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/PopeyePxx/BLaFA.

title: Tamper-Proofing with Self-Modifying Code
comments: 14 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Lean 4 formalization (Palomar entry PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000004 v1): https://github.com/GregoryMorse/SelfModTamper , tag palomar-v1
summary: Classical computability theory tells us that self-modifying code (SMC) on a deterministic universal Turing machine can be simulated by non-SMC code on the same model. That abstraction, however, omits the external timing inputs, concurrency, and microarchitectural state that dominate practical execution on modern processors. We argue that once timing, ordering, and self-introspective effects are treated as observables, a practically faithful non-SMC reproduction of timed SMC becomes detectably expensive on commodity systems. We present a tamper-proofing model that combines introspective and polymorphic SMC, reliable clocks, and runtime timing predicates to bind integrity checks to execution behavior. We distinguish static and dynamic SMC generation, characterize the timing semantics needed to avoid catastrophic pipeline clears, and give x86-64 design primitives for checksum-driven self-patching. We also report timer measurements, performance comparisons, and performance-monitoring counter evidence showing that careful engineering - especially loop unrolling and cross-page modification - substantially reduces the overhead of SMC while preserving its tamper-detection value. The paper concludes with an efficiency analysis, a threat model, and deployment guidance for trusted code executing in untrusted environments. The threat model is formalized in Lean 4, relative to an explicit platform contract: the security theorem, the necessity of each assumption and which assumptions each adversary level satisfies or breaks are machine-checked, and the development is registered with the Palomar registry.

title: A Lightweight Global-Target Framework for Multi-Domain No-Reference Image Quality Assessment in UAV Imagery
summary: Reliable image quality assessment is essential in applications where large volumes of images are acquired automatically and must be filtered before further analysis. In many practical scenarios, a pristine reference image is unavailable, making no reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) particularly important. This paper introduces Multi-Metric Image Quality Assessment (MM-IQA), a lightweight multi-metric framework for NR-IQA. It combines interpretable cues related to blur, edge structure, low resolution artifacts, exposure imbalance, noise, haze, and frequency content to produce a single quality score in the range [0,100].MM-IQA was evaluated on five benchmark datasets (KonIQ-10k, LIVE Challenge, KADID-10k, TID2013, and BIQ2021) and achieved SRCC values ranging from 0.647 to 0.830. Additional experiments on a synthetic agricultural dataset showed consistent behavior of the designed cues. The Python/OpenCV implementation required about 1.97 s per image. This method also has modest memory requirements because it stores only a limited number of intermediate grayscale, filtered, and frequency-domain representations, resulting in memory usage that scales linearly with image size. The results show that MM-IQA can be used for fast image quality screening with explicit distortion aware cues and modest computational cost.

title: Lower Bounds for Testing Directed Acyclicity in the Unidirectional Bounded-Degree Model
comments: The author has withdrawn this paper due to an error in the proof of the one-sided lower bound. In particular, the bound on the probability of a long blue path in Lemma 4.3 does not hold for adaptive exploration.
summary: We study property testing of directed acyclicity in the unidirectional bounded-degree oracle model, where a query to a vertex reveals its outgoing neighbors. We prove that there exist absolute constants $d_0\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every constant $d\ge d_0$, any one-sided $\varepsilon$-tester for acyclicity on $n$-vertex digraphs of maximum outdegree at most $d$ requires $\widetildeΩ(n^{2/3})$ queries. This improves the previous $\widetildeΩ(n^{5/9})$ lower bound for one-sided testing of acyclicity in the same model. We also prove that, under the same degree assumption, any two-sided $\varepsilon$-tester requires $Ω(\sqrt n)$ queries, improving the previous $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound. We further prove an $Ω(n)$ lower bound for tolerant testing for some absolute constant outdegree bound $d$ by reduction from bounded-degree $3$-colorability.

title: Model-Predictive Spill-Free Emergency Stopping for Liquid-Manipulating Robots
summary: Manipulating open liquid containers is challenging because liquids are highly sensitive to vessel accelerations and jerks. Although spill-free liquid manipulation has been widely studied, emergency stopping under unexpected hazards has received little attention, despite the fact that abrupt braking may cause hazardous spills. This letter presents an emergency stop system for robots manipulating liquids in open containers. We formulate emergency stopping as an optimal control problem and solve it in a model predictive control framework to generate time-optimal, spill-free stopping trajectories. The method operates as a plug-and-play safety layer on top of existing slosh-free motion planning methods, enabling immediate reaction to detected hazards while accounting for nonlinear liquid dynamics. We demonstrate, through simulation and on a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda robot, that the proposed approach achieves fast emergency stopping without spilling.

title: COSAC: Counterfactual Credit Assignment in Sequential Cooperative Teams
comments: To appear at NeurIPS 2026; 10 main text pages
summary: In cooperative teams where agents act in a fixed order and share a single team-level reward (multi-agent language systems, sequential robotic tasks), per-agent credit assignment is under-determined. Critic-based approaches scale poorly as the number of agents grows owing to the costly maintenance of joint/factored critic(s), whereas the existing critic-free alternatives have other issues: common credit across agents that couples every agent's signal to teammate noise, importance-sampling corrections for upstream-update staleness that incur variance exponential in team size, or per-agent counterfactual replay that isolates each agent's effect at the price of extra environment or reward calls. We propose COSAC, a critic-free policy gradient framework for sequential cooperative teams. COSAC fits an additive per-agent decomposition of the team reward by a single ridge regression on the rollout batch (giving each agent a learning signal decoupled from teammate noise), and computes each agent's counterfactual advantage from fictitious continuations of the current policy (policy forward passes that replace both importance-sampling reweighting and per-agent environment replay, at no extra environment or reward cost). The estimator instantiates the Sequential Aristocrat Utility (SeqAU), our extension of Wolpert and Tumer's (2001) aristocrat utility to sequential teams. We derive bias and conditional variance bounds for SeqAU credits: the direct-effect bound has no explicit team-size factor, while the indirect effect's reward-noise bound scales with the number of downstream agents. Sequential bandits test the analysis across team sizes up to K=16. In sequential multi-agent LLM fine-tuning, COSAC reduces training regret by 17% on consensus-based science reasoning relative to the best critic-free multi-agent baseline and by 61% on Python coding relative to MA-GRPO.
comment: To appear at NeurIPS 2026; 10 main text pages

title: GPUOS: A GPU Operating System Primitive for Transparent Operation Fusion
summary:
Modern deep learning workloads often consist of many small tensor operations, especially in inference, attention, and micro-batched training. In these settings, kernel launch overhead can become a major bottleneck, sometimes exceeding the actual computation time.
  We present GPUOS, a GPU runtime JIT system that reduces launch overhead using a persistent kernel architecture with runtime operator injection. GPUOS runs a single long-lived GPU kernel that continuously processes tasks from a host-managed work queue, eliminating repeated kernel launches. To support diverse operations, GPUOS uses NVIDIA NVRTC to just-in-time compile operators at runtime and inject them into the running kernel through device function pointer tables. This design enables operator updates without restarting the kernel or recompiling the system.
  GPUOS introduces four key ideas: (1) a persistent worker kernel with atomic task queues, (2) a runtime operator injection mechanism based on NVRTC and relocatable device code, (3) a dual-slot aliasing scheme for safe concurrent operator updates, and (4) transparent PyTorch integration through TorchDispatch that batches micro-operations into unified submissions. The system supports arbitrary tensor shapes, strides, data types, and broadcasting through a generic tensor abstraction.
  Experiments show that GPUOS achieves up to 15.3x speedup over standard PyTorch on workloads dominated by small operations, including micro-batched inference and attention patterns. GPUOS improves utilization while remaining compatible with the PyTorch ecosystem.

title: CHRep: Cross-modal Histology Representation and Post-hoc Calibration for Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables spatially resolved gene profiling but remains expensive and low-throughput, limiting large-cohort studies and routine clinical use. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides is a promising alternative, yet under realistic leave-one-slide-out evaluation, existing models often suffer from slide-level appearance shifts and regression-driven over-smoothing that suppress biologically meaningful variation. CHRep is a two-phase framework for robust histology-to-expression prediction. In the training phase, CHRep learns a structure-aware representation by jointly optimizing correlation-aware regression, symmetric image-expression alignment, and coordinate-induced spatial topology regularization. In the inference phase, cross-slide robustness is improved without backbone fine-tuning through a lightweight calibration module trained on the training slides, which combines a non-parametric estimate from a training gallery with a magnitude-regularized correction module. Unlike prior embedding-alignment or retrieval-based transfer methods that rely on a single prediction route, CHRep couples topology-preserving representation learning with post-hoc calibration, enabling stable neighborhood retrieval and controlled bias correction under slide-level shifts. Across the three cohorts, CHRep consistently improves gene-wise correlation under leave-one-slide-out evaluation, with the largest gains observed on Alex+10x. Relative to HAGE, the Pearson correlation coefficient on all considered genes [PCC(ACG)] increases by 4.0% on cSCC and 9.8% on HER2+. Relative to mclSTExp, PCC(ACG) further improves by 39.5% on Alex+10x, together with 9.7% and 9.0% reductions in mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE), respectively.

title: SLIDERS: Evidence Synthesis with Autonomous Database Reconciliation for Systematic Reviews
summary: Systematic reviews requires comprehensive evidence synthesis from large document corpora to answer targeted research questions and are foundational in finance, social sciences, and other technical fields. Manual construction of evidence tables is labor-intensive, and recent LLM-based assistants relying on embedding or keyword search often fail to meet the coverage standards of systematic reviews. We introduce SLIDERS, a novel LLM-based methodology for automatically assembling evidence tables tailored to research questions for systematic reviews. SLIDERS extracts full-text excerpts that serve as direct evidence or as provenance for structured data. Core to SLIDERS is an autonomous evidence reconciliation coding agent that iteratively writes SQL to analyze and reconcile extracted evidence, bringing together information fragmented across documents, resolving inconsistencies and removing duplicates across records. We evaluate SLIDERS on BrowseComp+, achieving 90% accuracy, and show that it outperforms all baselines on additional benchmarks within the LLM's context window. To assess scalability, we introduce two new evidence-synthesis benchmarks, WikiCeleb100 (3.9M tokens) and FinQ100 (36M tokens), which include follow-up questions beyond the original research query. Although SLIDERS synthesizes evidence knowing only the original question, it answers 78.9% and 55.2% of all questions correctly on WikiCeleb100 and FinQ100, respectively

title: ZFLean: a framework for set-level mathematics in Lean
summary: We present ZFLean, a Lean 4 library for doing core mathematics inside a model of ZFC with the ergonomics expected of typed Mathlib developments. Building on Mathlib's ZFC model, we contribute a relational calculus for sets with rewriting hints and small predictable tactics, canonical set-theoretic constructions -- Booleans, naturals, integers, sums/option -- and bridges between ZFC objects and Lean's native types enabling mixed set-level/typed proofs. The layer reduces boilerplate for extensional reasoning while remaining compatible with vanilla Mathlib. We discuss library organization and usage patterns that lower the friction of set-theoretic formalization in a dependently typed assistant. We demonstrate typical use of the framework with a case study exercising our constructions and relational calculus through a proof of an isomorphism theorem on curried functions.

title: Computational Complexity of the Interval Ordering Problem
summary: We study an interval ordering problem introduced by Dürr et al. [Discrete Appl. Math. 2012] which is motivated by applications in bioinformatics. The task is to order a given set of n intervals with the goal of minimizing a certain objective which is defined via a given cost function $f$ which assigns a cost to the exposed part of each interval (that is, the pieces not covered by previous intervals). We develop a dynamic programming approach which solves the problem with $O(2^n\text{poly}(n))$ oracle calls to $f$ and arithmetic operations. Moreover, our approach yields polynomial-time algorithms for all cost functions $f$ such that $f-f(0)$ is subadditive or superadditive. This answers an open question for the function $f(x)=2^x$. We contrast these results by proving a running time lower bound of $2^{n-1}$ for any algorithm that solves the problem for every function $f$ (with oracle access only) and further proving NP-hardness for some classes of simple functions. Thus, we significantly narrow the gap regarding the computational complexity of the problem.

title: Training Computer Use Agents to Assess the Usability of Graphical User Interfaces
summary: Recent HCI research leverages AI agents to assess graphical user interfaces (GUIs) usability, but current agents still struggle. Computer use agents (CUAs) that are used in these assessments are predominantly developed using objective task trajectories with verifiable outcomes and lack an operationalized definition of usability and necessary training data. This work presents a novel training objective that operationalizes usability to fine-tune CUAs to assess GUI usability through relative comparisons between interface variants. We apply our method to CUA models using a large-scale dataset of fully interactive UIs paired with usability labels mixed with human preferences.Two empirical evaluations across real and synthetic GUIs show that our method i) improved relative usability assessment accuracy across three off-the-shelf CUA models, ii) enabled our best model to outperform proprietary baselines, and iii) produced grounded usability assessments. Our work lays a data-driven foundation for agent-based usability assessment, enabling exploration of new forms of scalable usability evaluation and interface design.

title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
comments: 13 pages, 11 figures. Major revision with updated title, system design, and expanded evaluation. Preprint
summary:
Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue.
  We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/MARS_preview .
