title: From Prediction to Practice: A Task-Aware Evaluation Framework for Blood Glucose Forecasting
comments: Accepted to ML4H 2026 (Proceedings Track). This revision corrects hypoglycemia alarm matching, updates the advance-warning analysis and its claims, and replaces the simulator evaluation with four-hour Control-IQ experiments. Code and simulated data are publicly available
summary: Clinical time-series forecasting is increasingly studied for decision support, yet standard aggregate metrics can obscure whether a model is actually useful for the task it is meant to serve. In safety-critical settings, low average error can coexist with dangerous failures in exactly the high-risk regimes that matter most. We present a task-aware evaluation framework for blood glucose forecasting built around two downstream uses: hypoglycemia early warning and insulin dosing decision support. For early warning, we evaluate on real data from three clinical cohorts using event-level recall and false alarms per patient-day, metrics that reflect operational alarm burden rather than aggregate accuracy. We show that models appearing acceptable overall, with recall above 0.9 on the full test set, can fail badly in the post-bolus slice, where insulin-on-board is elevated and missed warnings carry the greatest clinical consequences. Standard forecasting evaluation, however, does not test whether a model can reason about the effects of actions, a requirement for supporting insulin dosing decisions. We therefore add a second, interventional arm using the FDA-accepted UVA/Padova simulator, where we evaluate whether forecasters can predict glucose responses to altered insulin plans in paired factual/counterfactual scenarios. We show that models that look strong on real-data forecasting often fail to predict the direction, magnitude, or ranking of intervention effects, and choose poor insulin doses when evaluated under a clinically motivated cost. Taken together, the two arms reveal a consistent gap between forecasting accuracy and task-relevant usefulness. We release the benchmark, the standardized preprocessing pipeline for public cohorts, and the simulator-based interventional dataset as a reproducible toolkit.
comment: Accepted to ML4H 2026 (Proceedings Track). This revision corrects hypoglycemia alarm matching, updates the advance-warning analysis and its claims, and replaces the simulator evaluation with four-hour Control-IQ experiments. Code and simulated data are publicly available

title: AI Alignment via Incentives and Correction
comments: 48 pages. v4: adds scalable-oversight screening protocol, abstention-suppression and smaller-auditor ablations, expanded related work
summary:
We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement. In these models, misconduct is not treated as an external failure, but as a strategic response to incentives: an actor weighs the gain from violation against the probability of detection and the severity of punishment. We argue that the same logic arises naturally in agentic AI pipelines. A solver may benefit from producing a persuasive but incorrect answer, hiding uncertainty, or exploiting spurious shortcuts, while an auditor or verifier must decide whether costly monitoring is worthwhile. Alignment is therefore a fixed-point problem: stronger penalties may deter solver misbehavior, but they can also reduce the auditor's incentive to inspect, since auditing then mainly incurs cost on a population that appears increasingly aligned.
  This perspective also changes what should count as a post-training signal. Standard feedback often attaches reward to the final answer alone, but a solver-auditor pipeline exposes the full correction event: whether the solver erred, whether the auditor inspected, whether the error was caught, and whether oversight incentives remained active. We formalize this interaction in a two-agent model in which a principal chooses rewards over joint correction outcomes, inducing both solver behavior and auditor monitoring. Reward design is therefore a bilevel optimization problem: rewards are judged not by their immediate semantic meaning, but by the behavioral equilibrium they induce. We propose a bandit-based outer-loop procedure for searching over reward profiles using noisy interaction feedback. Experiments on an LLM coding pipeline show that adaptive reward profiles can maintain useful oversight pressure and improve principal-aligned outcomes relative to static hand-designed rewards, including a substantial reduction in hallucinated incorrect attempts.
comment: 48 pages. v4: adds scalable-oversight screening protocol, abstention-suppression and smaller-auditor ablations, expanded related work

title: Learning Koopman operators for coupled systems via information on governing equations of subsystems
summary: Nonlinear coupled systems are ubiquitous in science and engineering. The analysis and modeling of such systems are challenging due to their high dimensionality and complex interactions among subsystems. In recent years, operator-theoretic methods based on the Koopman operator have attracted attention as a powerful tool for analyzing and modeling nonlinear dynamical systems. Extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) is one of the most popular methods for approximating the Koopman operator. However, EDMD is a purely data-driven method, and it may be unstable and inaccurate for coupled systems under limited data availability. In this paper, we propose a method to construct a finite-dimensional Koopman matrix for coupled systems using the differential equations governing each subsystem. By regularizing the Koopman matrix toward a prior constructed from the subsystem equations, the proposed method improves prediction accuracy when only a limited number of snapshot pairs are available. We also demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments on coupled oscillator systems.

title: QuIVer: Efficient Graph Indexing with Two-Bit Construction and Navigation
comments: 14 pages, 4 figures; substantially revised with expanded baseline comparisons, ablations, and SSD-backed reranking
summary: High-dimensional vector indices must balance construction time, memory, and query throughput. Two-bit comparisons reduce computation and storage, but preserving useful graph connections and search candidates requires scores suited to each stage. We present QuIVer, a graph index that uses a training-free sign-magnitude representation for construction and navigation while reserving original vectors for bounded final reranking. Construction discovers candidates with Hamming scores, orders them with an integer proxy, and defers reverse-edge pruning across parallel insertions. Search uses reconstruction norms and bitwise inner products to order both the frontier and retained candidates, without query calibration or an exact anchor. Experiments cover 21 datasets and compare 30 external baseline modes on three core workloads. QuIVer's validation-selected 95% configurations lie on the measured Pareto frontiers of achieved recall, throughput, index preparation time, and memory, whether memory counts navigation state alone or also the original vectors. On Cohere-5M, QuIVer reaches 95.90% Recall@10 at 3,075 single-thread queries/s, $11.74\times$ the throughput of Lucene BBQ with FP32 reranking at 95.83% recall. Against SymphonyQG at 95.87%, it retains 81% of single-thread and 97% of 32-thread throughput while reducing index preparation time by 54%, total logical memory by 47%, and navigation storage by 87%. An SSD mode with INT8 reranking serves Cohere-5M at about 5 GiB of steady-state process RSS. Controlled crossovers and candidate-coverage diagnostics connect these results to construction and retention quality. Across 21 datasets, high recall holds for most text and image embeddings, while non-negative descriptors, cross-modal queries, and random data expose the limits of the representation.
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures; substantially revised with expanded baseline comparisons, ablations, and SSD-backed reranking

title: Submodular Benchmark Selection
summary: Evaluating a new language model means running it on a large, growing collection of benchmarks, at considerable cost. Much of this cost is redundant: arranged as a matrix of models by benchmarks, scores are strongly correlated and concentrate in a few dimensions, so a few well-chosen benchmarks largely determine the rest. This allows us to run a new model on a few benchmarks and predict the rest with a simple Gaussian model that copes with missing scores. The key question is \emph{which few to run}. An answer comes from sensor placement, which chooses the observations that carry the most information, measured by entropy or mutual information. We argue that the objective should instead reward a selection for how well it predicts every benchmark. This leads to two coverage objectives: explained variance, the predictions' accuracy if the estimated correlations were exact, and facility location, which credits each benchmark with its best proxy among the selected ones. On eleven score matrices built from public evaluation results, the coverage objectives predict the scores of held-out models best wherever the correlations can be estimated. The information objectives fall behind because they favor benchmarks that the selection predicts poorly (entropy) or that the others predict well (mutual information), not benchmarks that predict the others. By contrast, facility location predicts practically as well as explained variance, holds up on the addition of newer models and under real costs, has classical guarantees (even under a budget), and gives readable selections.

title: Optimal Privacy-Utility Trade-Offs in LDP: Functional and Geometric Perspectives
comments: 20 pages, 2 figures. Compared to v1, relevant references have been newly added
summary: Local differential privacy (LDP) has emerged as a gold-standard framework for privacy-preserving data analysis. However, characterizing the optimal privacy-utility trade-off (PUT) and the corresponding optimal LDP channels remains largely fragmented, relying on problem-specific, case-by-case analyses. In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework that systematically characterizes the optimal PUT and optimal LDP channels for general privacy-preserving statistical decision-making problems. We first identify key functional properties of Bayesian and minimax risks as functions of the LDP channel, including the data processing inequality (DPI), direct-sum quasi-convexity (or additivity), concavity, and symmetry invariance. Leveraging these properties, we reduce the optimization domain required to compute the optimal PUT. To this end, we reinterpret the existing result implying the one-to-one correspondence between maximal LDP channels under the Blackwell order and a finite-dimensional polytope, through an alternative convex geometric derivation. This result renders the optimal PUT computationally tractable via vertex enumeration or linear programming. Furthermore, when the underlying problem exhibits symmetries characterized by a transitive group action, we show that the optimal PUT can be computed by comparing finitely many values, rather than optimizing over a high dimensional polytope. Our framework applies broadly beyond risk minimization, encompassing the maximization of information-theoretic measures. We demonstrate the efficacy of our theoretical framework by recovering or strengthening several known results, and deriving exact analytic expressions for the optimal PUTs in specific tasks that were previously unaddressed.
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures. Compared to v1, relevant references have been newly added

title: A Near-optimal SQ Lower Bound for Smoothed Agnostic Learning of Boolean Halfspaces
summary: We study the complexity of smoothed agnostic learning of halfspaces on $\{\pm 1\}^n$ under uniform marginals in the model of~\cite{KM25}, where each input coordinate is independently flipped with probability $σ\in (0, {1}/{2})$. We show that $L^1$ polynomial regression achieves runtime and sample complexity $\tilde{O}(n^{O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/σ)})$, and prove a nearly matching Statistical Query complexity lower bound of $n^{Ω(\log(1+σ/\varepsilon^2)/σ)}$. This complements the recent work of~\cite{DK26}, which established analogous bounds in the continuous setting under Gaussian marginals.

title: TIDE: Token-Level Credit Assignment via Entropy-Gated Bounded Deviation
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is central for aligning large language models (LLMs) with complex reasoning, yet the leading critic-free algorithm, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), broadcasts a single sequence-level advantage uniformly across long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generations and constrains exploration with an unbounded Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty, which dilutes token-level supervision and induces gradient instability and mode-seeking conservatism. We propose TIDE (Token-level Importance via Deviation and Entropy), a critic-free RL framework that reinterprets distribution deviation as a guiding signal rather than a rigid penalty. TIDE replaces the volatile reverse KL divergence with the bounded Hellinger distance, safely quantifying token-level exploration without risk of gradient explosion. To separate genuine reasoning breakthroughs from confident hallucinations, an entropy gating mechanism scales this deviation by the policy's predictive uncertainty, and the gated scores redistribute the sequence-level advantage across tokens. The resulting updates amplify exploratory steps while suppressing low-entropy deviations, without a value network and with negligible overhead. Across in-domain, held-out, and out-of-domain benchmarks, TIDE outperforms strong critic-free baselines: on the Qwen2.5-32B backbone it reaches 60.0% and 46.0% Avg@32 accuracy on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, respectively, above competitive baselines such as DAPO. Token-level attribution, causal perturbation, and exploration analyses further support the interpretation that the entropy-gated deviation identifies pivotal reasoning steps rather than merely perturbing optimization dynamics.

title: Common Principal Component Networks for Domain Generalization
comments: This version consolidates our previous works, merging the contributions of the earlier paper available at arXiv:2607.22117
summary: Domain Generalization (DG) aims to learn representations that generalize to unseen target domains under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. Despite recent advances in invariant representation learning, explicitly capturing shared structures across source-domain distributions remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we integrate Common Principal Component Analysis (CPCA) into deep learning to identify a common orthogonal basis across multiple domains, proposing two complementary end-to-end differentiable frameworks. First, we introduce Common Principal Component Network (CPCNet), which unrolls the iterative Flury-Gautschi (FG) algorithm into fully differentiable neural layers, enabling covariance-based joint diagonalization within end-to-end representation learning. Second, to address rank deficiency arising from mini-batch covariance estimation in small-sample regimes, we develop Projection Pursuit-based Common Principal Component Network (PP-CPCNet), which directly optimizes a common orthogonal basis without explicit covariance estimation. Experiments validate the joint diagonalization capabilities of both methods, while evaluations on four standard DG benchmarks demonstrate competitive zero-shot generalization performance with favorable computational efficiency.
comment: This version consolidates our previous works, merging the contributions of the earlier paper available at arXiv:2607.22117

title: Structural Correspondence and Universal Approximation in Diagonal plus Low-Rank Neural Networks
summary: Structured low-rank and sparse-plus-low-rank parameterizations, motivated by methods such as LoRA and low-rank factorization, impose strong structural constraints on the linear transformations within neural networks. We study the expressive consequences of these constrained structures from the perspective of universal approximation. We first characterize that purely low-rank neural networks, despite being able to exactly interpolate arbitrary finite scalar datasets, can fail to approximate continuous functions that vary along directions ignored by the low-rank hidden mapping. We show that augmenting the low-rank structure with a one-parameter diagonal component suffices to overcome this geometric bottleneck, yielding a Diagonal-plus-Low-Rank (DLoR) structure. We show that a full-rank linear transformation can be reconstructed using DLoR components either by expanding network width through additive decomposition or by extending network depth through multiplicative decomposition. We term this correspondence between additive width expansion and multiplicative depth extension the Structural Correspondence framework. By combining these constructions with local linearization of the activation function, we prove that DLoR neural networks restore universal approximation for general activation functions. These results characterize how architectural width and depth can compensate for severe rank constraints without requiring unrestricted dense hidden transformations. Diagonal terms are required for multiplicative construction, while additive expansion works with purely low-rank terms. We further determine its exact cost: both the minimal number of rank-$r$ DLoR factors representing $W$ and the minimal network depth for that layer equal $\lceilκ(W)/r\rceil$, where $κ(W)=\min_{γ\ne0}rank(W-γI)$, achieving a lower cost than its dense representation when $W$ is identity-centered.

title: $\mathcal{B}^{3}$-Net: Controlled Posterior Bridge Learning for Multi-Task Dense Prediction
summary: Multi-task dense prediction solves complementary pixel-level tasks in a unified model, such as semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal estimation, and edge detection. Existing decoder-side interactions use attention, prompts, routing, diffusion, Mamba, or bridge features to exchange task evidence, but most of them organize this evidence implicitly. They usually fuse task features by similarity or affinity, without explicitly modeling that evidence reliability varies across tasks and spatial locations. As a result, unreliable evidence may contaminate the shared representation and intensify negative transfer. We propose $\mathcal{B}^{3}$-Net, a controlled posterior bridge learning framework for multi-task dense prediction. Our method decomposes decoder-side interaction into reliability estimation, posterior bridge construction, and bounded redistribution. The Precision Field Estimator estimates patch-wise evidence precision from task-reference alignment and local variation. The Posterior Bridge Operator builds a precision-weighted posterior bridge through heteroscedastic evidence fusion, yielding a shared state more reliable than uniform or heuristic mixtures. The Contractive Dispatch Operator redistributes the bridge to each task branch through a bounded update, reducing uncontrolled feature injection. Experiments on NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, and Cityscapes show that $\mathcal{B}^{3}$-Net achieves competitive or superior trade-offs over representative CNN-, Transformer-, diffusion-, Mamba-, and bridge-feature-based methods. Backbone-matched comparisons and extensive analyses further verify that the gains arise from controlled posterior bridge learning rather than backbone capacity or decoder scale.

title: Retain-Neutral Surrogates for Min-Max Unlearning
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a Conference Paper
summary: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget designated training data while retaining performance on the rest. In min-max unlearning, an inner adversary perturbs the model to maximize the forget loss, and the model is updated to minimize the retain loss at the resulting surrogate point. When the forget and retain gradients are positively coupled, the standard perturbation also moves toward higher retain loss, and the retain step begins by recovering that loss. We propose Retain-Orthogonal Surrogate Unlearning (ROSU), which redefines the adversary to admit only perturbations orthogonal to the retain gradient. The one that raises the forget loss fastest has a closed form, and ROSU uses it to set the surrogate point and amplifies it into the forgetting step. Under positive coupling the ROSU surrogate avoids the retain cost that coupling induces in the standard surrogate, and the difference shrinks as the gradients approach orthogonality. ROSU has the smallest accuracy gap to retraining in every vision setting (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) and is competitive with the baselines on language benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP). The redefinition helps most under high positive coupling. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/machine-unlearning.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a Conference Paper

title: Learned Lagrangian Models of PDEs via Euler-Lagrange Residual Minimization
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (spotlight). 10 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables, 9 pages of appendices
summary: We present the first method to directly use a learned continuous Lagrangian to forecast the dynamics of systems governed by partial differential equations, exploiting the inherent conservative structure to achieve stable long-range predictions. We develop an integrator that minimizes the squared Euler-Lagrange residual via a discretization-agnostic, structure-preserving construction on local space-time patches. Different from integrators for analytical models, integrators for learned models should decouple model error (phase error) from integration error (conservation error). By minimizing the residual locally on overlapping patches, we bypass the global implicit solve inherent to fixed discretizations, which slows time- and space-stepping and complicates learning. Our method scales linearly with domain size via Jacobi iteration, and places no structural requirements on the learned network, allowing it to be coupled with existing physics-guided machine learning (ML) methods. We validate our approach on a learned representation of a double pendulum, a one-dimensional wave equation, and a two-dimensional wave equation. Our method achieves long-horizon predictions with error comparable to classical symplectic methods while generalizing to spatially varying dynamics and arbitrary boundary conditions without retraining.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (spotlight). 10 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables, 9 pages of appendices

title: Disambiguating 2D-3D Correspondences in Gaussian Splatting-based Feature Fields for Visual Localization
comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: https://misoleekr.github.io/SplitGS-Loc/
summary: While Gaussian Splatting-based Feature Fields (GSFFs) have shown promise for visual localization, this paper highlights that photometrically optimized GSFFs are inherently not suitable for 2D-3D matching. The volumetric extent of each Gaussian induces many-to-one pixel-to-point mappings that destabilize PnP-based pose estimation, while photometric optimization gives rise to superfluous Gaussians devoid of multi-view consistency. To address these issues, we propose SplitGS-Loc, a GSFFs construction framework for localization, which disambiguates 2D-3D correspondences by exploiting Gaussian attributes. Our key design, Mixture-of-Gaussians-based splitting, decomposes each Gaussian into smaller Gaussians, replacing ambiguous many-to-one with precise one-to-one correspondences. In parallel, we exploit composition weights from GS rasterization to select Gaussians that significantly and consistently contribute across multiple views and aggregate discriminative features through strong pixel-Gaussian associations. The resulting compact yet discriminative feature fields enable stable PnP convergence, achieving competitive performance on localization benchmarks. Extensive experiments validate that SplitGS-Loc extends the utility of photometric GSFFs to accurate and efficient localization by exploiting Gaussian attributes, without per-scene training for feature fields or iterative pose refinement. The code is available at: https://github.com/misoleekr/SplitGS-Loc.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: https://misoleekr.github.io/SplitGS-Loc/

title: A Marine Debris Detection Framework for Ocean Robots via Self-Attention Enhancement and Feature Interaction Optimization
comments: Language polishing only; no substantive changes to content, data, results, or conclusions
summary: Marine debris detection for ocean robot is crucial for ecological protection, yet performance is often degraded by low-quality images with blur, complex backgrounds, and small targets. To address these challenges, we propose YOLO-MD, an enhanced YOLO-based detection framework. A Dual-Branch Convolutional Enhanced Self-Attention (DB-CASA) module is designed to strengthen spatial-channel interactions, improving feature representation in degraded images. Additionally, a lightweight shift-based operation is introduced to enhance fine-grained feature extraction for objects of varying scales while maintaining parameter efficiency. We further propose SFG-Loss to mitigate class imbalance and optimization instability via dynamic sample reweighting. Experiments on the UODM dataset demonstrate that YOLO-MD achieves 0.875 precision, 0.822 F1-score, and 0.849 mAP50, outperforming the latest state-of-the-art methods. The effectiveness of this method has also been verified through real-world robotic edge deployment experiments.
comment: Language polishing only; no substantive changes to content, data, results, or conclusions

title: Meta-Scaling Laws: On the Invariance and Generality of Neural Scaling
summary: Neural scaling laws establish a predictable relationship between model performance and data or compute, offering crucial guidance for resource allocation in new domains and tasks. Yet such laws are most needed precisely where they are hardest to obtain: fitting one for a new model and task pair demands expensive sweeps that typically exhaust the very compute budget the law is meant to economize. We study meta-scaling laws: relations that characterize when neural scaling behavior is preserved and predict how it changes under data transformations, enabling forecasts across domains when the shift can be approximated by a compatible transformation. We address this by identifying the right invariants: scaling laws are preserved under bijective (information-preserving) transformations of the data and modified in predictable, information-theoretically grounded ways under non-bijective transformations that lower its information resolution $ρ$: a single axis along which a law fit in one domain can be transported to another. We validate this across language, vision, and speech, and demonstrate two cross-domain applications: predicting scaling for language models trained on electronic health records from laws fit on general text, and predicting time-series classification scaling under varying levels of noise injection, recovering the data-scaling exponents to within $3\%$ error.

title: Rethinking State Tracking in Recurrent Models Through Error Control Dynamics
summary: The theory of state tracking in recurrent architectures has predominantly focused on expressive capacity: whether a fixed architecture can theoretically realize a set of symbolic transition rules. We argue that equally important is error control, the dynamics governing hidden-state drift along the directions that distinguish symbolic states. We prove that affine recurrent networks, a class of models encompassing State-Space Models and Linear Attention, cannot correct errors along state-separating subspaces once they preserve state representations. Consequently, practical affine trackers do not learn robust state tracking; rather, they learn finite-horizon solutions governed by accumulated state-relevant error. We characterize the mechanics of this failure, showing that tracking remains readable only while the accumulating within-class spread remains small relative to the between-class separation. We demonstrate empirically on group state-tracking tasks that this breakdown is predictable: tracking collapses when the distinguishability ratio crosses the readability threshold. Across trained models, the point of this crossing predicts the horizon at which downstream accuracy fails. These results establish that robust state tracking is determined not only by an architecture's theoretical expressivity but crucially by its error control.

title: The Limits of AI-Driven Allocation: Optimal Screening under Aleatoric Uncertainty
summary: The rise of machine learning has shifted targeted resource allocation in policy and humanitarian settings toward algorithmic targeting based on predicted risk scores. This approach is typically cheaper and faster than traditional screening procedures that directly observe the latent vulnerability status through physical verification. Yet, even access to the true conditional vulnerability probability cannot eliminate misallocation: aleatoric uncertainty over individual vulnerability status is irreducible, and probabilistic targeting inevitably misallocates some resources. In this work, we study how screening and algorithmic targeting should be optimally combined in a two-stage allocation framework, in which a screening stage observes true outcomes for a subset of units before a final allocation stage assigns the resource under a fixed coverage budget. We show that the optimal strategy screens units at the margin of algorithmic allocation, while directly targeting the highest-risk units. We empirically characterize when screening and algorithmic targeting act as complements or substitutes: efficiency gains from screening grow as the aleatoric uncertainty in the population increases. Finally, we characterize the relative value of screening and direct allocation, which yields a simple rule for splitting a program budget between the two: the optimal cutoff depends only on their cost ratio. We illustrate our framework with applications in income-based social protection programs and humanitarian demining in Colombia, where the tension between screening costs and allocation efficiency is operationally consequential

title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Domain Shift in Permission-Based Android Malware Detection
summary: Machine learning-based Android malware detectors often fail in real-world deployment due to domain shift, where models trained on one data source perform poorly on applications from another. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the generalizability and interpretability of permission-based detectors under cross-domain conditions. Using two complementary datasets (PerMalDroid and NATICUSdroid) and five ensemble classifiers, we first establish an intra-domain baseline, where models achieve over 92% accuracy, and then quantify a severe asymmetric performance drop. While models trained on PerMalDroid generalize well to NATICUSdroid (86% accuracy), the reverse direction sees a drastic drop to 73% accuracy. Explainable AI analysis reveals bimodal feature distributions and shows that feature importance is highly unstable, with key permissions losing or gaining influence across domains. The predictive feature sets for different domains are fundamentally mismatched, as models rely on different, dataset-specific permissions. Most importantly, an ablation study demonstrates that for most models, training on a noisy feature set leads to poor generalization, confirming that domain-specific artifacts are a greater obstacle than missing features. To mitigate this, we validate a hybrid training strategy based on the intersection of common features and successfully recover cross-domain performance, achieving 88% accuracy on PerMalDroid and maintaining 97% on NATICUSdroid. These findings highlight the importance of explainable, cross-domain-robust malware detection systems and provide a practical pathway toward improving real-world deployment of permission-based Android malware detectors.

title: Prompt-Activation Duality: Improving Activation Steering via Attention-Level Interventions
summary: Activation steering controls language model behavior by adding directions to internal representations at inference time, but standard residual-stream steering can fail in stateful dialogue. We identify KV-cache contamination as a key failure mode: steered token states are stored and repeatedly reused, turning a local perturbation into cumulative coherence degradation. To address this challenge, we propose Gated Cropped Attention-Delta steering (GCAD), which extracts steering signals from system-prompt contributions to self-attention and applies them with token-level gating. Across persona-steering experiments, GCAD preserves trait control while substantially improving long-horizon coherence. On the main multi-turn benchmark, GCAD improves average coherence drift from -18.6 to -1.9 and raises turn-10 trait expression from 78.0 to 93.1. These results suggest that activation steering becomes more reliable when interventions follow the prompt-mediated pathways that models already use for behavioral control.

title: The Path-Extremal Conjecture for Zero Forcing: Distance-Hereditary Graphs and a Split-Decomposition Reduction
comments: This version strengthens the split-decomposition reduction: it allows arbitrarily many prime bags of order at most six, together with at most one additional prime bag whose label graph has every induced subgraph path-extremal, whereas the previous version restricted the total number of prime bags to at most one, subject to the same condition on its label graph. Also streamlined the exposition
summary:
A zero-forcing set of a graph is a set for which, after regarding each of its vertices as being blue, and applying the rule that a blue vertex with exactly one white neighbor forces said neighbor to become blue, all of the vertices in the graph are blue. Let $z(G;k)$ denote the number of zero forcing sets of size $k$. A conjecture of Boyer et al.\ asserts that the path $P_n$ maximizes these numbers coefficientwise among all $n$-vertex graphs. We prove this path-extremal conjecture for distance-hereditary graphs, which is the class of all graphs $G$ such that for each of the connected induced subgraphs of $G$, the distances between any two vertices in that subgraph are the same as they are in $G$. This extends the previously known tree case in which the path-extremal conjecture was known to be true to a much larger class that includes, in particular, all trees and all cographs.
  We then use canonical split decomposition to push the argument we used to show the distance-hereditary result into the more general setting of a connected graph with at most one prime bag in its canonical split decomposition. Specifically, we show that if a split-prime graph $H$ and all of its induced subgraphs are path-extremal, then every connected graph whose canonical split decomposition has a unique prime bag whose label graph is isomorphic to $H$ is also path-extremal. As a corollary of this result, for each fixed $m$, if every induced subgraph of every split-prime graph on at most $m$ vertices is path-extremal, then so is every connected graph whose canonical split decomposition has a unique prime bag of size at most $m$. Additionally, we prove that the path-extremal conjecture holds when all prime bags have order at most six, without restricting their number; under the preceding hereditary hypothesis, one additional prime bag labelled by $H$ is also allowed.
comment: This version strengthens the split-decomposition reduction: it allows arbitrarily many prime bags of order at most six, together with at most one additional prime bag whose label graph has every induced subgraph path-extremal, whereas the previous version restricted the total number of prime bags to at most one, subject to the same condition on its label graph. Also streamlined the exposition

title: Random Access Expectation in DNA Data Storage: Asymptotic Analysis Through Fountain Codes
summary: The expected number of coded symbols drawn from a linear code until a desired information symbol can be decoded is studied. This quantity is of interest in DNA data storage, where it is called the random access expectation. If the generator matrix of the code is binary and fully symmetric, the process of sampling symbols from the code is equivalent to the encoder of an LT code. Based on this observation, the random access expectation of binary fully symmetric codes under a peeling decoder is analyzed in the large blocklength limit. Asymptotically, a random access expectation, normalized by the number of information symbols, of $0.7869$ is achievable, while for a binary fully symmetric code under a peeling decoder it cannot be below $π/4\approx 0.7854$. The analysis is extended to the case where a set of information symbols needs to be decoded.

title: Principled Design of Diffusion-based Optimizers for Inverse Problems
summary: Score-based diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art performance for inverse problems, but their practical deployment is hindered by long inference times and cumbersome hyperparameter tuning. While pretrained diffusion models can be reused across tasks without retraining, inference-time hyperparameters such as the noise schedule and posterior sampling weights typically require ad-hoc adjustment for each problem setup. We propose principled reparameterizations that induce invariances, allowing the same hyperparameters to be reused across multiple problems without re-tuning. In addition, building on the RED-diff framework, which reformulates posterior sampling as an optimization problem, we further develop the OptDiff pipeline. OptDiff provides a simplified tuning framework that facilitates the integration of convex optimization tools to accelerate inference. Experiments on image reconstruction, deblurring, and super-resolution show substantial speedups and improved image quality.

title: LOFT: Low-Rank Orthogonal Fine-Tuning via Task-Aware Support Selection
summary: Orthogonal parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts pretrained weights through structure-preserving multiplicative transformations, but existing methods often conflate two distinct design choices: the subspace in which adaptation occurs and the transformation applied within that subspace. This paper introduces LOFT, a low-rank orthogonal fine-tuning framework that explicitly separates these two components. By viewing orthogonal adaptation as a multiplicative subspace rotation, LOFT provides a unified formulation that recovers the multiplicative core of representative orthogonal PEFT methods, including coordinate-, butterfly-, Householder- (with a learnable support) and principal-subspace-based variants (up to scaling and relaxation). More importantly, this perspective exposes support selection as a central design axis rather than a byproduct of a particular parameterization. We develop a first-order analysis showing that useful adaptation supports should be informed by the downstream training signal, motivating practical task-aware support selection strategies. Across language understanding, visual transfer, mathematical reasoning, and multilingual out-of-distribution adaptation, LOFT with task-aware supports improves performance at matched trainable-parameter and transform settings under a shared protocol. This suggests that, under a fixed transform and budget, the choice of support affects performance, making systematic support selection an important direction for improving orthogonal PEFT.

title: From Noise to Diversity: Random Embedding Injection in LLM Reasoning
summary: Recent soft prompt research has tried to improve reasoning by inserting trained vectors into LLM inputs, yet whether the gain comes from the learned content or from the act of injection itself has not been carefully separated. We study Random Soft Prompts (RSPs), which drop the training step entirely and append a freshly drawn sequence of random embedding vectors to the input. Each RSP vector is sampled from an isotropic Gaussian fitted to the entrywise mean and variance of the pretrained embedding table; the sequence carries no learned content, and yet reaches accuracy comparable to optimized soft prompts on math reasoning benchmarks in several settings. The mechanism unfolds in two stages: because attention has to absorb a never-seen-before random position, the distribution over the first few generated tokens flattens and reasoning trajectories branch, and as generation continues this influence dilutes naturally so the response commits to a single completion. We show that during inference RSPs lift early-stage token diversity and, combined with temperature sampling, widen Pass@N, the probability that at least one out of N attempts is correct. Beyond inference, we carry the same effect into DAPO training and demonstrate practical gains. Our contributions are: (i) RSP isolates the simplest form of soft prompt -- training-free, freshly resampled -- providing a unified lens for the structural effect of injection that variants otherwise differing in training and form all share; (ii) a theoretical and empirical validation of the underlying mechanism; and (iii) an extension from inference to training.

title: Efficient TV regularization of large-scale linear inverse problems via the SCD semismooth* Newton method with applications in tomography
summary: In this paper, we consider the efficient numerical minimization of Tikhonov functionals resulting from total-variation (TV) regularization of linear inverse problems. Since the TV penalty is non-smooth, this is typically done either via smooth approximations, which are inexact, or using non-smooth optimization techniques, which can often be numerically expensive, in particular for large-scale problems. Here, we present a numerically efficient minimization approach based on the recently proposed semismooth* Newton method, which employs a novel concept of graphical derivatives and exhibits locally superlinear convergence. The proposed approach is specifically tailored to TV regularization, suitable for large-scale inverse problems, and supported by strong mathematical convergence guarantees. Furthermore, we demonstrate its performance on two (large-scale) tomographic imaging problems and compare our results to those obtained via other state-of-the-art TV regularization approaches. Finally, an open-source Matlab implementation of the proposed method is made available online at https://github.com/HGfrerer/TVReg-2D-Semismoothstar-Newton.

title: PrivacySIM: Evaluating LLM Simulation of User Privacy Behavior
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but their ability to simulate individual privacy decisions is not well understood. In this paper, we evaluate whether a core set of user persona attributes can drive LLMs to simulate individual-level privacy behavior across various contexts. We introduce PrivacySIM, an evaluation suite that benchmarks LLM simulation of user privacy behavior against the ground-truth responses of 1,000 real users. These users are drawn from five published user studies on privacy behavior spanning LLM healthcare consultations, conversational agents, and chatbots. Drawing on these user studies and prior work in privacy behavior, we hypothesize three persona facets as plausible predictors of privacy decision-making: demographics, previous experiences, and stated privacy attitudes. We condition nine frontier LLMs on subsets of these three facets and measure how often each model's response to a data-sharing scenario matches the user's actual response. Our findings show that (1) zero-shot conditioning on these facets consistently improves simulation quality, but the performance of the best model (40.4% accuracy) suggests that richer and more nuanced persona facets are needed to reliably align with users' mental models for privacy decisions. (2) A user's stated privacy attitudes alone are often not the best predictor because they can diverge from the user's actual privacy behavior. (3) Users with high AI/chatbot experience are the most challenging to simulate. PrivacySIM is a first step toward understanding and improving the capabilities of LLMs to simulate user privacy decisions. We release PrivacySIM to enable further evaluation of LLM privacy simulation.

title: Black-Box Optimization of Mixed Binary-Continuous Variables: Challenges and Opportunities in Evolutionary Model Merging
summary: Model merging has emerged as a cost-effective paradigm for combining capabilities of multiple large language models (LLMs) without additional training. Among existing approaches, Data Flow Space (DFS) merging operates by selectively activating parameter groups across model layers, offering greater flexibility than naive parameter averaging. However, the optimization challenges underlying DFS merging remain poorly understood. In this paper, we formally characterize the DFS merging problem as a mixed binary-continuous black-box optimization problem, identifying three fundamental challenges: (1) mixed binary-continuous variable types, (2) high-dimensional search spaces with up to 291 parameter groups, and (3) conditional variable dependencies corresponding to Type-I interaction as characterized by Akimoto et al. [1]. We empirically evaluate seven merging methods on Mistral-7B models across official GSM8K (1,319 questions) and MMLU (14,042 questions, 57 subjects) benchmarks. Our structured approach achieves a 49.5% reduction in effective search space. Results reveal that all tested merging methods fail to surpass the stronger source model on official benchmarks, with TIES (13.72%) and DELLA (4.12%) performing catastrophically on GSM8K. Notably, DELLA scores below even the base model (6.67%), demonstrating that standard parameter space methods fail when merging base and instruction-tuned models. These findings directly validate the difficulty of the Type-I interaction structure we identify, and motivate the application of algorithms specifically designed for this challenge such as the concurrent IGBD work of Ong et al. [2].

title: Fill the GAP: A Granular Alignment Paradigm for Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Visual latent reasoning lets a multimodal large language model (MLLM) create intermediate visual evidence as continuous tokens, avoiding external tools or image generators. However, existing methods usually follow an output-as-input latent paradigm and yield unstable gains. We identify a feature-space mismatch behind this instability: dominant visual-latent models build on pre-norm MLLMs and reuse decoder hidden states as predicted latent inputs, even though these states occupy a substantially different norm regime from the input embeddings the model was trained to consume. This mismatch makes direct latent feedback unreliable. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose GAP, a Granular Alignment Paradigm for visual latent modeling. GAP aligns visual latent reasoning at three levels: data-level alignment grounds latent targets with inspectable auxiliary visual supervision; feature-level alignment maps decoder outputs into input-compatible visual latents through a lightweight PCA-aligned latent head; and model-level alignment assigns latent supervision selectively to examples where the base MLLM struggles. On Qwen2.5-VL 7B, GAP achieves the best aggregate perception and reasoning scores among all compared methods and is the only evaluated latent method that improves both over the base model. Inference-time interventions further show that generated latents carry task-relevant visual signal rather than merely adding token slots. Code is available at https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/GAP.

title: Routers Learn the Geometry of Their Experts: Geometric Coupling in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models enable scaling language models efficiently, but training them remains challenging, as routing can collapse onto few experts and auxiliary load-balancing losses can reduce specialization. Motivated by these hurdles, we study how routing decisions in SMoEs are formed mechanistically. First, we reveal a geometric coupling between routers and their corresponding experts. For a given token, the router weights for the selected expert and the expert weights processing it receive gradients along the same input direction, differing only in scalar coefficients. Thus, matched router--expert directions accumulate the same routed token history. This theoretical coupling also appears empirically in routing dynamics. In a $1$B SMoE trained from scratch, higher router scores predict stronger expert neuron preactivations, showing that routing decisions are mirrored inside the selected expert. Next, we analyze the effects of auxiliary load balancing on the router--expert geometric coupling, showing that such losses break this structure by spreading input-directed gradients across router weights, making distinct router directions nearly three times more similar to each other. Last, we demonstrate the centrality of geometric coupling for effective routing with a parameter-free online K-Means router, in which each expert maintains a running average of the hidden states routed to it and tokens are assigned based on cosine similarity. Compared with auxiliary-loss and loss-free balancing, this router achieves the lowest load imbalance with only a modest perplexity increase, indicating that geometric coupling captures a substantial part of what the router learns. Overall, our results explain how routers form assignment geometry that supports an effective division of labor.

title: MEME: Multi-entity & Evolving Memory Evaluation
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly operate in persistent environments where they must store, update, and reason over information across many sessions. While prior benchmarks evaluate only single-entity updates, MEME defines six tasks spanning the full space defined by the multi-entity and evolving axes, including three not scored by prior work: Cascade and Absence (dependency reasoning) and Deletion (post-removal state). Evaluating six memory systems spanning three memory paradigms on 100 controlled episodes, we find that all systems collapse on dependency reasoning under the default configuration (Cascade: 3%, Absence: 1% in average accuracy) despite adequate static retrieval performance. Prompt optimization, deeper retrieval, reduced filler noise, and most stronger LLMs fail to close this gap. The largest gain comes from a file-based agent paired with Claude Opus 4.7 as its internal LLM, which partially closes the gap at roughly 70x the baseline cost. Code and data are available on the project page: https://seokwonjung-jay.github.io/meme-eval/

title: Formal Conjectures: An Open and Evolving Benchmark for Verified Discovery in Mathematics
comments: 24 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
summary: As automated reasoning systems advance rapidly, there is a growing need for research-level formal mathematical problems to accurately evaluate their capabilities. To address this, we present Formal Conjectures (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures), an evolving benchmark of currently 7559 mathematical problem statements formalized in Lean 4. Sourced from areas of active mathematical research, the dataset features 1642 open research conjectures without known solutions for mathematical proof discovery, 2923 solved problems for proof auto-formalization, and 2994 supporting statements. Notably, the repository provides a structured interface connecting mathematicians who formalize and clarify problems with the AI systems and humans attempting to solve them. Demonstrating its immediate utility, the benchmark has already been leveraged for new mathematical discoveries, including the resolution of open research conjectures, and for the formal confirmation of major newly announced results. We describe our approach to ensuring the correctness of these formalizations in a collaborative open-source project where contributions stem from an active community. In this framework, AI-generated proofs and disproofs serve as a valuable auditing mechanism to iteratively improve the fidelity of the benchmark. Finally, we provide a standardized evaluation setup and report baseline results on frozen evaluation subsets, demonstrating a climbable signal that measures the current frontier of automated reasoning on research-level mathematics.
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Datasets and Benchmarks Track

title: Do Heavy Tails Help Diffusion? On the Subtle Trade-off Between Initialization and Training
summary: Recent works have proposed incorporating heavy-tailed (HT) noise into diffusion- and flow-based generative models, with the goals of better recovering the tails of target distributions and improving generative diversity. This motivation is intuitive: if the data are heavy-tailed, HT noise may appear better matched than light-tailed (LT) Gaussian noise. However, replacing Gaussian noise by HT noise also changes the underlying estimation problem. In this paper, we revisit this paradigm through a combined theoretical and empirical study, establishing sampling-error bounds for two representative diffusion models driven by HT and LT noise. We show that HT diffusion models can achieve exponentially fast initialization, but accumulated training errors may offset this advantage. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support our theoretical findings. Our results call into question a growing design trend in generative modeling and challenge the use of HT noise to improve rare-region exploration.

title: Exact Accepting-State Spectrum for Reversal of Permutation Automata
comments: Contains the strengthened result which, for $m,α\ge 2$, constructs a language $L$ with $\operatorname{asc}(L)=m$ and $\operatorname{asc}(L^R)=α$ such that the minimal DFAs recognizing $L$ and $L^R$ each have polynomially many states in $m$ and $α$, whereas the proof previously could use exponentially many states here. Contains additional streamlining of the exposition
summary:
In this paper we determine the accepting-state spectrum of the reversal operation on permutation automata, and moreover prove the conjecture conjectured by Rauch and Holzer in so doing. Namely, we show that reversal satisfies the spectrum $g^{\operatorname{asc}}_{R,\mathrm{PFA}}(0)=\{0\}$, $g^{\operatorname{asc}}_{R,\mathrm{PFA}}(1)=\{1\}$, and $g^{\operatorname{asc}}_{R,\mathrm{PFA}}(m)=\mathbb{N}_{\ge 2}$ for $m\ge 2$.
  We do this by, for every $m\ge 2$ and every $α\ge 2$, constructing a binary permutation automaton $A_{m,α}$ such that $ \operatorname{asc}(L(A_{m,α}))=m$ and $ \operatorname{asc}(L(A_{m,α})^{R})=α$. The spectrum above follows from this (combined with the trivial cases $m=0$ and $m=1$ and the fact that $1$ is magic for every $m\ge 2$).
  Thus our result shows that for $m \ge 2$, the reversal operation in permutation automaton attains ever single value positive value in the accepting-state complexity except for $1$.

title: Beyond Instance-Level Self-Supervision in 3D Multi-Modal Medical Imaging
summary: Self-supervised pre-training methods in medical imaging typically treat each individual as an isolated instance, learning representations through augmentation-based objectives or masked reconstruction. They often do not adequately capitalize on a key characteristic of physiological features: anatomical structures maintain consistent spatial relationships across individuals (instances), such as the thalamus being medial to the basal ganglia, regardless of variations in brain size, shape, or pathology. We propose leveraging this cross-instance topological consistency as a supervisory signal. The challenge arises from the inherent variability in medical imaging, which can differ significantly across instances and modalities. To tackle this, we focus on two alignment regimes. (i) Intra-instance: with pixel-level correspondences available, a cross-modal triplet objective explicitly preserves local neighborhood topology. (ii) Inter-instance: without such supervision, we derive pseudo-correspondences to control partial neighborhood alignment and prevent topology collapse across modalities. We validate our approach across 7 downstream multi-modal tasks, achieving average improvements of 1.1% and 5.94% in segmentation and classification tasks, respectively, and demonstrating significantly better robustness when modalities are missing at test time.

title: Beyond Bounded Variance: Variance-Reduced Normalized Methods for Nonconvex Optimization under Blum-Gladyshev Noise
summary: Stochastic optimization theory often assumes that gradient noise has uniformly bounded variance. However, this assumption can be inadequate even in simple settings; e.g., it does not hold for linear least squares regression. The Blum-Gladyshev ($\mathsf{BG}$-0) noise model instead allows the stochastic gradient variance to grow quadratically with the distance from the initialization and has recently been identified as the weakest known viable variance assumption. We study nonconvex stochastic optimization under $\mathsf{BG}$-0 noise and prove that normalized momentum converges with one stochastic gradient per iteration, reaching an $\varepsilon$-stationary point with the optimal $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$ complexity. We then show that, under mean-square smoothness, a variance-reduced normalized STORM method achieves the minimax optimal complexity of $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$. We further extend our analysis to the symmetric generalized smoothness framework, which captures objectives whose local curvature can scale with the gradient norm. To our knowledge, these are the first convergence guarantees for normalized methods in nonconvex stochastic optimization under $\mathsf{BG}$-0 noise without bounded domains.

title: Constructing Generalizable Parallel Algorithm Portfolios for Multi-Objective Binary Optimization via General-Purpose Instance Generation
summary: Despite progress in constructing generalizable parallel algorithm portfolios~(PAPs), no general-purpose method is yet available for multi-objective binary optimization problems~(MOBOPs) without problem-specific customization. To fill this gap, this work proposes domain-agnostic co-evolution of parameterized search for multi-objective binary optimization~(DACMO), the first general-purpose method for automatic PAP construction on MOBOPs. Its core, Unified Instance Representation~(UIR), represents and generates MOBOP instances with varying dimensions without knowledge of problem-specific instance structures. UIR separates common features of the target class from instance-specific features, preserving the common features learned from real instances during generation. DACMO co-evolves the training instances and PAP by alternating UIR-based instance augmentation with PAP updates. Experiments cover four structurally different MOBOP classes, including two black-box classes from real-world applications. Starting from five real training instances per class, DACMO constructs high-performance PAPs without problem-specific customization. On unseen instances from all four classes, these PAPs outperform portfolios of tuned classical multi-objective evolutionary algorithms and those constructed by the recent automatic PAP construction method EoH-S. DACMO also achieves overall performance comparable to the strong CEPS baseline and significantly outperforms it on two classes, without the substantial expert effort CEPS requires for problem-specific instance generator design.

title: Policy Library CBF: Finite-Horizon Safety at Runtime via Parallel Rollouts
summary: Safety-critical autonomy in unstructured environments poses significant challenges for online safety certification under evolving constraints, particularly when a single backup policy is not effective across operating conditions. We propose the Policy Library Control Barrier Function (PL-CBF), a runtime safety filter that evaluates a library of fallback policies via parallel finite-horizon rollouts. Among policies with constraint-satisfying rollouts and feasible CBF constraints, PL-CBF selects the policy maximizing the volume of its admissible control set and solves a single quadratic program to minimally modify the nominal input within that constrained input set. Using a finite-horizon language metric over closed-loop behaviors, we characterize when a finite policy library contains a constraint-satisfying rollout. Five simulation studies cover indoor robot navigation with a double-integrator model (4 states), highway driving under abrupt friction changes with a nonlinear vehicle model (8 states), and quadrotor flight control among dynamic obstacles (12 states), demonstrating improved safety performance compared with the evaluated baselines while maintaining millisecond-scale mean computation times. Hardware experiments on a mobile robot among moving pedestrians and a custom-built quadrotor among dynamic obstacles demonstrate real-time operation of PL-CBF.

title: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization
comments: 46 pages, 10 figures. v2 adds matched-baseline comparisons, residual diagnostics, and expanded long-context analysis
summary:
INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM.
  We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7 (358B parameters). On RULER-NIAH up to 128K tokens, OSCAR substantially outperforms QuaRot-style INT2 across context lengths. System-wise, OSCAR compresses KV-cache memory by nearly $8\times$, boosts multi-request throughput by up to $7.8\times$ at large batch sizes within the same memory budget, and accelerates batch-size-1 decoding by up to $3.1\times$ over BF16 by cutting KV memory traffic.
