title: Euclidean and Hermitian Self-Orthogonal Codes from Divisible Codes
summary: Self-orthogonality and divisibility are two fundamental properties of linear codes, and the relationship between them has long been of interest. Huffman and Pless (2003) showed that every binary \(4\)-divisible code is Euclidean self-orthogonal, that a ternary code is Euclidean self-orthogonal if and only if it is \(3\)-divisible, and that a quaternary code is Hermitian self-orthogonal if and only if it is \(2\)-divisible. The general case remained open for a long time. In 2024, Li and Heng settled the odd-characteristic case, proving that every \(p\)-divisible code over \(\F_{p^m}\), with \(p\) odd, that contains the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal. In this paper we treat the even-characteristic case: we prove that every \(4\)-divisible code over \(\F_{2^m}\) containing the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal. We also prove that, for every prime \(p\), every \(p\)-divisible linear code over \(\F_{q^2}\), where \(q=p^m\), that contains the all-one vector is Hermitian self-orthogonal. In addition, we generalize the Hermitian criterion to the Galois self-orthogonal case, proving that any $p$-divisible linear code over $\gf_{q^r}$ that contains the all-one vector is $\ell$-Galois self-orthogonal for \(\ell\in\{1,\dots,r-1\}\). These criteria make the construction of self-orthogonal codes from divisible codes simple and efficient. As applications, we recover the known Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonality of generalized Reed--Muller codes and obtain several infinite families of new Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonal codes, which give rise to infinite families of quantum codes with excellent parameters.

title: Communication-Learning Co-Design for Pinching-Antenna-Assisted Federated Learning in Heterogeneous Wireless Networks
summary: Wireless federated learning (FL) suffers from two coupled bottlenecks: statistical heterogeneity across clients and communication-constrained model synchronization over unreliable wireless links. Instead of focusing on algorithmic design and/or wireless resource optimization, this paper provides a systematic study of pinching antenna (PA)-empowered FL for heterogeneous wireless networks and develops a unified communication-and-learning framework. Specifically, we integrate a segmented waveguide-enabled pinching antenna (SWAN) architecture with a heterogeneity-robust FL algorithm based on client variance reduction and dual quantization, so as to jointly mitigate communication bottlenecks and client drift. On this basis, we further develop a two-stage SWAN-assisted downlink protocol and formulate fairness-oriented uplink optimization problems for PA positioning, bandwidth allocation, and quantization design. Efficient solution frameworks are then derived for the resulting downlink and uplink optimization problems. Experimental results show the superiority of the proposed design in convergence speed and final accuracy under non-independent and identically distributed data and communication bottlenecks.

title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
summary: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
summary: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. However, existing methods primarily represent skills as natural language documents, intertwining procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and making skills difficult to maintain and evolve. To address this limitation, we propose PASE (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution), a program-aided framework that iteratively evolves skills by associating them with executable programs. Unlike prior approaches that encode trajectory-derived experience primarily in natural language, PASE separates reusable procedural logic into editable programs, enabling targeted updates to executable components while reducing the need to repeatedly revise natural language skills. Extensive experiments across diverse models and benchmarks demonstrate that PASE consistently outperforms all baselines, by achieving over 2.8% improvements. Further analyses show that PASE exhibits greater evolutionary stability and generalisation capability, highlighting the critical role of programmatic knowledge in skill evolution. We will release all data and code via GitHub.

title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for high-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs
comments: 69 pages (26 pages main manuscript, 43 pages Supplementary information)
summary: The time to solution of an iterative solver depends on the number of iterations and the cost per iteration. This paper develops algorithms that reduce both for elliptic problems discretized with high-order continuous finite elements on distributed GPUs, implemented in a unified matrix-free code supporting CUDA, HIP and SYCL. A distributed direct fast-diagonalization (FD) Poisson solver provides exact solutions on tensor-product meshes with direction-wise grading and coefficients varying along one coordinate direction. Its tensor data remain distributed, moved between slab layouts using collective transposes or kept in place by a Schur-complement approach. A two-level hybrid Schwarz preconditioner with FD cell solves (HS-FD) is extended to 2:1 hanging-node octrees with exact local cell inverses, while a p-multigrid preconditioner with Chebyshev--Jacobi smoothing (CJ-pMG) resolves hanging-node constraints at every level within fused kernels. Both approaches exploit FP32, where cell shapes and coefficients allow, within an FP64 conjugate-gradient iteration, adaptively select replicated or distributed coarse levels, support block solves for multiple right-hand sides and determine all parameters from the operator without case-specific tuning. Comparisons with Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients (Jacobi PCG), MFEM, nekRS and deal.II span uniform, graded and octree meshes, layered coefficients, and four applications across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs. The direct solver is two to three orders of magnitude faster than Jacobi PCG on uniform meshes. HS-FD converges in 11 iterations for the generalised Poisson problem on octree meshes across 8 to 1024 MI250X graphics compute dies. These results provide practical guidelines for solver selection based on mesh structure and coefficient characteristics.
comment: 69 pages (26 pages main manuscript, 43 pages Supplementary information)

title: An AI Assistant for Automating Anti-Corruption Expertise of Draft Legislation Based on the TRACE Framework
summary: We present an AI assistant for automating anti-corruption expertise of draft legislation based on the TRACE architecture, designed to screen bills for corruption risks: pinpoint provisions an expert would criticise and name the regulatory defect in each. The pipeline combines a deterministic parsing core, model-guided single-provision qualification, rule-based factor assignment, and external human oversight. To evaluate the assistant, we constructed an open benchmark from the published conclusions of Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK), comprising 132 draft laws with 474 model-extracted findings. A system flag agrees with a finding when it targets a compatible provision and an LLM judge rates the risk as the same (strict) or partly the same (lenient). On 100 draft laws, the pipeline matches 0.28 of the findings within its top ten flags using the local Gemma 4 31B model, 0.30 with Sonnet 5.5, and 0.43-0.46 across all flags (non-blind; the frozen blind baseline achieves 0.21, 95% CI 0.16-0.26). Across all runs, most misses occur on provisions that the system located but qualified as a different risk, and none of the 32 legal-collision findings was matched. On 21 acts held out from tuning, the pipeline outperforms a monolithic prompt containing the full methodology under the strict measure, though not under the lenient one, and Opus 5.5 adds nothing over Sonnet. The reported scores reflect agreement with model-extracted findings rated by an LLM judge whose two access routes agree on 73 of 74 labels, without human expert validation.

title: UniFlow-RS: Unified Generative Prediction for Heterogeneous Remote-Sensing Tasks
summary: Remote-sensing foundation models increasingly unify representations across sensing modalities and downstream tasks, yet their prediction mechanisms remain largely task-specific. Separate decoders, prediction heads, and objectives leave prediction fragmented across tasks. This naturally raises a question: can heterogeneous remote-sensing tasks share the prediction process? UniFlow-RS answers this question with a single latent flow-matching predictor shared across tasks. This requires addressing two key challenges: unifying heterogeneous prediction spaces and harmonizing joint optimization across tasks. First, we cast heterogeneous task outputs into structured visual targets in a common latent space, allowing them to be modeled by the same pretrained flow predictor. Task-dependent conditioning further accommodates differences in input configurations. Second, we optimize all tasks with a common Flow Matching objective, eliminating task-specific prediction losses. To mitigate optimization mismatch across tasks and modalities, we introduce Task-Modality Adaptive Timestep Sampling (TMAS), which dynamically allocates training timesteps according to the online learning state of each task-modality group. Using a single shared model, UniFlow-RS handles six tasks and thirteen datasets, surpassing recent task-specific state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks while remaining competitive on the others. Beyond these benchmarks, the same checkpoint demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer across unseen datasets, task settings, occlusion conditions, and near-infrared false-color imagery, without target-specific adaptation. Codes are available at https://github.com/MindVision-AI/UniFlow-RS.

title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
summary: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.

title: Reliable and explainable analysis of AVS/RS by Statistical Model Checking and Process Mining
comments: 66 pages, 11 figures. Author accepted manuscript for Expert Systems with Applications, revised following peer review. Replaces the original pre-review version
summary: Automated Vehicle Storage and Retrieval Systems (AVS/RS) are increasingly adopted to boost warehouse throughput while containing operational costs. We present a tool-supported analysis workflow that combines discrete-event simulation, Statistical Model Checking (SMC), and Process Mining (PM) techniques to quantify and explain AVS/RS performance. SMC, implemented through the MultiVeStA tool, delivers statistically reliable estimates of key indicators, such as cycle times and inventory consolidation, across alternative stocking and picking policies with user-specified confidence levels. MultiVeStA orchestrates multiple independent simulations in a black-box manner, enabling automated verification. PM ingests the resulting event logs to uncover the behavioural patterns and bottlenecks that drive those indicators, closing the interpretability gap typical of simulation studies. We instantiate the framework on a new open-source AVS/RS simulator configured according to recent industrial guidelines and evaluate multiple control strategies and different scenarios. Results show that the coordinated use of SMC and PM supports both predictive what-if analyses and post-hoc diagnostics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of a combined SMC-PM workflow to AVS/RS operations, complemented by a reusable open-source simulation and analysis toolchain.
comment: 66 pages, 11 figures. Author accepted manuscript for Expert Systems with Applications, revised following peer review. Replaces the original pre-review version

title: New linear codes over GF(7), GF(8) and GF(9) from quasi-cyclic codes and Construction X
comments: 12 pages, 1 table. Ancillary files: verification program and generator matrices. v2: three more codes and two more derived codes added. summary: We present linear codes with parameters [88,8,64]_7, [90,8,65]_7, [98,7,75]_8, [97,8,72]_8, [44,7,31]_9, [97,8,71]_7, [85,6,67]_8 and [78,8,56]_7. The remaining one, the [90,8,65]_7 code, is obtained from the first by appending two coordinates. The parameters and all weight counts were obtained by exhaustive enumeration, and a short program that repeats these computations is included.

title: Accurate predictions of properties of energetic materials with tabular foundation models
summary: We use TabPFN, a recently developed tabular foundation model, to predict three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature and crystal density. Without any hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN outperforms the best published models for all three properties. It also substantially outperforms a wide range of established machine-learning models, including tuned gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forests and Gaussian processes. This holds both when the models are given hand-crafted molecular descriptors and when they are given learned representations from Chemprop's message-passing neural network. In particular, for all three properties, TabPFN applied to Chemprop's own embedding is more accurate than Chemprop's predictions. TabPFN is also among the fastest models we consider, more than an order of magnitude faster than XGBoost. As TabPFN predicts the entire distribution of the target rather than just a single value, it offers built-in uncertainty quantification, which we compare with the empirical distributions of compounds with repeated measurements. Finally, we interpret the predictions using Shapley values, which rank the features by their importance.

title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
comments: 39 pages, 24 figures, 2 tables, Accepted at 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.
comment: 39 pages, 24 figures, 2 tables, Accepted at 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
comments: 51 pages, 13 figures. Code and run records: https://github.com/unifyai/continual-arc
summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
comment: 51 pages, 13 figures. Code and run records: https://github.com/unifyai/continual-arc

title: Efficient Multi-Organ Segmentation Using SpatialConfiguration-Net with Low GPU Memory Requirements
summary: Even though many semantic segmentation methods exist that are able to perform well on many medical datasets, they are often not designed for direct use in clinical practice. The two main concerns are generalization to unseen data with a different visual appearance, e.g., images acquired using a different scanner, and efficiency in terms of computation time and required Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) memory. In this work, we employ a multi-organ segmentation model based on the SpatialConfiguration-Net (SCN), which integrates prior knowledge of the spatial configuration among the labelled organs to resolve spurious responses in the network outputs. Furthermore, we modified the architecture of the segmentation model to reduce its memory footprint as much as possible without drastically impacting the quality of the predictions. Lastly, we implemented a minimal inference script for which we optimized both execution time and required GPU memory.

title: A Unified Algorithmic Framework for Dynamic Assortment Optimization under MNL Choice
summary: We consider assortment and inventory planning problems with dynamic stockout-based substitution effects, and without replenishment, in two different settings: (1) Customers can see all available products when they arrive, a typical scenario in physical stores. (2) The seller can choose to offer a subset of available products to each customer, which is more common on online platforms. Both settings are known to be computationally challenging, and the current approximation algorithms for the two settings are quite different. We develop a unified algorithm framework under the MNL choice model for both settings. Our algorithms improve on the state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of approximation guarantee and runtime, and the ability to manage uncertainty in the total number of customers and handle more complex constraints. In the process, we establish various novel properties of dynamic assortment planning (for the MNL choice model) that may be useful more broadly.

title: Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
comments: 99 pages, includes appendix. Accepted for publication in Management Science
summary: We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.
comment: 99 pages, includes appendix. Accepted for publication in Management Science

title: Boolean combinations of graphs
summary: Boolean combinations allow combining given combinatorial objects to obtain new, potentially more complicated, objects. In this paper, we initiate a systematic study of this idea applied to graphs. In order to understand expressive power and limitations of boolean combinations in this context, we investigate how they affect different combinatorial and structural properties of graphs, in particular $χ$-boundedness, as well as characterize the structure of boolean combinations of graphs from various classes.

title: FACE: Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion for Cross-subject EEG Emotion Recognition
summary: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples. This article introduces the few-shot adapter with a cross-view fusion method called FACE for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition, which leverages dynamic cross-view fusion and effective subject-specific adaptation. Specifically, FACE incorporates a cross-view fusion module that dynamically integrates global brain connectivity with localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights to provide complementary emotional information. Moreover, the few-shot adapter module is proposed to enable rapid adaptation for unseen subjects while reducing overfitting by enhancing adapter structures with meta-learning. Experimental results on three public EEG emotion recognition benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FACE under few-shot cross-subject evaluation.

title: Projective Variety Recovery from Unknown Linear Projections
comments: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:math/0208099, arXiv:math/0110157 by other authors. Code and computations: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24114814
summary: We study how a smooth irreducible variety $X$ of dimension $n$ and degree $d$ in $\mathbb{P}^m$, $m\geq n+2$, can be recovered from the equations of its images under two generic projections from unknown centers. This extends earlier results on curves in $\mathbb{P}^3$ and surfaces in $\mathbb{P}^4$ to any dimension. Since $X$ is the normalization of each image, one image determines $X$ modulo the projective group when $X$ is linearly normal; what two images add is the configuration, that is the pair of projections. For complete intersections we prove unconditionally that the set of configurations compatible with the two images and their Hilbert polynomial is finite, of size at most $|\mathrm{Lin}(X)|$, the projective automorphism group of $X$. The argument is effective and the bound is attained. We then introduce an equation generalizing Kruppa's equation, relating the duals of the images to a fundamental matrix, encoding the pair of projections modulo the projective group. We give a necessary condition for its solution variety to be finite, a bound on its isolated points, and a sufficient condition under which the true fundamental matrix is rigid: no quadric may contain a generic line $L$ together with the locus of points of $X$ whose tangent space meets $L$. Rigidity is unconditional for curves; in higher dimension it holds under a first-order liftability hypothesis, which we certify for a del Pezzo quartic surface in $\mathbb{P}^4$. Global finiteness of that solution variety remains open, necessarily so, as it contains solutions realized by no variety; for $\dim X<\mathrm{codim}\,X-1$ the obstruction amounts to knowing the fundamental matrix itself. Once the projections are known, $X$ is recovered from the two cones over the images: in codimension two their intersection is $X$ plus a component of degree $d(d-1)$; in higher codimension $X$ is its unique component of maximal dimension.

title: Computing Projective Implicit Representations from Poset Towers
summary: A family of simplicial complexes connected by simplicial maps and indexed by a finite poset $P$ is called a poset tower. Poset towers subsume multi-parameter filtrations, zigzag filtrations, and one-parameter simplicial towers, while allowing arbitrary finite posets and simplicial maps. The homology of a poset tower is a $P$-persistence module. To compute it globally over $P$, we consider the chain complex segment of $P$-persistence modules $C_{\ell-1}\xleftarrow{\partial_{\ell}}C_\ell \xleftarrow{\partial_{\ell+1}}C_{\ell+1}$ induced by the simplices of the tower. Unlike in one-critical multi-filtrations, the chain modules $C_\ell$ need not be projective and may have a complicated structure. We address the problem of replacing this segment by projective modules and $P$-graded matrices while preserving homology. The resulting projective implicit representation (PiRep) plays the role of the graded boundary-matrix representation in the classical persistence algorithm: it converts simplicial data into algebraic input on which persistent homology can be computed globally over $P$. In particular, a PiRep can be used as input to algorithms for computing minimal presentations of persistent homology. We give an efficient algorithm to compute a PiRep from a poset tower. It constructs degreewise minimal presentations and asymptotically minimal second terms of projective resolutions of the chain modules $C_\ell$, lifts the boundary maps $\partial_\ell$ to these resolutions, and assembles the resulting data into a PiRep using an additional correction term. The method is tailored to chain complexes induced by poset towers and computes the required algebraic data combinatorially, exploiting their special structure and avoiding general-purpose algebraic reduction. In the context of poset towers, it is fully general and can serve as a foundation for efficient algorithms on specific posets.

title: Lilith: Developmental Modular LLMs with Chemical Signaling
comments: This paper has been withdrawn by the author as it represents early, preliminary work that the author no longer endorses.
summary: Current paradigms in Artificial Intelligence rely on layers of feedforward networks which model brain activity at the neuronal level. We conjecture that expanding to the level of multiple brain regions with chemical signaling may be a productive step toward understanding the emergence of consciousness. We propose LILITH, a novel architecture that combines developmental training of modular language models with brain-inspired token-based communication protocols, mirroring chemical signaling in the brain. Our approach models distinct brain regions as specialized LLM modules including thinking, memory, sensory, and regulatory components that communicate through emergent token-based signaling protocols analogous to neurotransmitter networks. Unlike traditional pre-trained systems, LILITH would employ developmental training where untrained LLM architectures learn through simulated life experiences, developing communication pathways and cognitive abilities through environmental interaction and evolutionary optimization. This framework would enable direct empirical investigation of consciousness emergence using Integrated Information Theory metrics while providing unprecedented insight into inter-module signaling patterns during development. By optimizing for consciousness emergence rather than task performance, LILITH could provide insight into different emergent phenomena at multiple levels of neural correlates, contrasting neuronal-level processing with multi-region coordination dynamics. The goal of this paper is to put the idea forward while recognizing the substantial challenges in implementing such a system.

title: Re-evaluating Heart Rate Variability Biomarkers for Glucose Sensing: The Impact of Age Normalisation and Subject-Independent Validation
summary: Heart rate variability (HRV) from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals may indicate glycemic status, but prior studies often combine distinct glucose targets and use validation strategies vulnerable to data leakage. Since HRV declines with age, aging may be confounded with diabetes-related autonomic dysfunction. We tested whether age-dependent HRV normalisation improves glycemic estimation. We analysed ECG features from 43 male patients with type 2 diabetes. Outcomes were glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c; n=29) and fasting blood glucose (FBG; n=38). We used leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, with feature selection and standardisation within each training fold. We compared 20 machine-learning algorithms, six age-adjustment methods, and 20 normalisation parameter combinations. Validation included 500 permutations and bootstrap confidence intervals. Extra Trees regression performed best: R2=0.222 (r=0.476, p=0.009) for HbA1c and R2=0.086 (r=0.344, p=0.034) for FBG. Mean absolute errors were 1.18 percentage points and 2.27 mmol/L, respectively. Permutation testing supported both associations (p=0.002). Contrary to our hypothesis, no age-adjustment method or parameter combination improved performance. Tree ensembles retained positive performance under strict validation, whereas linear models had negative R2 values; neural networks performed poorly. Strict within-fold preprocessing materially changed model performance and revealed potential inflation from conventional validation. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were [0.13, 0.82] for HbA1c R2 and [0.10, 0.72] for FBG R2. Although findings support HRV-glycemic associations, performance remains insufficient for standalone clinical use. The study highlights the importance of separating glycemic targets, subject-independent validation, within-fold preprocessing, and comprehensive baselines in non-invasive glycemic monitoring research.

title: The C-index Multiverse
comments: 21 pages main text with 6 figures and 3 tables. 22 pages of supplementary material
summary: Quantifying out-of-sample discrimination performance for time-to-event outcomes is a fundamental step for model evaluation and selection in the context of predictive modelling. The concordance index, or C-index, is a widely used metric for this purpose, particularly with the growing development of machine learning methods. Beyond differences between proposed C-index estimators (e.g. Harrell's, Uno's and Antolini's), we demonstrate the existence of a C-index multiverse among available R and python software, where seemingly equal implementations can yield different results. This can undermine reproducibility and complicate fair comparisons across models and studies. Key variation sources include tie handling and adjustment to censoring. Additionally, the absence of a standardised approach to summarise risk from survival distributions, result in another source of variation dependent on input types. We demonstrate the consequences of the C-index multiverse when quantifying predictive performance for several survival models (from Cox proportional hazards to recent deep learning approaches) on publicly available breast cancer data, and semi-synthetic examples. Our work emphasises the need for better reporting to improve transparency and reproducibility. This article aims to be a useful guideline, helping analysts when navigating the multiverse, providing unified documentation and highlighting potential pitfalls of existing software. All code is publicly available at: www.github.com/BBolosSierra/CindexMultiverse.
comment: 21 pages main text with 6 figures and 3 tables. 22 pages of supplementary material

title: Robust Amortized Simulation-Based Inference via Learned Error Models
summary: Recent advances in neural density estimation have enabled amortized Bayesian inference for complex stochastic simulators. However, these methods rely on simulators accurately reflecting the true data-generating process and can degrade significantly under model misspecification. We consider the setting where multiple unlabeled observations are available and introduce robust variational neural posterior estimation (RVNP), an amortized Bayesian inference method that uses an importance-weighted autoencoder to jointly learn a misspecification-robust posterior proxy and an explicit error model that captures the simulation-to-reality gap. Our results show that RVNP can recover robust posterior inference in a data-driven and interpretable manner, outperforming previous methods on multiple metrics across misspecified benchmarks.

title: Model Order Reduction for Quantum Molecular Dynamics
summary: Quantum molecular dynamics (QMD) provides a high-fidelity physical framework for modeling atomic and molecular phenomena from first principles. However, its mathematical formulation requires solving iterative, high-dimensional electronic structure problems at every physical state step. Within the broader data-driven computational mechanics paradigm, we present a projection-based model order reduction framework for electronic structure calculation in QMD. By discovering a low-dimensional manifold of the electronic solution space within Kohn-Sham density functional theory, our approach projects the governing variational formulation onto an intrinsically reduced subspace. This avoids full-space iterative wavefunction optimization while preserving rigorous physical symmetries and state consistency. We demonstrate this methodology on a water molecule, demonstrating strong agreement with high-fidelity reference solutions across structural trajectories and thermodynamic observables through canonical coordinate alignment and structured manifold sampling.

title: QuantGraph: A Receding-Horizon Quantum Graph Solver
comments: P. Vaidhyanathan and A. Papatheodorou contributed equally to this work. Published in Physical Review Applied. 17 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, 2 algorithms
summary: Dynamic programming is a cornerstone of graph-based optimization. While effective, it scales unfavorably with problem size. In this work, we present QuantGraph, a two-stage quantum-enhanced framework that casts local and global graph-optimization problems as quantum-searches over discrete trajectory spaces. The solver is designed to operate efficiently by first finding a sequence of locally optimal transitions in the graph (local stage), without considering full trajectories. The accumulated cost of the resulting candidate acts as a threshold that prunes the search space (up to 60% reduction for certain examples). The subsequent global stage, based on this threshold, refines the solution. To achieve scalability and robustness, we draw on principles from control theory and embed QuantGraph's global stage within a receding-horizon model-predictive-control scheme. This classical layer stabilizes and guides the quantum search, improving precision and reducing computational burden. In practice, the resulting closed-loop system exhibits robust behavior and lower query complexity. Notably, for a fixed control horizon and query budget, QuantGraph supports approximately twice as many control discretization bits while still benefiting from Grover-search's inherent quadratic speedup compared to classical methods.
comment: P. Vaidhyanathan and A. Papatheodorou contributed equally to this work. Published in Physical Review Applied. 17 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, 2 algorithms

title: Block-Fitness Modeling of the Global Air Mobility Network
summary: Accurate representations of the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, high-resolution, real-time data on the WAN are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model of the WAN that treats air travel as a stochastic process within a maximum-entropy framework. The model uses airport-level passenger flows to probabilistically generate connections while preserving traffic volumes across geographic regions. The resulting reconstructed networks reproduce key structural properties of the WAN and enable simulations of dynamic spreading that closely match those obtained using the real network. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for forecasting and policy design in global mobility systems.

title: The Leibniz adjunction in homotopy type theory, with an application to simplicial type theory
summary: Simplicial type theory extends homotopy type theory and equips types with a notion of directed morphisms. A Segal type is defined to be a type in which these directed morphisms can be composed. We show that all higher coherences can be stated and derived if simplicial type theory is taken to be homotopy type theory with a postulated interval type. In technical terms, this means that if a type has unique fillers for $(2,1)$-horns, it has unique fillers for all inner $(n,k)$-horns. This generalizes a result of Riehl and Shulman for the case $n = 3, k \in \{1, 2\}$. Our main technical tool is the Leibniz adjunction: the pushout-product is left adjoint to the pullback-hom in the wild category of types. While this adjunction is well known for ordinary categories, it is much more involved for higher categories, and the fact that it can be proved for the wild category of types (a higher category without stated higher coherences) is non-trivial. We make profitable use of the equivalence between the wild category of maps and that of families. We have formalized the results in Cubical Agda.

title: Learning pharmacokinetic dynamics with structured neural ODEs for precision dosing
summary: Individualized dosing requires predicting how a patient's drug exposure would change under a different dose or schedule. However, a model that accurately predicts exposure at the current dose may not reliably predict what happens when treatment changes. We developed two neural models that learn pharmacokinetic dynamics from data without predefined pharmacokinetic equations. The first predicts exposure after a dose change, while the second also allows changes in dosing schedules. In simulations, the second model predicted exposure under new dosing schedules more accurately than competing neural models. On real data of kidney transplant recipients treated with tacrolimus, both models showed lower prediction errors than Bayesian estimation when predicting exposure at a later visit. These findings suggest that incorporating pharmacokinetic principles into neural models can improve predictions needed for individualized dosing.

title: Functional Stochastic Localization
summary: Eldan's stochastic localization is a probabilistic construction that has proved instrumental to modern breakthroughs in high-dimensional geometry and the design of sampling algorithms. Motivated by sampling under non-Euclidean geometries and the mirror descent algorithm in optimization, we develop a functional generalization of Eldan's process that replaces Gaussian regularization with regularization by any positive integer multiple of a log-Laplace transform. We further give a mixing time bound on the Markov chain induced by our localization process, which holds if our target distribution satisfies a functional Poincaré inequality. Finally, we apply our framework to differentially private convex optimization in $\ell_p$ norms for $p \in [1, 2)$, where we improve state-of-the-art query complexities in a zeroth-order model.

title: Assessing Per-Sample Membership Inference Vulnerability without Retraining
summary: Recent work in the privacy literature shows that sample-targeted membership inference attacks (MIAs) significantly outperform untargeted approaches by a wide margin. Motivated by this observation, we address the following question: can the privacy vulnerability of individual training points be assessed without training shadow models? We show that per-sample exposure to MIA is governed not only by a point's loss, but also by a data-dependent geometric measure. In the linear setting, we derive a closed-form decomposition of individual black-box MIA vulnerability into a population leverage score and a residual loss term, making explicit how sample-dependent geometry translates into privacy exposure. Since the final layer of most modern architectures is linear, we extend this framework to deep networks and propose a surrogate score operating on last-layer representations that requires only a single trained model and no shadow models. Empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and architectures show that our score outperforms loss and gradient-norm baselines at identifying the highest-risk points under state-of-the-art attacks, providing a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded tool for per-sample privacy risk assessment.

title: A characterization of interval nest digraphs
comments: Small mistake correction with respect to the published version. A necessary condition in a related paper was (wrongly) stated buy us as a characterization, we have now corrected that mistake
summary:
A digraph consisting of a set of vertices $V$ and a set of arcs $E$ is called an interval digraph if there exists a family of closed intervals $\{I_u,J_u\}_{u \in V}$ such that $uv$ is an arc if and only if the intersection of $I_u$ and $J_v$ is non-empty. Interval digraphs naturally generalize interval graphs, by extending the classical interval intersection model to directed graphs. Several subclasses of interval digraphs have been studied in the literature-such as balanced, chronological and catch interval digraphs-each characterized by admitting interval representations that satisfy specific restrictions. Among these, interval nest digraphs are the ones that admit an interval representation in which $J_u$ is contained in $I_u$ for all vertices $u$ of $V$.
  In this work, we provide a complete characterization of interval nest digraphs in terms of vertex linear orderings with forbidden patterns, which we call nest orderings. This result completes the picture of vertex-ordering characterizations among the main subclasses of interval digraphs.
comment: Small mistake correction with respect to the published version. A necessary condition in a related paper was (wrongly) stated buy us as a characterization, we have now corrected that mistake

title: Foundational Analysis Of The Solvability Complexity Index
comments: Important: [arXiv:2603.18955v2]: additional discussions about evaluation-induced topologies, Kihara-style piecewise-continuity reducibilities, and feasible real RAM models and their connection to the SCI [arXiv:2603.18955v3]: Short+focused version on main results; this version: densified revised version with additional examples, algebraic properties of general algorithms
summary: The Solvability Complexity Index (SCI) provides an extensional limit-height formalism for recovering a target map $Ξ$ from finite samples of an evaluation interface $Λ\subseteq\mathbb C^Ω$ by finite-height towers of pointwise limits. We first give a foundational analysis of what this extensional framework does and does not determine. In second place, we give a concrete non-trivial bridge result from a comparable SCI object to the well known limit rank of Weihrauch theory.

title: Pseudo-Labeling for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation with Kernel GLMs
comments: 62 pages, 6 figures. Python solvers and experiment scripts are available at: https://github.com/nathanweill/pseudolabel-uda-experiments
summary: We propose a principled framework for unsupervised domain adaptation under covariate shift in kernel Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), encompassing kernelized linear, logistic, and Poisson regression with ridge regularization. Our goal is to minimize prediction error in the target domain by leveraging labeled source data and unlabeled target data, despite differences in covariate distributions. We partition the labeled source data into two batches: one for training a family of candidate models, and the other for building an imputation model. This imputation model generates pseudo-labels for the target data, enabling robust model selection. We establish non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds that characterize adaptation performance through an "effective labeled sample size", explicitly accounting for the unknown covariate shift. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate consistent performance gains over source-only baselines.
comment: 62 pages, 6 figures. Python solvers and experiment scripts are available at: https://github.com/nathanweill/pseudolabel-uda-experiments

title: HRIR-Former: Grid-Free Time-Domain Reconstruction of Head-Related Impulse Responses with a Spatially Encoded Transformer
comments: Published in Interspeech 2026. Demo: https://shaohenry.github.io/HRIR-Former. Code: https://github.com/ShaoHenry/HRIR-Former
summary: Individualized head-related impulse responses (HRIRs) enable binaural rendering, but dense per-listener measurements are costly. We address HRIR spatial up-sampling from sparse per-listener measurements: given a few measured HRIRs for a listener, predict HRIRs at unmeasured target directions. Prior learning methods often work in the frequency domain, rely on minimum-phase assumptions or separate timing models, and use a fixed direction grid, which can degrade temporal fidelity and spatial continuity. We propose HRIR-Former, a time-domain, grid-free binaural Transformer for reconstructing HRIRs at arbitrary directions from sparse inputs. It uses sinusoidal spatial features, a Conv1D refinement module, and auxiliary interaural time difference (ITD) and interaural level difference (ILD) heads. On SONICOM, it improves normalized mean squared error (NMSE), cosine distance, and ITD/ILD errors over prior methods; ablations validate modules and show minimum-phase preprocessing is unnecessary.
comment: Published in Interspeech 2026. Demo: https://shaohenry.github.io/HRIR-Former. Code: https://github.com/ShaoHenry/HRIR-Former

title: Conformal Risk Control under Non-Monotone Losses: Theory and Finite-Sample Guarantees
comments: 84 pages, including references and supplementary material
summary:
Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees for controlling the expected loss at a user-specified level. Existing theory typically assumes that the loss decreases monotonically with a tuning parameter that governs the size of the prediction set. However, this assumption is often violated in practice, where losses may behave non-monotonically due to competing objectives such as coverage and efficiency.
  In this paper, we study CRC under non-monotone loss functions when the tuning parameter is selected from a finite grid, a setting commonly arising in thresholding and discretized decision rules. Revisiting a known counterexample, we show that the validity of CRC without monotonicity depends critically on the relationship between the calibration sample size and the grid resolution. In particular, reliable risk control can still be achieved when the calibration sample is sufficiently large relative to the grid size.
  We establish a finite-sample guarantee for bounded losses over a grid of size $m$, showing that the excess risk above the target level $α$ scales on the order of $\sqrt{\log(m)/n}$, where $n$ is the calibration sample size. A matching lower bound demonstrates that this rate is sharp for the CRC selection rule under the same population-safe endpoint condition. We also derive refined guarantees under additional structural conditions, including Lipschitz continuity and monotonicity, and extend the analysis to settings with distribution shift via importance weighting.
  Numerical experiments on synthetic multilabel classification and real object detection data illustrate the practical implications of non-monotonicity. Methods that explicitly account for finite-sample uncertainty achieve more stable risk control than approaches based on monotonicity transformations, while maintaining competitive prediction set sizes.
comment: 84 pages, including references and supplementary material

title: ISAC with Backscattering RFID Tags: Beamforming and Codebook Design
comments: 16 pages, 10 figures. Accepted in IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: This paper explores an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system with backscattering radio frequency identification (RFID) tags. In this setup, an access point employs communication beams to serve communication users while leveraging a sensing beam to interrogate RFID tags. Under the total transmit power constraint of the system, our objective is to design a joint sensing and communication beamforming codebook by considering the tag interrogation and communication requirements. To lay a foundation for the codebook design problem, we first study the beamforming design problem in the single-tag scenario and investigate two approaches: a two-stage zero-forcing-based design with optimized power allocation and a joint beamforming design that minimizes the total transmit power. Extending our study to the multi-tag scenario, we propose a site-specific beamforming codebook design. The proposed approach partitions the region of interest into angular sectors and jointly optimizes the sensing and communication beams for each sector. The simulation results show that the proposed beamforming designs can effectively mitigate the mutual interference between sensing and communication functionalities, thus enhancing the interrogation range of the tags while minimizing transmit power. Also, the efficacy of the proposed site-specific codebook design has been demonstrated in terms of interrogation success rate, offering a promising approach for ISAC backscattering systems.
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures. Accepted in IEEE Transactions on Communications

title: Cloning is as Hard as Learning for Stabilizer States
comments: 10 + 33 + 8 pages. Corrected small errors in classical sample amplification statements and proofs; new quantum cloning lower bound proof strategy that avoids an incorrect structured random purification claim in V1; new no-go theorems for structured random purification
summary: The impossibility of simultaneously cloning non-orthogonal states lies at the foundations of quantum theory. Even when allowing for approximation errors, cloning an arbitrary unknown pure state requires as many initial copies as needed to fully learn the state. Rather than arbitrary unknown states, modern quantum learning theory often considers structured classes of states and exploits such structure to develop learning algorithms that outperform general-state tomography. This raises the question: How do the sample complexities of learning and cloning relate for such structured classes. We answer this question for an important class of states. Namely, for $n$-qubit stabilizer states, we show that the optimal sample complexity of cloning is $Θ(n)$. Thus, also for this structured class of states, cloning is as hard as learning. To prove this result, we relate stabilizer state cloning to a variant of the sample amplification problem for probability distributions that was recently introduced in classical learning theory. This allows us to obtain our cloning lower bounds in analogy to new sample amplification lower bounds for classes of distributions with an underlying linear structure. Our results provide a more fine-grained perspective on No-Cloning theorems, opening up connections from foundations to quantum learning theory and quantum cryptography.
comment: 10 + 33 + 8 pages. Corrected small errors in classical sample amplification statements and proofs; new quantum cloning lower bound proof strategy that avoids an incorrect structured random purification claim in V1; new no-go theorems for structured random purification

title: Duality for the Adversarial Total Variation
summary: Adversarial training of binary classifiers can be reformulated as regularized risk minimization involving a nonlocal total variation. Building on this perspective, we establish a characterization of the subdifferential of this total variation using duality techniques. To achieve this, we derive a dual representation of the nonlocal total variation and a related integration-by-parts formula, involving a nonlocal gradient and divergence. We provide such duality statements both in the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity on proper metric spaces and for the space of essentially bounded functions on separable metric spaces. Furthermore, under some additional conditions we provide characterizations of the subdifferential in these settings.

title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
comments: A conference version of this paper was accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Published conference version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=kh57rITtAA. Paper website: https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/
summary: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but may be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can calibeat the original score, improving it both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while replacing the fitted isotonic score by its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship between existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin and van der Laan, 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.
comment: A conference version of this paper was accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Published conference version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=kh57rITtAA. Paper website: https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/

title: There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
summary:
In this paper, we make the case that a scientific theory of deep learning is emerging. By this we mean a theory which characterizes important properties and statistics of the training process, hidden representations, final weights, and performance of neural networks. We pull together major strands of ongoing research in deep learning theory and identify five growing bodies of work that point toward such a theory: (a) solvable idealized settings that provide intuition for learning dynamics in realistic systems; (b) tractable limits that reveal insights into fundamental learning phenomena; (c) simple mathematical laws that capture important macroscopic observables; (d) theories of hyperparameters that disentangle them from the rest of the training process, leaving simpler systems behind; and (e) universal behaviors shared across systems and settings which clarify which phenomena call for explanation.
  Taken together, these bodies of work share certain broad traits: they are concerned with the dynamics of the training process; they primarily seek to describe coarse aggregate statistics; and they emphasize falsifiable quantitative predictions. We argue that the emerging theory is best thought of as a mechanics of the learning process, and suggest the name learning mechanics. We discuss the relationship between this mechanics perspective and other approaches for building a theory of deep learning, including the statistical and information-theoretic perspectives. In particular, we anticipate a symbiotic relationship between learning mechanics and mechanistic interpretability.
  We also review and address common arguments that fundamental theory will not be possible or is not important. We conclude with a portrait of important open directions in learning mechanics and advice for beginners. We host further introductory materials, perspectives, and open questions at learningmechanics.pub.

title: Strategically Robust Linear Quadratic Dynamic Games
comments: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
summary: We study linear quadratic dynamic games where players are uncertain about each other's control policies or goals and consequently seek to be strategically robust. Building on recent work on strategically robust and risk-averse game theory, we first formalize the problem of strategically robust linear quadratic dynamic games. We show that these can be rewritten as simple transformations of linear quadratic games in which each player chooses a controller in a fictitious game in which they are faced with an adversary who is penalized for deviating from the other players' policies. This formulation naturally induces a novel notion of dynamic equilibrium, which we call a strategically robust dynamic equilibrium. We establish existence and uniqueness (in the subgame-perfect sense) of such equilibria and show that the equilibrium policies are Markovian, linear, and can be efficiently computed via coupled backward Riccati equations. Through numerical simulations, including experiments in a network game, we illustrate the benefits of strategic robustness in designing robust and resilient decentralized control schemes. Our experiments also expose a "free-lunch" phenomenon in games in which robustness does not incur a corresponding loss in performance but can yield improvements in players' utilities and social welfare.
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)

title: R Package iglm: Regression under Interference in Connected Populations
summary: We introduce R package iglm, which implements a unifying regression framework for studying relationships among binary, count-, and real-valued predictors and outcomes in connected populations with interference due to spillover, contagion, and other complex phenomena. On the computational side, the regression framework provides scalable methods that can be applied to small and large data sets, by solving a convex optimization program based on pseudo-likelihoods via accelerated Minorization-Maximization algorithms. On the statistical side, the regression framework comes with provable theoretical guarantees for statistical estimators, including consistency results and rates of convergence for maximum pseudo-likelihood estimators. To increase the versatility of iglm, users can add custom-built model terms. We showcase iglm using data on hate speech on the social media platform X and communications among students.

title: Equation-Free Digital Twins for Nonlinear Structural Dynamics
comments: Added more details of the theory as well as real experimental validation also included in the results. Now the manuscript is more defensible
summary:
Monitoring floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) under stochastic excitation and sensor failure requires computationally efficient and physically interpretable estimators. This paper introduces an equation-free, output-only digital twin framework combining Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel-DMD), sparse-sensor reconstruction, and a stochastic Kalman extension. A sufficient identifiability condition is derived for modal amplitudes recovered from delay-embedded measurements, while Tikhonov regularization addresses ill-conditioned sensor layouts. Correlation-domain identification improves damping estimates under stochastic forcing and distinguishes structural modes from rotor harmonics.
  The framework is validated using OpenFAST simulations of an NREL 5-MW spar turbine and experimental basin-test measurements from a 1:70-scale IEA 15-MW semi-submersible. In simulations, the identified tower modes agree with established operational modal analysis methods (MAC at least 0.99), while the Kalman estimator achieves R-squared values of 0.91 to 0.99 under severe sensor sparsity. Experimental results identify tower modes at 0.430 and 0.415 Hz with MAC of 1.00 against SSI-COV and reconstruct tower-base bending moments on unseen runs with R-squared values of 0.83 to 0.89 using three of four sensors. The framework provides a computationally efficient, sensor-failure-resilient structural-state estimation layer for digital twins.

title: TRACED-X enables in vivo imaging of cellular microstructure, intrinsic extracellular diffusivity, tortuosity, and membrane permeability in human glioma patients
comments: 14 pages and 8 figures (main text), plus 4 pages and 3 figures (supplementary material). Under review at Magnetic Resonance in Medicine. This version adds experiments in response to reviewer suggestions. Earlier TRACED work was presented at ISMRM 2026 (program nos. 505-03-010 and 651-02-005). A TRACED-X abstract was submitted for consideration at ISMRM 2027
summary: The lack of analytical models describing diffusion time dependence at intermediate time scales in complex tissue microstructure limits accurate quantification of extracellular diffusivity and tissue microstructure. Cell membrane water permeability modulates the signal in complex ways and is often disregarded in tumor microstructure models. We introduce TRACED-X, a Monte Carlo-based model that incorporates diffusion time dependence and membrane permeability in cell distributions to quantify pathologically-relevant properties in solid tumors. Monte Carlo simulations of water diffusion in semipermeable spheres were used to train neural network regressors for parameter estimation. A separate neural network was trained to predict the extracellular effective diffusivity, enabling the estimation of extracellular space tortuosity. Diffusion data from eight mixed-grade glioma patients were fitted with TRACED-X and analyzed in conjunction with clinical images. Simulation results demonstrate improved parameter estimation compared to comparator models. TRACED-X enabled the simultaneous in vivo quantification of intracellular volume fraction, cell size distribution, intrinsic extracellular diffusivity, tortuosity, and membrane permeability in glioma patients. Parameter maps show coherence with radiological findings and expected tumor phenotypes. TRACED-X permits the rapid estimate of unique biophysical properties in solid tumors, such as intrinsic extracellular diffusivity, tortuosity, and membrane permeability, in addition to cell microstructure. TRACED-X maps show promise in identifying heterogenous tumor subregions before and after treatment. Neural network implementations of diffusion time-dependence and tortuosity showed behavior consistent with coarse-graining and effective medium theory, respectively. Future work will explore the clinical utility of TRACED-X parameters in additional patients.
