title: ARIA: Anti-diagonal Reduced-cost Index-masked Adaptive BLMS Algorithm
summary: The block least-mean-square (BLMS) algorithm supports high-throughput adaptive filtering but incurs high computational cost as the filter length and block size increase. This letter proposes anti-diagonal reduced-cost index-masked (ARIA) adaptive BLMS, which reduces coefficient-update multiplications through anti-diagonal index masking and tap-wise step-size scaling while keeping the filtering exact. Mean-square error (MSE) analysis establishes an explicit step-size bound, and misadjustment. An extension, ARIA-MF (ARIA with masked filtering), also applies the mask during filtering; its analysis shows that the excess MSE is redistributed across block rows while its block average is approximately preserved. Simulations validate the analysis and shows very good agreement with the estimates

title: Learning-enabled Acceleration of Scenario-based Model Predictive Control
summary: Scenario-based model predictive control (SBMPC) is a variant of model predictive control (MPC) that explicitly accounts for uncertainty by optimizing control actions over multiple predicted scenarios. However, its computational complexity increases rapidly with the number of scenarios and prediction horizon, limiting its applicability to real-time planning and control. This paper presents a learning-accelerated Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for efficiently solving SBMPC problems by leveraging parallel computing and Moreau envelope learning, while maintaining high solution accuracy. We reformulate the SBMPC problems into consensus forms that can be decomposed via ADMM, separating the scenario-dependent dynamics from non-anticipativity constraints and enabling parallel updates across scenarios and time steps. Building on this decomposition, we utilize a learning-to-optimize scheme that leverages Moreau envelope learning of the cost function to accelerate the primal update in ADMM, thereby reducing computation time. The proposed framework is evaluated on a microgrid energy management problem subject to load and renewable generation uncertainties. Comparisons with IPOPT and MadNLP, two popular and modern nonlinear programming solvers, demonstrate substantial computational speedups while maintaining reliable closed-loop control performance.

title: Physics-informed Learning for Orbital Uncertainty Propagation with Error Bounds
comments: Accepted to Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics
summary: The Fokker-Planck partial differential equation (FP-PDE) governs uncertainty evolution in stochastic dynamical systems. In orbital dynamics, solving the FP-PDE is challenging because of nonlinear motion, high-dimensional states, and large space-time domains. We develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach that approximates the FP-PDE solution as a single space-time probability density, while also quantifying its worst-case approximation error. This approach is, in principle, independent of the choice of state coordinates and neural network architecture. Specifically, to enforce probability density function (PDF) properties into the neural network, we design a Physics-informed Gaussian mixture model (PINN-GMM). Then a companion error PINN learns the dynamics of the approximation error and yields time-dependent bounds that define an ambiguity set of PDFs. This ambiguity set enables rigorous computation of upper and lower bounds on event probabilities through tractable linear programs. Numerical studies on illustrative 1D examples and several 4D--6D orbital test cases demonstrate accurate uncertainty propagation, correct and informative error bounds, and improved reliability over common uncertainty-propagation baseline methods (Gaussian approximation, unscented transform, and Gaussian mixture model). Constructing the PINN-GMM requires offline training, making it costlier than the baseline approximations; once trained, however, a single forward pass returns the density at any time in sub-millisecond time $(0.16~\mathrm{ms}$ in our implementation).
comment: Accepted to Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics

title: Benign Geometry and Distributional Robustness of $\mathcal{H}_2$ Synthesis
summary: In this paper, we study standard and distributionally robust $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis problem of a stabilizing state-feedback controller for discrete-time linear time-invariant systems. Without requiring a nonsingular disturbance controllability Gramian or a positive-definite control penalty, we establish that stationarity of a stabilizing gain in standard $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis is equivalent to global optimality and derive an exact Pythagorean identity for the performance difference. We then generalize the $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis problem by considering i.i.d. disturbances with zero mean and uniformly bounded second moments, and extend the stationarity-optimality equivalence to the corresponding distributionally robust $\mathcal{H}_2$ synthesis. Moreover, we show that every standard $\mathcal{H}_2$-optimal gain is simultaneously optimal for every such distributionally robust problem. Finally, we specialize the framework to Frobenius, Kullback--Leibler, and Wasserstein-2 ambiguity sets and obtain explicit characterizations of their worst-case covariances, which, in turn, provide performance certificates for a common optimal controller.

title: Dynamic Programming for A Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
summary: We consider an infinite-horizon discounted dynamic programming (DP) problem for a countable-innovation belief-state model. The model is a surrogate for a linear-Gaussian dual control problem involving an unknown parameter vector and Gaussian observation noise. The surrogate preserves the first two moments of the Gaussian innovation and the resulting posterior second-moment structure. We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.

title: The role of distributed friction dynamics on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and simulations
summary: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.

title: Neuromorphic Camera for Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition and Tracking in Free Space Optical Communication
summary: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.

title: Filon Methods for Highly Oscillatory Controlled Quantum Systems
summary: Fast and accurate classical simulation of quantum systems is a central challenge in the design and control of quantum computers, but the highly oscillatory dynamics of these systems severely limit the efficiency of standard numerical methods. To address this, we adapt Filon quadrature for oscillatory integrals into two numerical methods, called Filon and Controlled Filon, for solving linear systems of ODEs with highly oscillatory solutions. We tailor both methods for efficient implementation in controlled quantum systems, and the Controlled Filon method additionally accounts for the oscillatory structure of the control pulses. We show by numerical experiments that these methods significantly reduce the computational cost of accurately simulating systems of superconducting transmon qubits by decreasing the number of timesteps needed to reach a given level of precision, with only a modest increase in the cost per timestep. For a realistic simulation of the dynamics of a CNOT gate, the Controlled Filon method is the most efficient method tested at every target accuracy, outperforming the best Hermite method by up to 6x and the Hermite method of the same order by up to 500x.

title: An energy-stable and accuracy-preserving finite volume scheme for wall-distance computations
summary: The distance to the nearest wall provides a length scale in models of wall-bounded turbulence. Computing this distance accurately on highly stretched meshes is challenging because small near-wall cells restrict explicit pseudo-time steps and geometric singularities can induce spurious oscillations. To address these challenges, this paper presents a semi-implicit finite-volume scheme based on a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) for solving the pseudo-time Eikonal equation on unstructured meshes. An upwind weighted least-squares reconstruction supplies the gradients used to evaluate the cell-averaged Eikonal residuals. The artificial-viscosity term is discretized using a two-point face flux whose coefficient vanishes as the regularized residuals in both adjacent cells tend to zero. The SAV update advances the semi-discrete system in pseudo-time by evaluating the residuals and viscosity coefficients explicitly and coupling the wall-distance averages and auxiliary variables implicitly. The analysis establishes unconditional energy stability under homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, permitting a grid-independent global pseudo-time step. The system's M-matrix structure guarantees nonnegative cell averages of the physical wall distance under a separate step restriction, while residual regularization and artificial viscosity preserve the formal order of spatial accuracy. Numerical tests confirm second-order spatial convergence for the quarter-cylinder case and demonstrate robust wall-distance computation on highly stretched meshes typical of Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes simulations. The SAV formulation is independent of the reconstruction scheme, providing a basis for extensions to higher-order finite-volume methods and other nonconservative scalar equations.

title: Towards Exact Multidimensional Fluxes: A Structure-Preserving Data-Informed Framework for Riemann Solvers
summary:
Finite volume and discontinuous Galerkin methods evolve the discrete solution using space-time flux integrals over mesh faces, which typically depend on solutions to local Riemann problems. In the multidimensional Riemann problem setting, this integral is difficult to evaluate exactly because of complex wave interactions. In this work, we show that the exact space-time flux integral is a polynomial in the time step and face dimensions. This motivates a learning-based approach, as only the mapping from the initial states to the polynomial coefficients needs to be learned. We propose a structure-preserving, data-informed Riemann solver framework that uses a neural network trained on high-resolution simulation data to learn this mapping. Key structural properties, including consistency and mirror symmetry, are enforced by construction. Provided that the high-resolution simulations converge to the exact flux integrals and the network accurately predicts the coefficients, this framework yields near-exact flux integrals for use in numerical simulations.
  We demonstrate the framework using classical implosion and explosion problems for the two-dimensional Euler equations. In an unsplit MUSCL-Hancock scheme, the learned Riemann solver remains stable at a CFL number of 0.9, whereas the same scheme using the exact one-dimensional Riemann solver fails. Compared with the latter scheme at CFL=0.45, the learned scheme is slightly more accurate and requires approximately 30% less computational time.

title: Linearize or Discretize First? Error Estimates under Mesh-Uniform Regularity and Exponential Stability for the KdV Equation with Boundary Dissipation
comments: 36 pages. Ancillary files: the Lean 4 development for Theorems 4.1-4.4. Companion paper: arXiv:2611.12585
summary:
We study the Korteweg-de Vries equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation, and its spatial semidiscretization by a weighted cubic Hermite Galerkin method. A small nonlinear wave can be approximated by a linear discrete simulation in two orders: linearize first and then discretize, or discretize first and then linearize. Both orders lead to the same total error. They divide this error differently between linearization and discretization. The difference of the two divisions is what we call the ordering error. We show that it is quadratic in the size of the initial datum and carries a positive power of the mesh size, for all time. It can be used to assess the effect of a coarse-mesh correction for nonlinear problems.
  For the continuous problem, the solution map is analytic, and the semigroup of the linearized equation has Crandall-Pazy regularity with the exact index 3/2. For the weighted scheme, the discrete semigroups of the linearized equation inherit exponential stability, Kato smoothing and Crandall-Pazy regularity, with bounds uniform in the mesh size. The nonlinear solution maps are analytic, also uniformly in the mesh size.
  These properties give error estimates in which the error and the datum are measured in the same norm: in the energy norm, in $H_0^1$ and in $H^2$. On every interval $[t_0,\infty)$, $t_0>0$, same-norm convergence holds uniformly on balls at algebraic rates. The ordering error is of order $h^{1/6}$ times the square of the energy norm of the datum, uniformly for all $t\ge0$.
comment: 36 pages. Ancillary files: the Lean 4 development for Theorems 4.1-4.4. Companion paper: arXiv:2611.12585

title: Ignoring Blow-Ups for Approximations
summary: It is well known that for SDEs with non-Lipschitz coefficients, the Euler scheme can fail to converge in an Lp sense. It is also widely observed that convergence fails only due to rare explosive trajectories, that distort the expectation. In this work we demonstrate that almost any method of removing these rare explosive trajectories leads to convergence in a suitable strong and weak sense. We apply this framework to coefficients that grow faster than linearly at infinity and Lennard-Jones type coefficients that explode like a reciprocal power on a compact set.

title: Hierarchical Empirical-Bayes Forecasting of Sparse Counts with Exposure: An Application to Airline Demand and Premium-Cabin Capacity Sharing
summary: Sparse count forecasting arises when events are rare, exposure varies across observational units, and short histories contain many zeros. Using thin-market airline demand as a motivating application, this paper develops a hierarchical exposure-adjusted Poisson-Gamma (HEPG) framework for probabilistic forecasting. Conditional counts follow a Poisson model with an exposure offset and pooled calendar effects, while unit specific baseline intensities receive a Gamma prior whose hyperparameters are estimated empirically across the population. The resulting posterior is Gamma and the posterior predictive distribution is negative binomial, providing closed-form partial pooling and explicit propagation of parameter uncertainty. This is especially useful for zero-history or low-exposure units, where independent maximum-likelihood estimates are unstable or collapse to zero. An adaptive extension, A-HEPG, adds a moment-matched negative-binomial variance correction when residual extra-Poisson variation remains. In synthetic experiments with 400 heterogeneous markets, HEPG improves average negative log predictive probability relative to complete pooling and independent route-level Poisson estimation. At a mean latent rate of 0.15 requests per exposure unit, the score is 0.525 for HEPG, compared with 0.585 for pooled Poisson and 0.731 for route-level Poisson maximum likelihood. Under strong overdispersion, A-HEPG reduces the score from 0.552 to 0.529. A downstream cabin-capacity example links the predictive distribution to a seat-protection rule based on predictive survival probabilities and fare ratios. The study emphasizes coherent probabilistic inference, partial pooling, and diagnostic model escalation for sparse applied count data.

title: Time-Domain and Spectral Decomposition of Dynamic Coupling with Instantaneous and Time-Lagged Causality: Methodological Evaluation and Application to Cardiovascular Variability
summary: The quantification of dynamic interactions in coupled physiological time series is a central question in biomedical signal processing. A critical issue is the presence of instantaneous dependencies, often neglected in conventional Granger causality (GC) analyses despite potentially reflecting physiologically meaningful effects. We investigate time- and frequency-domain measures of causality within the linear autoregressive (AR) framework, treating instantaneous dependencies according to three formulations: (i) the classical strictly causal AR model, providing spectral measures of time-lagged GC and instantaneous interaction; (ii) the Geweke approach, assigning instantaneous dependencies to the direction opposite to that under investigation; (iii) a single extended AR model incorporating causally-oriented instantaneous dependencies, yielding spectral GC measures accounting for both instantaneous and time-lagged causality. The three approaches are evaluated in simulated Gaussian systems, where dynamic measures can be derived analytically and compared with the expected coupling structure. The single extended AR model emerges as the most consistent formulation when instantaneous dependencies have a physiologically meaningful causal direction and is then applied to cardiovascular interactions between heart period (HP) and systolic (SAP) or diastolic arterial pressure (DAP) in healthy subjects during postural and mental stress. Accounting for instantaneous dependencies substantially affects HP-SAP and HP-DAP interactions, enabling better quantification of baroreflex and cardiac run-off mechanisms and characterization of their responses to stress and of low- and high-frequency dynamics. Overall, the framework provides consistent representation of causal interactions across time and frequency and highlights the importance of accounting for instantaneous dependencies in physiological coupling.

title: Forecasting Daily Household Electricity Demand in a Hot-Arid City: A Comparative Benchmark of Local, Global, Deep and Foundation Models on ESHED-38
summary: This study benchmarks 24 forecasting configurations on ESHED-38, daily smart-meter consumption for 38 homes in Erbil, Iraq, collected from May 2020 to June 2025 with station weather and a household survey. The configurations span five base families, plus two cross-family ensembles: naive baselines, per-house statistical models, global gradient-boosted trees, global deep networks, and zero-shot time-series foundation models. All are evaluated on the same 54,720 forecasts from 48 weekly origins over a 359-day held-out period, at lead times up to 30 days, using scaled absolute error, the continuous ranked probability score, calibration, and Friedman, Nemenyi and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests. The best configurations cut the scaled error of a seasonal-naive forecast by 20 to 25 percent, and the leading models beat it in all 38 houses. Chronos-2, used without training, is significantly the most accurate model one day ahead; at one week it is statistically tied with TimesFM-2.5, Chronos-Bolt and a pre-specified ensemble, and the two ensembles lead at 30 days. Deep networks trained from scratch do not outperform exponential smoothing on average, and the household survey adds negligible skill. Metered demand peaks in winter and falls as temperature rises. Recorded weather did not improve any model run with and without it. A quality screen helps explain why: on 68 percent of dates a temperature value recurs exactly on other dates, in three annual blocks covering almost all of the test period, suggesting that much of the weather record reuses one annual sequence. The value of weather information is therefore treated as unresolved, and the protocol is released as a baseline.

title: A Hidden Markov Analysis of Wet-Weather Tyre Crossover in Formula One
summary: Detecting a wet-weather regime and deciding when to replace slick tyres are distinct tasks. This study examines their relationship through a retrospective analysis of the 2024 British Grand Prix. A three-state hidden Markov model (HMM) represents normalized lap time and precipitation, while an entry rule requires both a high filtered Wet-state probability and sufficient pace deterioration. The analysis includes 642 car-laps and 33 complete lap-bin observations within the available precipitation record. Each completed-lap signal takes effect on the following lap. The combined rule enters on lap 27, matching the team-weighted modal reference; removing the pace or state condition advances entry to laps 25 and 20, respectively. The combined entry is retained in all 10 team-exclusion refits, but refitting a specification with larger off-diagonal transition probabilities produces entry on lap 20. These comparisons illustrate how state inference can contextualize a performance criterion while exposing dependence on model assumptions. Because estimation and rule development use the same event, the correspondence establishes neither prospective accuracy nor a race-time advantage.

title: Bayesian Evidence Fusion for Capability Tracking-A Simulation Study and Historical CI Pilot
summary: SaaS capability assessments can become stale between questionnaires, while delivery telemetry offers incomplete and correlated evidence. Continuous assessment and Bayesian delivery analysis already exist, leaving uncertainty about how biased surveys and missing observations should influence capability estimates.We implement SAAS-MATURITY-TWIN, an anchored Gaussian state model that jointly filters capability proxies and persistent survey offsets. Source covariance prevents correlated observations from being counted independently. Conditional uncertainty supports forecasting and budgeted intervention screening, with action effects estimated from randomized synthetic cohorts. Ten seeds generate forty paired worlds spanning reference observations, extensive missingness, informative missingness, and increased noise. Reference latent root mean squared error is 0.1261, compared with 0.1452 for a tuned moving average; nominal ninety percent intervals cover 90.3 percent. Improved state recovery produces only small incident forecasting differences. Adaptive conformal inference and an adapted conformal PID controller are evaluated separately for observed telemetry, where noise shifts expose calibration limitations. A licensed TravisTorrent pilot evaluates build prediction on 13 074 held out builds from 224 projects. Logistic regression achieves a Brier score of 0.1289, close to random forests. These results support reproducible methodological testing, but do not establish real organizational maturity, intervention effectiveness, or production readiness. Independent calibration and longitudinal validation remain necessary.

title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
comments: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.
comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

title: Where Does EEG Sleep-Onset Forecasting Skill Arise? A State-Conditioned Evaluation
summary: Sleep is scored afterwards in 30-second epochs as wake (W), the transitional stage N1, or N2. We study EEG forecasts, issued every 30 s from the preceding 30 s of EEG alone, of whether the first scored N2 epoch will begin within five minutes, on Sleep-EDF. A Brier score pooled over decisions made before and after the input is scored N1 does not show when the gain arose. In our own prespecified one-shot held-out comparisons, the spectral model SpecLR-18 improved on a training prevalence constant by 18.3% in the internal test, whereas its prespecified external result was inconclusive. Joining the retrospectively scored stage of each input epoch to the same frozen predictions, almost all of that internal-test Brier difference was attributed to N1-scored decisions; a diagnostic reference told only the scored stage reached 26.3% in the internal test and 29.5% in the external cohort, above the spectral forecasts in point estimate though not every difference excluded zero; and within-stage EEG advantages seen in single cohorts were not consistent across cohorts, with no consistent wake-stratum improvement. These references use labels unavailable online and cannot reveal what a model represents; they show why pooled forecasting scores need state-conditioned interpretation before being read as early anticipation.

title: Methodological Pitfalls in Predicting Ship Turnaround Time at Brazilian Ports: An Empirical Audit and a Reproducible Pipeline
summary: Two recent studies on ship turnaround time at Brazilian ports report models with R-squared scores above 0.80 on data from the national waterway transportation agency. We audit their published datasets and reveal these results are inflated by structural data leakage. Specifically, 97 percent of berthing events in their random row-level split appear in both training and testing partitions. We demonstrate that a model's R-squared drops from 0.82 to 0.20 when the data is properly split at the berthing level. We further document additional methodological flaws, including survivorship bias, undocumented target truncation, and the retention of variables that algebraically reconstruct the target. To address these issues, we propose a reproducible pipeline that aggregates cargo to the berthing level, utilizes conditional imputation, and represents high-cardinality cargo variables through weighted averages of multilingual sentence embeddings. Evaluating six time targets and thirty seeds, our pipeline reveals that cargo embeddings yield statistically significant improvements on four operational targets, while administrative waiting times remain unaffected. Prior works missed this per-target heterogeneity by conflating genuine signal with leaked identity.

title: Empirical Bayes mirror testing for persistent widening of achievement gaps in U.S. school districts
summary: Unequal recovery from pandemic learning losses raises concerns about widening achievement gaps between economically disadvantaged students and their peers. This study seeks to identify districts whose mathematics gaps widened in every annual interval from 2022 to 2025. The analysis uses estimates from the Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA) for 5,600 U.S. school districts. Identifying such districts requires accounting for correlated errors and differing precision in the estimated annual changes, as well as multiplicity. The true annual gap changes in each district form an effect vector, and persistent widening means that every component is positive. To address this class of multiple testing problems, we propose an empirical Bayes mirror procedure. It uses an estimated distribution of effect vectors to guide ranking and covariance-adjusted mirror observations to calibrate selection. The procedure achieves finite-sample false discovery rate (FDR) control under a Gaussian observation model, without requiring accurate estimation of the posterior null probabilities used for ranking. Simulations demonstrate power gains from incorporating information about the distribution of effect vectors. At a target FDR of 25%, the SEDA analysis identifies eight districts in five states with evidence of widening gaps in every annual interval.

title: GrAFT-PDX: Growth and Failure-Time Modeling of Patient-Derived Xenograft Experiments
summary: Cancer drugs are often evaluated for efficacy in mice before proceeding to human clinical trials. To do this, human tumors are engrafted onto immune-incompetent mice to create a patient-derived xenograft (PDX). Engrafted tumors can be propagated to evaluate multiple drugs, but the time and costs involved in PDX studies limit high throughput drug screens in mice. Here we present GrAFT-PDX, a Bayesian model of PDX drug screens that aims to reduce the PDX screening burden by enabling imputation of missing experiments and early stopping of likely unsuccessful drugs. Unlike conventional survival or growth models, GrAFT-PDX jointly predicts tumor growth and survival outcomes using a learned latent function decomposition. In experiments on a large-scale PDX dataset, GrAFT-PDX outperforms Cox proportional hazards models at predicting time of death, outperforms machine learning baselines at predicting tumor growth, and recovers known gene-treatment relationships without genomic input.

title: Is generative AI really changing public sector work? Evidence from a multi-country survey
summary: Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform how public services are delivered, with important implications for public service productivity. But how widely is the technology actually being used - and is it making any difference? Our survey of 3,362 public sector workers across the UK, the USA, South Africa and the EU finds widespread use of AI in every region. Our findings suggest that this spread is being driven by bottom-up individual adoption rather than top-down institutional adoption. In the EU, for example, 65\% of respondents use AI, while only 19\% say their organisation has formally adopted it. Most users are positive about its effects, with 79\% saying AI has improved their productivity. However, only 29\% say it has increased what is expected of them at work, raising questions about how truly transformative the technology is so far. Across regions, South Africa is a clear outlier, with the highest levels of use, organisational adoption, optimism and awareness of guidelines.

title: Clustering professional football players using Gaussian mixture models: A case study of the English Premier League 2024/25
summary: The increasing availability of detailed football performance data has created new opportunities for identifying player archetypes and informing recruitment and tactical decision-making. Most existing clustering approaches assign each player to a single group, despite the reality that many modern footballers perform hybrid roles spanning multiple stylistic categories. Performance data for 314 outfield players from the 2024/25 English Premier League season are analysed using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) applied to principal component representations of player statistics. Unlike hard-assignment methods such as k-means, the GMM provides probabilistic cluster memberships, allowing uncertainty and role hybridity to be quantified. Seven player archetypes are identified in the full dataset. Posterior membership probabilities reveal a subset of players whose profiles span multiple clusters, providing an objective measure of tactical flexibility and stylistic ambiguity. Further analyses within defender, midfielder, and forward groups recover position-specific sub-archetypes and highlight exceptional outliers. The results demonstrate that model-based clustering provides a flexible and interpretable framework for identifying latent structure in high-dimensional performance data while explicitly quantifying uncertainty in cluster membership. More broadly, the approach is readily transferable to other sports and domains in which individuals exhibit overlapping characteristics and cannot be adequately represented by hard cluster assignments alone.

title: Bayesian modeling of predictive stability under generalized Arrhenius non-linear kinetics
comments: 28 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Predictive stability modeling is widely used in pharmaceutical development to establish product shelf-life by identifying the kinetic parameters that govern degradation behavior and using these parameters to extrapolate out in time. Recent approaches typically assume linear degradation dynamics and rely on the Arrhenius equation to model temperature-specific reaction rates. However, observed degradation profiles may reflect nonlinear reaction dynamics and more complex temperature-specific reaction rates, potentially leading to reduced accuracy in long-term predictions and motivating a more flexible approach. We propose a novel Bayesian framework which extends predictive stability modeling beyond simple Arrhenius low-order kinetic dynamics and accommodates complex degradation mechanisms. The degradation process is modeled through the Sestak-Berggren kinetic formulation, a flexible ordinary differential equation encompassing many classical degradation models as special cases. To facilitate model interpretability and model exploration, probabilistic model selection on kinetic parameters automatically determines whether nonlinear reaction components are supported by the data, allowing the model to adaptively collapse to simpler dynamics when appropriate. To address departure from classical Arrhenius kinetics, we develop a generalized temperature reaction rate formulation in which temperature-specific reaction rates are shrunk toward Arrhenius predictions through a hierarchical shrinkage prior while allowing departures when supported by the data. This approach yields robustness to misspecification and reduces sensitivity to potentially influential high-temperature observations commonly encountered in accelerated stability experiments. The resulting framework provides a principled and flexible statistical tool for model-informed shelf-life determination.
comment: 28 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables; includes supplementary material

title: Regularized trimmed Factorial and Reduced K-means for contaminated high-dimensional data: separating geometry, search and selection
summary: Factorial and Reduced K-means estimate a partition and a low-dimensional clustering subspace jointly, which makes them attractive when the variables that separate groups are not those that dominate total variance. On contaminated high-dimensional data they face three linked problems: trimming can make the scatter matrices singular, the criterion has many local optima, and the rank, number of groups and trimming proportion are unknown and interact. We propose REG-HD-TFKM and REG-HD-TRKM, regularized trimmed versions of the two methods, together with a selection procedure that handles these problems as separate decisions. A ridge-stabilized spectral step keeps every fit well defined; heterogeneous multistart search explores alternative solutions; method-specific agreement and reproducibility scores choose among them; and trimming is applied only when a radial diagnostic or the path over trimming levels supports it. A simulation study with 41 design cells shows why the separation matters. Two representations of euro-area bank balance sheets show that similar partitions can rest on nearly orthogonal subspaces, and that the same selected structure can describe different retained samples.

title: Introducing and Repealing an EV Subsidy: Evidence from New Zealand's Clean Car Discount
summary: New Zealand's Clean Car Discount (CCD) was a feebate scheme that offered rebates for low-emission vehicles from July 2021, added fees for high-emission vehicles from April 2022, and was abolished at the end of December 2023. Shortly afterwards, road user charges were introduced for electric vehicles (EVs). We study how EV adoption responded to the introduction and the abrupt repeal of the scheme, using monthly vehicle registration data from 2014 to 2024. A structural break analysis following Bai and Perron, combined with a regression discontinuity in time, shows that breaks in the registrations of battery electric, plug-in hybrid and conventional vehicles coincide with the policy dates. To estimate causal effects, we apply a difference-in-differences approach with Queensland, Australia, as a comparison region and Newey-West standard errors. Because the New Zealand market was about four times larger, the analysis uses log-transformed registrations, so that parallel trends refer to equal growth rates. The results are asymmetric. After the introduction of the rebates, EV registrations in New Zealand rose strongly, but by a similar proportion as in Queensland, and the average effect relative to Queensland is not statistically significant. A specification allowing for a change in slope suggests a gradual acceleration of EV uptake. After the repeal, EV registrations fell by about 72% relative to Queensland, and the decline persisted in 2025. Both policy dates were preceded by a rush of purchases. The average CO2 emissions of newly registered vehicles fell markedly during the scheme and rebounded after its end. The results suggest that an abrupt end of EV purchase incentives can cause a large and lasting drop in EV uptake, and that a gradual, pre-announced phase-out may be preferable.

title: Functional Regression with Interacting Latent Mean and Variance Processes
summary: In many applications, variability itself carries important predictive information beyond the mean, and its association with an outcome may further depend on the underlying mean trajectory. However, existing functional regression approaches primarily rely on mean-based representations of functional predictors, while variability is often ignored or reduced to scalar summaries. We propose a functional regression framework that incorporates latent mean and variance processes as predictors, together with their mean-variance interaction, allowing the predictive contribution of variability to depend on the underlying mean trajectory. We establish consistency and convergence rates for the estimated coefficient functions and interaction surface, accounting for reconstruction errors, increasing observation frequency, and diverging truncation dimensions without requiring independence between the latent processes. Applications to real data demonstrate substantial gains in predictive accuracy from incorporating the variance process, with the proposed approach outperforming competing functional regression methods in the Tecator application and revealing localized mean-variance interaction patterns.

title: Improving Algorithmic Trading for BESS on Intraday Electricity Markets through Distributional Price Forecasts
summary: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are becoming increasingly important in short-term energy markets, where they help balance fluctuations in variable renewable generation. In many countries, the continuous intraday market is the most important wholesale market for BESS to monetize their flexibility. In this paper, we propose an extension to the myopic rolling intrinsic policy that incorporates intraday price forecasts tailored specifically to the BESS trading problem. While a large literature addresses intraday price forecasting, most existing work focuses on volume-weighted prices during the last hours of trading and consequently fails to capture the features most relevant to BESS trading. Our approach addresses this gap by introducing a novel target variable derived from the limit order book and its dynamics. The resulting forecasts are designed to inform the optimization about future profit opportunities while preserving computational efficiency and avoiding the burden of full stochastic optimization. In a realistic high-frequency simulation setting covering 2023 and 2024, our method improves profits by up to 42% over the naive rolling intrinsic formulation. We further analyze the relationship between forecast accuracy, stability, and financial performance, establishing a clear inverse relationship between accuracy and stability. Finally, we find evidence that BESS size and duration jointly influence both overall profitability and the marginal benefit of incorporating forecasts.

title: A market-initialised accelerated failure time model for in-play football forecasting
comments: 25 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Substantially revised: doubled evaluation sample, revised model specification, additional benchmarks, and updated results and conclusions
summary: In-play football forecasting models are rarely compared with betting exchange prices, which aggregate information from many market participants. We make this comparison for several goal-arrival models, focusing on a Weibull accelerated failure time model with two extensions: initialising team strength parameters from Betfair Exchange prices at kick-off to capture pre-match market information, and including cumulative shots as a time-varying covariate to capture in-play information. The initialisation, which fits team-strength parameters to 1X2 and over/under prices by squared-error minimisation, applies to any intensity-based goal arrival model. Evaluated across 280 English Premier League matches at minute intervals, the market-initialised model remains measurably weaker than Betfair in-play prices (classification accuracy 68.5% versus 69.5%, ranked probability score 0.1325 versus 0.1281), but retains interpretable team-level parameters and covariate effects. A comparison with a market-implied Poisson model, a Cox process and a Bayesian birth process, all initialised from the same pre-match odds, confirms that market initialisation is the dominant driver of predictive accuracy. A betting simulation against Betfair in-play odds yields a 1.0% return on investment over 37,467 bets (95% interval -3.8% to 5.9%), which we regard as preliminary given the limited sample of matches and prices that may not have been executable.
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Substantially revised: doubled evaluation sample, revised model specification, additional benchmarks, and updated results and conclusions

title: A Family-Level Graphical Gatekeeping Procedure with Iterative Retesting
comments: 42 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Includes proofs in the appendix
summary: Confirmatory clinical trials often involve multiple objectives grouped into families according to scientific priorities. At the intersection of graphical multiple testing and gatekeeping methods, we develop a Bonferroni-based family-level graphical procedure with partial-rejection-based transfers and iterative re-testing. Families are tested sequentially within each stage, using fixed component tests and a prespecified transition matrix. The updating rule combines current-stage forward contributions based on current family levels with previous-stage backward contributions based on initial allocations. We establish strong global familywise error rate control at a prespecified level under arbitrary dependence. The construction permits backward feedback while retaining fixed component tests and transition coefficients, distinguishing its implementation from forward-only family-level procedures and the specified superchain algorithm. Simulations demonstrate gains over the corresponding No-retest procedure, while identifying an efficiency cost relative to a hypothesis-level graphical comparator with matched initial allocations and edge weights. Clinical illustrations show how the procedure implements family-level priorities and feedback, and an extension accommodates a two-layer structure with multiple families per layer.
comment: 42 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Includes proofs in the appendix

title: Aproximación práctica a los métodos de selección de portafolios de inversión
summary:
This paper explores the practical approach to portfolio selection methods for investments. The study delves into portfolio theory, discussing concepts such as expected return, variance, asset correlation, and opportunity sets. It also presents the efficient frontier and its application in the Markowitz model, which employs mean-variance optimization techniques. An alternative approach based on the mean-semivariance model is introduced. This model accounts for the skewness and kurtosis of the asset return distribution, providing a more comprehensive view of risk and return. The study also addresses the practical implementation of these models, including the use of genetic algorithms to optimize portfolio selection. Additionally, transaction costs and integer constraints in portfolio optimization are considered, demonstrating the applicability of the Markowitz model.
  --
  Este documento explorar la aproximación práctica a los métodos de selección de portafolios para inversiones. El estudio profundiza en la teoría de los portafolios, discutiendo conceptos como el rendimiento esperado, la varianza, la correlación entre activos y los conjuntos de oportunidades. También presenta la frontera eficiente y su aplicación en el modelo de Markowitz, que utiliza técnicas de optimización media-varianza. Se introduce un enfoque alternativo basado en el modelo media-semivarianza. Este modelo tiene en cuenta la asimetría y la curtosis de la distribución de retornos de los activos, proporcionando una visión más completa de riesgo y rendimiento. El estudio también aborda la implementación práctica de estos modelos, incluyendo el uso de algoritmos genéticos para optimizar la selección de portafolios. Además, se consideran los costos de transacción y las restricciones enteras en la optimización del portafolio.

title: Conflict Forecasting via Conformal Prediction for Markov Processes
summary: Whether or not a country is at war, or experiencing escalating or deescalating levels of conflict, has massive ramifications on a country's national and foreign policy. Given a country's history of conflict, or lack thereof, future predictions about the war-status of a country are valuable information. In this paper, we present the use of conformal prediction on temporally-dependent data to obtain prediction sets of possible future conflict state-sequences. More specifically, we compare the results of conformal prediction to a likelihood-based prediction strategy when the data are assumed to come from a discrete-state Markov process. A point-prediction may not supply sufficient information because the penalty for a wrong prediction is extreme, and so we consider a machine learning alternative that gives valid uncertainty quantification and is robust to model misspecification. In the data analysis, we present real forecasts of conflict dynamics across multiple countries. Lastly, we assess the differences between the conformal and likelihood-based prediction sets applied to training data which fall under a pervasive edge-case, not discussed in existing literature.

title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
summary: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: at least 50% of the observational causal studies we review in leading journals state or imply it, while 7% describe an imputation model. We develop a framework for when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect (ATE). With a constant unit-level treatment effect, two checks suffice: whether covariates and the missingness indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools within-covariate comparisons appropriately, possibly using inverse propensity weighting. A collider--mediator illustration highlights the first check: the same missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism can require different adjustment choices. With heterogeneous effects, conditional effects must be transportable to the population and be reweighted to its population distribution. These formal results provide practical checks for applied researchers to run complete case regressions, recover existing guidance as special cases, and are illustrated with applications across fields.

title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
summary:
Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised.
  We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation.
  Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks.
  The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

title: Gatheral's Conjecture: General sufficient conditions for refutation
summary: In this paper we give general sufficient conditions for a stochastic volatility model to be a counterexample for Gatheral's conjecture. The conditions, achieved by asymptotic properties of integrated variance derivatives and Wiener chaos expansions, show that a general class of rough volatility models are generally counterexamples to Gatheral's conjecture. For stochastic volatility models with Markovian variance, the conjecture fails under a relationship on the coefficients of the SDE defining the variance process. Particular examples are provided.

title: Idiosyncratic Market Effects in Global Time Series Momentum
summary: Time series momentum is a pervasive explanatory factor in financial markets whereby a market's recent historical average return positively predicts future returns. Recent applications of statistical learning augment the traditional linear model definition with a more descriptive global nonlinear factor model. We extend the work of \citet{MoskowitzNonlinear} and demonstrate that models fit at the individual market level exhibit response curves that are distinct from the global factor model. We highlight the heterogeneity of forward market returns as a function of time series momentum and provide a framework that enables each feature-market pair to express its unique prediction behaviour. Empirical results demonstrate that, despite substantially smaller sample sizes, fitting nonlinear models to individual markets is a robust and often overlooked modelling approach that can result in a marginal improvement in out-of-sample performance.

title: Global Seasonality Factor Investing
summary: We study seasonality as a factor for predicting risk-adjusted returns across global futures markets. We document five seasonality anomalies that, in aggregate, are pervasive across bond, commodity and equity markets. We demonstrate that each seasonality factor produces excess returns that are not reasonably explained by established global time series carry, momentum and skewness factors. We apply recent innovations in statistical learning and fit nonlinear seasonality models at the individual market level, thereby allowing each feature-market pair to express its unique seasonal prediction pattern. We discuss candidate economic rationales for the existence and persistence of each seasonality anomaly. Walk-forward out-of-sample testing demonstrates that fast-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-week and day-of-month, produce strong gross performance but with extremely high turnover, resulting in negative performance net of transaction costs. In contrast, slower-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-quarter, day-of-half-year and day-of-year, produce positive gross performance and, with the exception of day-of-quarter, positive net performance. An equal-weight ensemble of seasonality models produces an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio that is competitive with, and uncorrelated to, established global time series factor portfolios. Empirical results demonstrate that adding seasonality to a global factor portfolio increases the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio by approximately $30\%$ over the full evaluation period.

title: Novel Esscher concepts for informational risks and valuation in market models under random horizon
summary: This paper considers the setting constituted by the triplet $(S,\mathbb{F},τ)$. The pair $(S,\mathbb{F})$ is the initial model where $S$ is the discounted price process of risky assets (Stocks) and $\mathbb{F}$ is the ``public" flow of information that is available to all agents over time. $τ$ is an arbitrary random time, which might not be seen through the flow $\mathbb{F}$, and it represents a default time in credit risk and a death time of an insured in life insurance where mortality and/or longevity risks present serious challenges. For simplicity, we suppose $S$ follows a geometric jump-diffusion model with stochastic volatiles and $\mathbb{F}$ is generated by a Brownian motion and Poisson process. In this setting, we address how the Esscher densities and/or measures notions can evolves with the informational risk induced by $τ$. In fact, we introduce the notion of Esscher with degrees-of-freedom associated to the informational risks generated by $τ$. On the one hand, we give various and complete characterizations of these Esscher notions in our informational setting. On the other hand, we fully characterize the Escher-prices bounds, for vulnerable claims (claims built on the occurrence of $τ$), using constrained backward stochastic differential equations (CBSDEs for short hereafter) that appear to be novel as well.

title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: In real-time bidding, marketing agencies must balance campaign performance, transaction margins and the use of a finite advertising budget. A key difficulty is that market-clearing prices are typically observed only when bids are successful, so the information available for subsequent decisions depends on the bidding policy. We formulate this problem using a continuous-time stochastic control model with a latent price process. To construct a price signal, we consider parallel exploratory subcampaigns in which bids are randomized subject to an upper bound. Under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the resulting price estimator is consistent and satisfies a mean-square error bound of order $N^{-1}$, where $N$ is the number of exploratory observations. We then describe a model-based approach combining forward-equation calibration with Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, alongside an entropy-regularized actor-critic approach based on observable information in a model-free setting. Synthetic experiments illustrate the estimator and the computational procedures. The framework clarifies the decision and information trade-offs faced by the agency, while distinguishing full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies from the genuinely partially observed control problem.

title: Price-impact Martingale optimal transport
summary: Martingale optimal transport (MOT) provides model-independent bounds for option prices calibrated to vanilla options, assuming frictionless trading in the underlying. In this work, we consider the case where dynamic trading incurs quadratic temporary price impact. First, we prove a duality result for the superhedging price. In particular, the primal of the duality relaxes the strict martingale constraint by penalizing the deviation from a specific martingale. Second, for one asset and one trading period, we interpret this price-impact martingale optimal transport (PIMOT) as a weak optimal transport (WOT) problem, and provide a characterization in the spirit of Wasserstein projection. Finally, we justify that PIMOT is an interpolation between MOT and classical optimal transport (OT), and derive the convergence rate to both sides. Numerical examples with SPX option data show how the price bounds per claim depend on the order size.

title: Convergence rates for truncated and discretised signature expansions
summary: Linear expansions in Brownian Stratonovich signatures, which originate in stochastic Taylor expansions, are increasingly used to represent and model processes with memory. Their numerical use requires truncating the signature at a level $M$ and discretising the driving path along $N$ steps. Under a simple growth condition on the coefficients of the linear expansion, we establish strong and weak convergence rates for both approximations, uniformly in time. The strong truncation error decays like $(B^M/(M!)^\varepsilon)^a$ for some constant $B$, uniformly in $N$, where $\varepsilon$ measures the growth of the coefficients and $a$ the regularity of the test function; the weak error does not improve on it. The discretisation error is of order $N^{-a/2}$ in $L^p$, and $N^{-1}$ weakly for polynomial test functions, uniformly in $M$. All these rates are sharp for polynomial test functions, and $M$, $N$ can be chosen independently. We extend the estimates to errors in probability, on distribution functions and on risk measures, and illustrate them on stochastic delay equations, Volterra processes and option pricing in signature volatility models.

title: On the continuity of martingale optimal transport in higher dimensions
summary: We investigate qualitative and quantitative continuity of martingale optimal transport under perturbations of both marginals in dimensions $d\geq2$. We assume that each pair of marginals admits a reference martingale coupling whose density relative to the product of its marginals is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly along the sequence. If the limiting target measure is not carried by a hyperplane, we prove continuity under $W_1$-convergence for continuous costs of at most linear growth, assuming only finite first moments. For Lipschitz costs, a uniform $p$-moment bound on the targets, $p>1$, yields an explicit stability estimate with exponent $(1-1/p)/2$; uniformly bounded target supports give exponent $1/2$. The proof constructs a correction of couplings with small martingale bias while preserving both marginals. Truncated moment corrections allow the target measure to have unbounded support. The construction also shows that every martingale coupling of the limiting marginals can be approximated in $W_1$ by martingale couplings of the approximating marginals. We also discuss counterexamples showing that neither the uniform density condition nor non-degeneracy of the limiting target measure can be omitted in general.

title: Incomplete-market CAPM equilibria in continuous time
summary: We study continuous-time CAPM equilibria with general mean-variance preferences of the form $U(μ,σ)$, where $U$ is strictly quasiconcave, increasing in the mean $μ$ and decreasing in the volatility $σ$ of terminal wealth. Our framework accommodates both financial and productive assets with nontradeable endowments. We allow for equilibria driven by general semimartingales in the case of linear mean-variance preferences and by continuous semimartingales in the case of general mean-variance preferences. The key insight is a connection between mean-variance efficiency and quadratic utility maximisation. We first characterise quadratic equilibria through an explicit family of equilibrium price processes indexed by the aggregate risk tolerance. We then show that each agent's optimal mean-variance strategy corresponds to a quadratic optimum with an endogenously determined risk tolerance. This correspondence reduces the mean-variance equilibrium problem to a one-dimensional fixed-point problem, whose solvability we establish using fine properties of (dynamic) mean-variance hedging and a novel stability result for quadratic BSDEs with BMO growth at the origin. Finally, examples illustrate how unspanned stochastic-volatility risk interacts with aggregate endowments to affect equilibrium asset prices, and how nonlinear mean-variance preferences influence equilibrium risk tolerance and asset-price comparative statics.
